She saw the white canopy lean, recover, and lean again. Figures in ceremonial coats moved toward the stairs. Governor Dault was among them. Arce stood near the rail, staring down as though the machinery had betrayed him personally.

For one instant, Ilyra felt the old satisfaction return.

There. Look.

Look at what the water remembers.

The thought was bright and poisonous. It carried her through the years of being sent back to the archive, of hearing her calculations called dockside resentment, of watching ration lines shorten while Crown fountains ran through the night. It carried Tomas’s ledger, Sella’s cough, her father’s missing safety harness. It carried every meeting where officials had asked for projections and then chosen the answer they wanted.

She had wanted them afraid.

She had wanted them to stand where the Low Quarter stood: beneath a force whose direction had been chosen elsewhere.

The western camp lights trembled below.

A second chain snapped.

The western gate opened another span.

Water struck the storage fields with a sound like a wall breaking.

Ilyra recoiled from the observation slit.

The clean memory ended there.

The next part came in pieces.

A child’s red scarf caught on a fence.

A woman carrying two cooking pots above her head.

A man climbing a roof while the roof came apart under him.

The lanterns, so many lanterns, lifting and vanishing in the dark.

She had believed there would be time to correct the error. That was the lie she told herself afterward. She had believed the first surge would fill the abandoned basins, lose force through the industrial terraces, and leave the camps enough height to escape. She had believed she could stabilize the western gate, then reduce the central opening, then send a warning through the civic lenses.

In the present, she understood that each belief had depended on the next.

A tower groaned. The warning bell stopped.

Ilyra seized the central wheel and tried to turn it down.

The mechanism fought her. Pressure had shifted too quickly. The wheel kicked in her hands, wrenching her wrists. She braced one boot against the housing and pulled.

The sluice began to descend.

At once, the eastern gauge leapt.

The needle crossed the red line.

The lower channels were taking the force.

In the darkness beyond the chamber, something gave way with a distant, muffled collapse.

She stopped turning.

The wheel shuddered beneath her hands.

Open, and the western camps drown.

Close, and the Low Quarter drowns.

There was no third position in the machinery.

Perhaps there had been one before the valves were removed. Perhaps the old map had contained another sequence, a slower distribution, a method requiring six operators and time enough for people to be warned. She had chosen to enter alone because she did not trust the Council, because she did not trust Arce, because she did not trust anyone to keep her purpose from being altered.

She had made herself the missing sixth operator.

Now the entire city rested against her hands.

A voice came through the maintenance tube.

At first she thought it was another mechanical vibration. Then the words separated from the noise.

“Engineer!”

The tube ran from the lower access corridor to the control chamber. A worker was shouting into it.

“Engineer Voss! The west door is jammed! Do you hear me?”

Ilyra leaned toward the tube.

“How many?”

The reply broke into static and water.

“—workers—some families—door—”

“How many?”

A fist struck the far end. Once. Twice.

Then a voice she recognized.

“Nera?”

The tube filled with breath.

“Ilyra?”

Nera’s voice was smaller than it had been in the Annex, where she had spoken quickly and confidently over blueprints. Here it trembled with the effort of being heard.

“Where are you?”

“Below the west gallery. The lower corridor is filling. We can’t reach the release stairs.”

“Is the emergency door intact?”

“It’s sealed.”

“I know.”

“Can you open it?”

Ilyra looked at the central wheel.

If she opened the emergency door, the lower corridor would flood the machinery chamber. It might destroy the western controls, perhaps the central mechanism as well. The pressure would disperse through the open chamber, but without controlled gates it would seek the lowest routes. She could save the people in the corridor and lose the barrage.

Or she could keep the system closed, preserve the calculations, and let the water decide which bodies were acceptable.

“Nera,” she said.

The tube crackled.

“Don’t open the door,” Ilyra told her.

Silence.

The chamber seemed to draw breath around them.

“What?”

“Stay where you are. Keep the others above the threshold. I’m coming to the west control.”

“You can open it from there?”

“I can stabilize the gate.”

“You said the fields were empty.”

The words entered her with more force than the broken chain.

Ilyra closed her eyes.

“I was wrong.”

Another fist struck the tube.

Someone behind Nera was crying. Someone else shouted that the water had reached the steps.

“You told us—” Nera began.

“I know.”

“No, you told us there was capacity.”

“I know.”

“You said the old survey was current.”

“I said it was more reliable than the Council’s.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“No.”

The admission seemed to travel down the tube and settle between them.

Ilyra opened her eyes.

Through the slit, the western lanterns were fewer now. The raised road had disappeared beneath the water. On the ceremonial platform, officials crowded the eastern stairs. The white canopy tore loose and flew into the river, its fabric spreading like a pale hand.

Somewhere beyond the chamber, a public lens clicked and rotated. The Council’s surveillance network had found her.

She could imagine Pell narrating the scene already. The unauthorized engineer. The stolen seal. The deliberate opening. The moment when she refused to close the gate. Every decision would become a clean line drawn backward from the dead.

She had spent years believing that if she controlled the sequence, she could control the judgment.

But the water did not care where a story began.

Ilyra forced herself away from the central wheel.

The western control platform bucked beneath her. She took three steps and fell against the railing. Below, the severed chain writhed in the dark, its broken end striking the drum each time the gate shifted. She could reach the manual brake. She could perhaps lower the gate by inches, if the housing held. She could not make the missing valves return. She could not make the storage fields empty. She could not restore the warning she had failed to send.

At the edge of the platform, she looked once more toward the camps.

A lantern had stopped moving.

Another was climbing.

The person carrying it had reached high ground, or was being lifted by someone else. Around that single light, other figures gathered. The lantern swung toward the tower.

Not a signal.

A question.

Ilyra placed her hand on the brake lever.

Behind her, the central sluice roared.

Ahead, the western gate groaned open.

Below, the city waited in both directions.

“Nera,” she said into the tube.

“I’m here.”

“I am going to try to bring the western gate down.”

“And the central?”

Ilyra looked at the wheel.

“I don’t know yet.”

It was the first answer she had given Nera that contained no instruction.

The machinery surged.

The brake lever tore against her hand, and the chamber filled with the sound of iron beginning to fail.

chapters.name: The Door Below
chapters.content:
## The Door Below

The western gate had no intention of obeying her.

Ilyra leaned into the brake wheel and felt it turn a fraction beneath her hands. Somewhere inside the wall, a tooth caught and slipped. The gate answered with a deeper movement, like a mountain settling in its sleep.

“Again,” she told herself.

The platform shook. Water sprayed through the seams in the stone and struck her face. Below, beyond the grated walkway, the western channel had become a white trench. The gate’s raised slab shuddered while the flood poured toward the storage fields.

Lanterns moved in the distance.

Not moved. Fled.

Canvas roofs spun through the water. People clung to poles, crates, sections of fencing. Their voices rose and vanished beneath the barrage’s thunder.

Ilyra pulled again.

The brake wheel turned half a tooth, then lurched back. The chain snapped tight around her wrist and burned through her glove. For an instant she saw herself reflected in the black water below, a white-coated figure bent over the machinery as if pleading with it.

The maintenance tube clanged.

Three sharp strikes. A pause. Two more.

Ilyra crossed the platform and dropped beside the brass tube set into the wall. Its red paint had long ago flaked away around the rim.

She pressed her mouth to it. “Who is there?”

At first there was only coughing.

Then Nera said, “You know who.”

Her voice was thin and distorted by the tube, but unmistakable.

“How many?”

“Workers from the lower inspection crew. Families from the fields. I don’t know. Thirty, perhaps more.”

“Are you injured?”

“Not yet.”

The words passed through Ilyra with greater force than the water striking the barrage.

“Where are you?”

“Below the western access. The corridor split when the first surge came through. We reached the emergency door, but it’s sealed.”

“Can you open it from your side?”

“No. The wheel is jammed.”

Ilyra looked toward the western control assembly. The emergency door lay directly beneath the platform, at the bottom of a shaft connecting the lower corridor to the control chamber. The original plans showed a drainage passage beyond it, beneath the western gate and out toward the old stone basins.

The current plans called the shaft obsolete.

The current plans also called the storage fields empty.

“Listen to me,” Ilyra said. “How high is the water?”

“Above the first landing. Rising.”

“How long until it reaches the door?”

“It’s already at the door.”

Ilyra turned toward the brake wheel.

The western gate was still rising.

She had perhaps three minutes before the water reached the control chamber floor. Less, if the lower corridor had collapsed farther than Nera knew. If she opened the emergency door, the flood would pour into the shaft, fill the chamber, and destroy the controls. The western gate might drop when the mechanism flooded. Or it might remain open. The central sluice would continue carrying force toward the eastern wall, and every valve in the chamber would become inaccessible.

But the people behind the door would have a path out.

She put her hand on the release lever.

“Nera,” she said. “There is a release on my side.”

“Then use it.”

“If I open the door, the chamber will flood.”

“Close the gate first.”

“I can’t.”

Silence.

“You said the western gate would bleed pressure,” Nera said.

“It should have.”

“You said the fields were clear.”

“They were marked clear.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Ilyra’s hand tightened on the lever.

The barrage roared around them, force without language, a body pressing against every wall and joint.

“I was wrong,” Ilyra said.

It was the first time she had answered Nera without qualification.

The water rose another mark on the gauge.

Nera breathed into the tube. “Open the door.”

Ilyra looked at the gauges. The eastern needle trembled just below red.

If she flooded the chamber, the central sluice would lose its regulating drive. The flow would surge toward the eastern embankment: the Low Quarter, the old tenements, the dyehouses and mills, the streets where Tomas had carried ration ledgers and Sella had waited for water.

If she kept the chamber dry, the people below would drown.

The arithmetic arranged itself in clean columns.

Western camps: thirty, perhaps more.

Eastern districts: thousands.

Machinery: necessary to preserve the greater number.

The figures did not become less terrible because they were large.

“Keep everyone above the landing,” she said.

“We can’t hold the water back.”

“Use the inspection braces. There should be two in the wall.”

“There are no braces.”

“Stack anything you have against the door. Timber. Carts. Bodies if you must.”

“You want us to build a wall?”

“I want you to buy time.”

“For what?”

Ilyra watched the lanterns vanish among the fields. “For me to lower this.”

The voices around Nera rose. Panic came through the tube in fragments: prayers, curses, names, someone shouting that his leg was caught. Nera spoke over them, trying to restore order.

Ilyra replaced the cap and returned to the wheel.

The chain had cut through her glove and opened her palm. She removed the glove with her teeth, tied it around the chain, and took hold with both hands.

“Lower,” she said.

She pulled.

Nothing.

She braced one foot against the base and pulled again. The wheel resisted, then gave with a sudden turn. The chain screamed through its guides. Somewhere below, the western gate descended a handspan.

Another handspan.

The gauge fell.

The eastern gauge rose.

She stopped.

The gate hung between positions, its weight suspended by the damaged chain. The western pressure could be reduced without fully redirecting it east. The camps might have minutes. The people below might have minutes.

Never enough.

She turned the wheel another fraction.

The eastern gauge crossed red.

The wall cracked.

A concussion passed through the chamber. Dust fell from the ceiling. The platform dropped several inches, and Ilyra struck the railing. The wheel tore free of her hands.

At the same instant, the maintenance tube rang with pounding.

“Open it!” Nera shouted. “Ilyra, open the door!”

The voices below were no longer distinct. Water thundered through the corridor. A child cried. Someone screamed for a mother.

Ilyra stared at the emergency lever.

She knew what would happen. The door would rise. Water would enter the chamber in a solid mass, take the lower controls first, then the platform. The central drive would short beneath the flood. The eastern sluice would open wider or lock where it stood. The barrage would cease to be a machine she could influence and become a set of broken weights and channels.

But the people below would come through.

She reached for the lever.

In the Flood Cells, Magistrate Pell leaned back from the table.

“Your own report says you heard them.”

The room was dry, white, and without windows. A drain whispered beneath Ilyra’s chair. Beyond the glass partition, a civic lens watched her face.

“I heard them,” she said.

“And you refused to open the door.”

“I refused to flood the control chamber.”

“Another way of saying you refused to open the door.”

“Words are not interchangeable because you arrange them in a sentence.”

Pell glanced toward the clerk. “Record that the accused remains evasive.”

The stylus moved.

Ilyra looked at the lens. She had designed its first relay network as a warning system, a way for every district to receive the same information. The Council had added delay locks, authorization tiers, and a central override.

Now it recorded her silence and made it evidence.

Pell folded his hands. “How many would have died if you had opened the emergency door?”

“I cannot give an exact number.”

“An estimate.”

“Several thousand, if the eastern wall failed.”

“Because of your machinery.”

“Because the central sluice was already carrying the pressure.”

“Because you opened it.”

“Because the Council narrowed it, removed the western valves, and transferred water through an untested private line.”

“We are not discussing the Council.”

“We are discussing the conditions under which the door became a choice.”

“And yet you made the final decision.”

The barrage returned.

The emergency lever was inches from Ilyra’s hand.

She heard Nera through the tube.

“Please.”

Not an argument now. Not a demand.

Please.

Ilyra had once believed pleading was merely pressure applied by those without instruments. She had been wrong. It could not be converted into a useful unit.

She gripped the lever.

Above the barrage, the Feast bells began to ring. Their notes came down through layers of stone, warped and hollow. The city was celebrating the renewal of its waterworks. Officials were telling the crowd that the failure had been contained, that Crown engineers were in command.

Ilyra pictured Governor Dault beneath the white canopy.

She pictured his face when the platform tilted.

For an instant she wanted the door open because it would destroy the machinery beneath him. She wanted the flood to rise into the chamber, to erase every control he believed belonged to him. She wanted the people above to feel the helplessness of those below.

Then she saw Tomas coughing in the winter dark.

Sella lifting an empty cup.

The child on the roof, one hand reaching toward her, while the valve key weighed in her palm.

A choice could be necessary and still belong to the person who made it.

Ilyra pulled the lever down.

The emergency mechanism groaned. The door below shuddered in its frame.

For one breath she thought she had opened it.

Then the warning bell sounded.

A red lamp flared above the release.

“Manual override,” she whispered.

The door had been sealed from the lower side with a civic lock. A maintenance authorization was required from the chamber console, across the platform, beyond the western wheel and the spray.

Ilyra crossed toward it.

The platform shifted. She fell to one knee. Water swept over the grating, carrying a wrench and pieces of broken brass. She caught the railing and hauled herself forward.

The console’s glass face was cracked. Beneath it, bronze studs waited for the six-operator authorization. She had opened the central sluice alone using the stolen seal. She could do the same here.

Her hand went to the forged seal at her belt.

Then she stopped.

The seal was not the problem.

The system had been designed to prevent one person from making this decision. Six operators. Six witnesses. No solitary hand could flood a chamber, sacrifice a district, or call the act inevitable.

There were no six operators left.

Only her.

Nera struck the tube again.

“Ilyra!”

“I’m here.”

“The door is bending.”

“Move back from it.”

“There’s nowhere to move!”

“I know.”

“You told us to wait.”

“Yes.”

“You told us to trust the sequence.”

Ilyra placed the seal against the first bronze stud.

The console remained dark.

“No,” Nera said. Her voice sharpened. “You are choosing.”

The words entered the chamber cleanly.

The floodwater was at the lower landing. A seam opened in the wall, and black water burst through it.

“Tell them to climb,” Ilyra said.

“What?”

“Use the service ladder. North wall. There should be a vertical shaft above the old filter room.”

“There isn’t a shaft.”

“There is. It was removed from the current plans.”

“You said there were braces.”

“I was wrong about the braces. I am not wrong about the shaft.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“No.”

“Then come here and open the door.”

Ilyra looked at the wheel, the broken chain, the eastern gauge, and the water pouring into the chamber.

If she opened the emergency door, the machine would die.

If she left it closed, the people behind it might die.

If she abandoned the chamber, the western gate would rise again and the camps would disappear beneath it.

There was no clean decision. No number that could make the dead consent.

“I can’t open it,” she said.

Nera inhaled sharply.

“Not yet,” Ilyra continued. “If I open it now, the pressure will take the eastern wall. I have to hold the gate.”

“You have to hold the gate,” Nera repeated.

“Yes.”

“And we wait.”

Ilyra could not answer.

Behind the tube came the sound of people moving, slipping, shouting. Nera began issuing orders, sending them toward the hidden shaft Ilyra had described.

Ilyra placed both hands on the western wheel.

“I will come back,” she said.

Nera did not reply.

The red lamp flashed faster.

Through the tube came the scrape of water, the cries of the trapped, and the heavy groan of the emergency door bending inward.

Ilyra did not look at it again.

She pulled until the skin of her palms opened, and listened to the people below waiting for a decision that had already been made.

chapters.name: The Child on the Roof
chapters.content:
## The Child on the Roof

The western gate shuddered beneath Ilyra’s hands.

Each tremor traveled through the wheel into her wrists. The metal was hot from friction, though the chamber air was cold. Water climbed the lower steps behind her, entering through seams in the floor and gathering in the grooves worn by generations of maintenance boots.

“Again,” Nera called through the maintenance tube.

Her voice came warped by brass and distance. “The shaft is there. I can feel air.”

“Then climb.”

“We’re climbing.”

“Faster.”

People shouted behind Nera. A child cried out, then was hushed. The sound entered the chamber with the water, as if the flooded corridor were breathing.

Ilyra looked toward the eastern gauge.

The needle trembled just below the red mark.

Not enough. The western pressure still rose, and every handspan she lowered the gate sent more force toward the eastern wall. The barrage had become a divided body with both arteries blocked. She could preserve one side only by injuring the other.

Beyond the grating, the central sluice roared. The Feast crowd had fled when the platform tilted. Officials had shouted for Crown engineers. Someone had called Ilyra’s name through the civic lenses.

The city had found its monster again.

She gripped the wheel until her split palms slipped.

For one instant, the chamber disappeared.

She was standing on a roof in the Low Quarter, and a child was reaching for her.

***

The flood had come at night.

People remembered that part incorrectly. They imagined an alarm bell, a red flare above the barrage, citizens waking in orderly rooms and carrying their possessions to marked shelters.

There had been no order.

Water had risen from below, forcing itself through drains and cellar grates. By the time the first bell rang, the lower rooms of the tenements were full.

Ilyra had been at the east pump station, knee-deep in water, when the emergency channel opened.

“Pressure’s gone west,” Arce said over the speaking tube.

His voice was breathless, but not frightened. “Get the east valves balanced.”

“The wall is holding.”

“Then keep it holding.”

“Where are the evacuation crews?”

“Crown first.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“Voss.”

The tube clicked dead.

She had looked at the gauge board. The old numbers were scratched beneath the newer ones, as if the barrage had been rewritten over itself. Central flow was high. Western relief was inconsistent. Somewhere beyond the walls, the Low Quarter was filling.

She took a service skiff through streets that had ceased to be streets.

The boat scraped over market stalls and struck the upper branches of drowned trees. Lamps swung from balconies, their flames reflected in water darkened by oil and silt. People called from windows. Some held babies above their heads. Others clutched ledgers, ration tins, bundles of clothing.

At the corner of Sella Row, a woman clung to a chimney while a body turned against the roofline below her. Ilyra recognized the red scarf. She did not stop. The pump station had reported a surge through the western feeder, and she carried the only calibrated valve key that could reach the auxiliary housing.

That was how she explained it afterward.

The key was needed. It was the difference between a controlled release and a rupture. It could save thousands.

All of those statements were true.

None contained the whole truth.

The roof belonged to a dyehouse. Its chimney had collapsed, and blue runoff slicked the tiles. A child stood near the ridge, ankle-deep in floodwater, wearing a yellow sleep shirt and one red boot. The other floated against a gutter.

Ilyra guided the skiff toward the building, but the current drove it sideways. The boat struck a shutter and spun. The valve key lay beneath the bench, wrapped in oilcloth. She had one hand on the oar and one on the gunwale.

“Hold on!” she shouted.

The child did not move.

“Come down!”

The western spill channel opened behind the dyehouse. Water poured through it toward the pump station. If it reached the station, the auxiliary controls would drown, and the eastern wall would take the pressure.

Ilyra saw the route in her mind: the gate positions, the force vectors, the places where water would climb. She also saw the child’s red boot.

The skiff struck the building again. The oar broke in her hands.

Ilyra seized the rope at the bow and leapt.

The water reached her chest. She caught a drainpipe and pulled herself toward the roof.

“Come to me,” she called.

The girl shook her head.

Tiles tore loose. The skiff broke free and drifted toward the pump station. The oilcloth bundle remained beneath the bench, black against the pale wood.

Ilyra pulled herself higher. The rope had caught on a submerged post. She tugged once, twice. It would not give. The valve key flashed in the drifting boat.

The eastern warning bell began to ring.

One strike.

A pause.

Two strikes.

The wall had shifted.

The child began to cry. Not loudly. She made a small, bewildered sound, as if the flood were an adult argument she had entered by mistake.

Ilyra released the rope and reached the roof edge. She swung against the wall, then hauled herself up with one arm. The girl slipped.

Ilyra caught her wrist.

The child weighed almost nothing. That was what Ilyra remembered most: how little force it took to hold her, and how little more it would take to lose her.

“Don’t let go,” the girl whispered.

“I won’t.”

The eastern bell struck again.

The pump station was nearly inundated.

Ilyra looked toward the skiff. The valve key’s brass teeth flashed whenever the boat turned. Without it, she could not open the auxiliary housing. Without the housing, the eastern wall would fail. The water would sweep through the Low Quarter in a wave taller than the tenements.

Perhaps that was true.

Perhaps it was the only story she could bear to believe.

The roof shifted. The girl fell.

Ilyra caught her again, but the movement drove her knee into the tiles. Pain flashed white. Below them, the current dragged at the child’s body.

She had a choice.

Not an impossible choice. There was a roof, a rope, a child’s wrist in her hand. No Council officer held her back. No official ordered her to release the girl.

There was also the key.

She could have followed the child into the water. She could have stayed and held her until help came, though no help was coming. She could have abandoned the pump station and allowed the wall to decide what Veyr had already decided was expendable.

Instead, she pried the child’s fingers from hers.

The girl screamed once.

Ilyra slid from the roof and dropped into the water.

She did not look back until she reached the skiff.

The child was gone.

***

“Voss!”

Senn’s voice shattered the memory.

The barrage chamber returned: wet iron, red lamps, the western wheel, Nera calling through the tube. Senn stood on the maintenance stair above, his uniform soaked to the thighs. A civic lens hovered behind him, its glass eye shining.

“You’re losing the gate,” he said.

“I know.”

“You said you could hold it.”

“I said the gate could be held.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

The western gate climbed another fraction. The eastern needle jumped.

Senn descended one step. “My sister told me what she saw.”

Ilyra’s hands tightened on the wheel.

“Is she alive?”

“She was alive long enough to tell me.”

He came lower. Water streamed from his hair and collected along his jaw.

“She said you looked at the child.”

“I did.”

“She said you had the girl’s hand.”

“I did.”

“And you let go.”

Ilyra said nothing.

The lens clicked as it adjusted focus. Pell would be listening. Every word could be placed beside the forged order and stolen seal. Every silence could be called evasion.

Senn’s mouth twisted. “You told the court you were saving the district.”

“I told the court what happened.”

“No. You told them what the numbers said happened.”

The wheel bucked. Ilyra braced her shoulder against it.

“Your sister was not the only person there,” she said.

“She was the only one who remembered your face.”

“I was trying to reach the auxiliary housing.”

“She remembered the child.”

“I know.”

“She remembered the girl asking you not to let go.”

The words struck more deeply than he could know.

Ilyra turned the wheel. Her palms opened again, blood running over the metal and vanishing beneath the spray.

Behind the emergency door, something hammered three times.

Nera.

Three knocks. A pause. Two knocks.

The pattern was the same as the unexplained sound beneath the Flood Cells. The chamber floor tilted. The gate groaned.

Senn reached for the railing. “Open the door.”

“If I do, this chamber floods.”

“Then move.”

“If I abandon the wheel, the western gate rises.”

“Let it.”

“The eastern wall will take the force.”

“People are behind that door.”

“So are people beyond the wall.”

His face hardened. “You always have another crowd ready.”

“I have a district.”

“You have an answer.”

Below, Nera struck the door again.

“Ilyra!”

She looked toward the emergency console. Its red lamp glowed. Manual authorization required. The original system had required six operators to agree before opening a door capable of flooding a chamber or sacrificing a district.

She had broken that principle once by acting alone.

She had called it courage. She had called it necessity. But on the dyehouse roof, no Council stood above her with a hand on hers. The key had been in her own hand.

She had made that choice.

***

At the pump station, Ilyra had torn away the oilcloth and fitted the valve key into the auxiliary housing.

Her clothes were heavy with river water. Her fingers shook, but the brass teeth caught. She turned the key.

Pressure burst through the lower pipes. The station screamed. Water struck the walls from within, but the eastern gauge began to fall.

Three points.

Five.

Seven.

The warning bell stopped.

The Low Quarter did not vanish. That fact became her certificate. She had saved the wall. She had prevented the full rupture. The casualty count, though terrible, was not the catastrophe first predicted.

For weeks, officials repeated this in private.

For months, Ilyra repeated it to herself.

The child’s body was never found.

Lysa Renn survived with a broken arm and fever. She told the inquiry that strangers had pulled her onto a roof. She had seen Ilyra choose the key. Her statement was excluded from the technical record because she could not identify the pressure readings or explain the gate sequence.

But she knew what a hand looked like when it opened.

***

“Ilyra.”

Nera’s voice was quieter now.

Senn had moved lower on the stair. He was close enough to seize her if the wheel slipped, though she doubted he would help.

“I told them to climb,” Ilyra said.

“You don’t know if the shaft holds.”

“No.”

“You don’t know if they can reach it.”

“No.”

“You don’t know how many are behind this door.”

“No.”

“Then you know nothing.”

Ilyra turned the wheel another fraction. The eastern needle crossed the red line.

A crack opened along the wall behind the gauge.

Senn saw it. “Stop.”

“If the gate rises—”

“Stop!”

Water burst through the crack in a narrow jet and struck his shoulder. The chamber shook. Dust sifted from the ceiling.

Nera’s voice came through the tube. “Open it!”

Ilyra closed her eyes.

The child on the roof had asked her not to let go.

Nera had not asked for faith. She had asked for a decision. Ilyra had given the trapped workers time by holding the gate, but time was not mercy if it only postponed who would pay.

She opened her eyes.

The wheel was still in her hands. The emergency console was three steps away. The eastern wall was failing by increments. Beyond it lay the Low Quarter, the old streets and rebuilt streets, the people whose names would become figures if she let them.

Behind the door were Nera and the others.

There was no clean mathematics.

There had never been clean mathematics.

Only choices made by hands, and the stories those hands later told about themselves.

Ilyra eased the wheel back.

The western gate rose.

Pressure shifted with a roar. The eastern needle dropped below red. Somewhere beyond the wall, water changed course. It would still flood the storage fields. It would still tear through the lower camps. But the wall held.

For now.

Senn stared at her.

“You chose them,” he said.

“I chose the wall.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Below, the emergency door gave a long metallic shriek.

Ilyra released the wheel.

Then she ran toward the console.

chapters.name: The Drowned Quarter
chapters.content:
The key turned in Ilyra’s hand, and the water changed its voice.

Until then it had been one immense roar, a beast pressed against the walls of the world. When the auxiliary housing opened, the sound separated: water struck stone below, tore through the eastern channel, and fell through the pump shaft in a hard silver sheet. Somewhere above, a bell began ringing.

The pressure gauge trembled.

Twenty-two.

Twenty-one.

Twenty.

For one breath, Ilyra believed she had done it.

Then the eastern embankment gave way.

The sound was soft at first, an internal crack beneath mud. A seam opened along the wall. Water pushed through in a dark fan, carrying timber, a door, and half a roof. The pump station shook. Dust fell from the beams and turned to paste on her face.

“Close it!” Arce shouted through the speaking tube.

His voice came thin and distant, stripped of authority by the metal.

Ilyra ran to the second wheel. Its spokes were already turning. She caught one and burned her palm. The mechanism bucked. Behind her, the auxiliary channel swallowed the street.

She remembered thinking that the wall had held four minutes longer than the model predicted.

She remembered thinking that four minutes was not nothing.

Then the first tenement collapsed.

It went down from the bottom. The upper floors hung for a moment in the air, windows lit from within. People stood behind the glass, faces pale and small. A woman lifted a baby above her head. Someone struck a shutter with an iron bar. Someone else opened a window and disappeared.

The building folded inward.

A wave crossed the street and broke against the dyehouse. Ilyra saw the water reach the second-floor windows. A man ran with a child beneath his coat, slipped, rose, and vanished as the current took them.

There had been warnings. Maps, orders, reports, sealed channels, and the measured rise of water against foundations. There had been a Council that knew which streets would fill first and reinforced the terraces where ministers kept summer rooms.

She had not made the water.

She had only opened the gate.

The distinction became less useful with every street that vanished.

At the pump station, the emergency crew fought to keep the eastern valves balanced. The station had been designed for twelve operators. Seven had come. One had already been swept from the lower platform. Another knelt beside the boiler, vomiting river water.

“Pressure is climbing in the lower main,” said the woman at the gauge.

“Close the third intake.”

“It’s jammed.”

“Use the bypass.”

“The bypass is Crown-side.”

“It connects below the split.”

“It will feed the Crown terraces.”

Ilyra looked at the map spread across the table. Its edges were soaked and curling. Red pencil marked the streets beneath the eastern embankment: Low Quarter, dyehouses, ropewalk, foundry lane, the old grain market. The Crown terraces were marked in blue.

“Open the bypass,” she said.

The woman stared at her.

“Open it.”

The woman obeyed.

Far above them, the governors’ ceremonial platform took the first strike.

The Feast of Renewal had been built over the central channel so the Council could stand above the water and declare its mastery. White decking crossed the river. Bronze rails gleamed beneath an embroidered canopy. Governor Dault, Master Engineer Arce, three ministers, and the visiting merchants stood beneath it.

When the central current surged, the decking lifted like a raft.

For a heartbeat, the crowd cheered.

Then the platform struck the western pier.

The canopy tore free. One minister fell through the railing. Arce caught a bronze post with both hands. Dault was thrown against the lectern, his ceremonial crown rolling across the boards.

A private barge emerged from beneath the riverwalk.

It had been concealed under the platform, where only authorized boats could dock. Guards pulled Dault aboard. He did not look back at Arce or the minister. He stepped over the fallen man and seized the cabin rail.

The barge turned toward the Crown locks.

A woman on the platform saw it go and screamed. Others followed her gaze. Their fear became anger, though anger did not make them less helpless. They crowded the stairs and trampled one another, reaching for boats already full.

Ilyra watched Dault pass beneath the gold-trimmed archway.

For an instant, satisfaction moved through her. He was frightened, forced to flee through the water he had priced and rationed.

Then the eastern market bell began to ring.

It rang seventeen times before the tower fell.

The sound traveled over the roofs and into the pump station. Each strike grew duller. On the eighteenth, there was only a concussion, and then the quarter was quiet except for water.

That silence was worse than the roar.

People called from roofs. Families shouted names. Neighbors tied ropes between chimneys and pulled strangers from attic windows. Beneath the streets, hands struck at cellar doors while water pressed against the other side.

A workshop on Tallow Lane filled from its drains. Workers sleeping in the upper room climbed toward the rafters. The rafters broke. One man clung to a loom as it floated past; another reached the roof and found the hatch nailed shut.

At the tannery, vats of dye burst from their frames and stained the flood purple. At the ropewalk, coils of hemp unwound through the streets, catching around legs and wagon wheels. A rescue cart overturned when its horse became entangled. The people inside were dragged beneath the surface together.

At the old grain market, sacks split open and pale grain spread through the water.

Ilyra heard fragments afterward. No account held the whole night. Survivors carried one room, one face, one sound.

A boy on a chimney remembered the taste of soot.

A woman who lost three daughters remembered a red scarf floating past her window.

An old cooper remembered that the water entered his house warm, because buried pipes had cracked beneath the floor.

Lysa Renn remembered the child in the yellow sleep shirt.

Ilyra remembered the valve key.

The memory came in no order. Sometimes the child fell before Ilyra reached the skiff. Sometimes the child was already gone, and the hand belonged to Nera. Sometimes Tomas was on the roof, older than he had ever lived to be, asking why she had chosen a wall over him.

The machinery did not care which version she believed.

It continued to shudder.

“Engineer,” called the gauge woman. “The lower main is failing.”

Ilyra forced herself to look at the numbers.

The bypass had reduced pressure beneath the Low Quarter. The Crown terraces were taking the force instead. Gardens disappeared, then retaining walls, then storage buildings where grain had been held against winter shortages. Water rose around the governor’s warehouses and broke open their doors.

Barrels of wine rolled into the flood.

Crates of imported fruit followed.

People from the Low Quarter tried to swim after them. Some drowned beneath the crates. Others struck the barrels with stones until wine ran red into the river.

The calculations worked.

That was the horror.

The bypass performed as the model predicted. The Crown properties flooded. The eastern wall held. If she closed the intake, water would return to the lower main and the Low Quarter would be destroyed in a single surge.

If she left it open, the quarter might survive.

Not safely. Not wholly. But the wall would remain standing.

Ilyra wrote the figures on the edge of the map.

18: eastern main  
14: Crown intake  
9: lower pressure  
7: structural integrity

Her hand shook. She rewrote them more neatly.

The woman beside her began to cry.

“Stop,” Ilyra said.

“I’m not—”

“Read the gauge.”

The woman wiped her face. “Seven.”

“Again.”

“Seven.”

Ilyra nodded. The number became a fact. Facts could be held. Facts did not ask to be forgiven.

Outside, the Low Quarter continued to drown.

Water reached the third floors of the tenements. Families crowded onto roofs beneath blankets and doors ripped from hinges. A mother lowered her infant in a cooking pot toward a rescue boat, but the boat tipped when three men climbed aboard. The pot spun away. The child floated for several seconds, wrapped in white cloth, then vanished beneath a bridge.

At the north schoolhouse, the headmaster opened the doors to everyone he could admit. The lower hall filled to the windows. Children climbed onto desks while the oldest students broke through roof tiles. When the bell rope fell and wrapped around a girl’s ankle, two boys held her while a teacher cut it with a kitchen knife.

The school survived.

Of the thirty-eight people inside, twenty-three were found alive the next morning.

At the infirmary, the sick were left in their beds because there were not enough hands to carry them. Water rose across the wards, lifting mattresses and medicine bottles. A physician stood on a table and shouted for help until the roof caved in.

The bells stopped one by one.

First the market.

Then Saint Orra’s.

Then the watchtower at the eastern gate.

The last belonged to the Low Quarter civic office. It rang without rhythm as the tower leaned, struck the water, and broke.

After that, there was only the groan of masonry settling into the flood.

By dawn, the rain had thinned.

The city emerged in pieces. Roofs showed above the water. Chimneys smoked where people burned furniture for warmth. Bodies snagged on railings and branches. Boats moved through streets that had held carts the night before. White festival banners hung from gutters, stained brown and purple.

The ceremonial platform had broken apart. One section lodged against the eastern bridge. Another turned in the current, carrying three survivors and the dead minister toward the western locks.

Governor Dault was gone.

Notices stated that he had been “relocated to coordinate relief efforts.” Nothing mentioned the hidden dock, the prepared guards, or the minister left behind.

Arce was found on the roof of the Hall of Civic Judgment with a broken arm. He refused treatment until he learned whether the Crown retaining wall remained intact.

The wall did.

So did the Hall.

The Low Quarter did not.

Ilyra remained at the pump station because the water had not finished moving. She slept for nine minutes against a warm pipe and woke when someone stepped over her legs. The emergency crew had been reduced to four. One was injured. One had not spoken since the child on the roof. The gauge woman had wrapped both hands in cloth and continued working.

“Can we drain the lower streets?” she asked.

Ilyra studied the ruined map.

The auxiliary housing had warped. The eastern main was blocked by debris. The Crown bypass remained open, pouring water through gardens and warehouses. If they diverted it too quickly, the lower pressure would rise. If they waited, the water would settle into the quarter and become a second disaster: contamination, disease, foundations collapsing beneath the dead.

“We can open the old drainage run,” Ilyra said.

“It’s marked sealed.”

“It was sealed in the revised plan.”

The woman looked at her. “Can you open it?”

Ilyra wanted to say yes.

The answer was forming already: the angle, the pressure, the failure points. She could direct the others, take the wrench, make the decision before doubt spread among them. She could be the one person who understood the buried structure of the city.

Instead she said, “I don’t know.”

The woman’s face tightened.

“Then find someone who does.”

They searched beneath a collapsed cabinet and found an old drainage schematic. The lines were faint, drawn in blue ink nearly washed away. Ilyra spread it across the floor and held the corners with bolts.

The old run led beneath the dyehouses, under the grain market, and out toward the western marsh.

The marsh was full.

Opening the run might drain the quarter.

It might also draw the flood back through the foundations and pull down the remaining tenements.

Ilyra traced the line with one finger.

She could not tell whether she wanted the system to work because people still lived in the upper rooms, or because success would prove the original diversion justified. The two desires occupied the same space, indistinguishable as water beneath darkness.

“Your order,” said the woman.

Outside, someone began calling the names of the missing.

They called until their voice broke, then started again.

Ilyra closed her hand around the valve key and gave the order.

The old drainage run opened with a violence that shook the station. Water withdrew from one street and rose in another. A tenement wall folded into the gap. People on its roof screamed as the building slid downward, but the roof settled against the neighboring house, making a bridge.

Three children crossed it.

Two adults fell.

The water kept moving.

By the third day, the Council had counted 4,812 dead.

The number appeared on every civic lens in clean black figures beneath Veyr’s seal. It was repeated by announcers, printed on broadsheets, spoken at churches and ration queues. Four thousand eight hundred and twelve: precise enough to sound complete.

Survivors said it was higher.

They named tenants whose leases had never been registered, laborers sleeping in workshops, children born without civic papers, families living in the storage fields the maps called empty. They named Lysa Renn’s child, though no one knew the child’s name. They named those carried into locked courtyards and sealed basements.

The Council called such claims grief making patterns from confusion.

At the ruined pump station, Ilyra continued turning valves.

Each time the water fell, she recorded the level. Each time a wall collapsed, she recorded that too. She told herself the figures were for the inquiry that would come, a record officials could not alter.

But when the lower gauge dropped by two points, satisfaction returned.

The calculation was right.

The wall had held.

The water had gone where she directed it.

Ilyra stared at the number until it blurred. Then she bent over the gauge and kept working, unable to decide whether she was saving the city or asking the ruined quarter to prove that she had been correct.

chapters.name: The Arrest
chapters.content:
Two days after the flood, the pump station still breathed.

Warm, wet air rose through the grates, carrying silt, oil, drowned timber, and the sweet rot of things trapped below. The pumps had stopped before dawn, but water continued moving beneath the floor and inside the walls. Every few minutes, the masonry answered with a knock.

Ilyra sat beside the largest pump, one hand wrapped in a strip of her coat. With the other, she turned the screw on the manual drainage assembly. The screw resisted, then gave a fraction. Somewhere below, a submerged valve clanked.

One quarter turn.

She marked it in charcoal.

Thirty-seven marks covered the floor.

Beyond the station windows, Veyr was a ruin of roofs and chimneys. Brown water filled the lower streets. Furniture floated in alleys. The Hall of Civic Judgment remained dry on its hill, its white walls untouched behind the Crown retaining wall.

The wall had held.

She could not stop thinking that. She had opened the Crown-side bypass when the eastern embankment began to fail, sending pressure toward ministers’ terraces, gardens, warehouses, and stored grain. The flow had slowed beneath the Low Quarter. Thousands had reached higher ground.

The bypass had also taken the market tower, the dyehouses, the ropewalk, and three rows of tenements.

It had taken the girl in the yellow sleep shirt.

Ilyra turned the screw again. A jet of black water struck the grating and sprayed her face.

For an instant, she felt cold fingers close around hers.

A child’s hand.

The valve key drifting away.

Her own hand pulling free.

The pump coughed, and the memory vanished.

At the far side of the station, survivors waited beside the relief cistern. Some had come from the Low Quarter. Others had slept in the storage fields before the western flow rose. They watched Ilyra without speaking.

A bell sounded outside.

Eight strokes.

A pause.

Eight more.

The outer doors opened. Civic officers entered through the floodwater, their gray coats clean above the knees. Two lens-carriers followed, brass recording cases strapped to their backs. At their center walked Magistrate Oren Pell in a plain black coat untouched by mud.

He carried a folded document sealed with red wax.

Ilyra rose. Her knees shook.

“Where are the rescue crews?” she asked.

“They are attending to the emergency,” Pell said.

“You are the emergency.”

An officer seized her arm. Another raised a restraint collar.

The survivors shifted. One man with a burned cheek stepped forward, then stopped when the lenses turned toward him.

Pell opened the document. “Ilyra Voss, civic engineer of the Third Class, you are charged with unlawful seizure of the North Barrage, destruction of public infrastructure, deliberate release of floodwater into inhabited districts, and the deaths of—”

“How many?”

Pell glanced at the page. “The provisional count is four thousand eight hundred and twelve.”

A woman at the cistern began to sob.

“Provisional,” Ilyra said. “You have not searched the storage fields.”

“The fields were designated unoccupied.”

“They were not.”

“You have not searched the lower ropewalk.”

“The ropewalk is full of bodies.”

“Ilyra,” Pell said, “this is not the place.”

“It is exactly the place. You came here because the bodies are here.”

The officer twisted her arm behind her back. The metal band closed around her wrists.

“The east pump can be restarted,” Ilyra said. “Open the intake. Close it after twelve counts. The pressure must fall before—”

“You have no authority here.”

“I built the intake system.”

“You destroyed it.”

“Not this station.”

Pell folded the charge sheet. “The Council will determine what was destroyed.”

“The Council already determined what could be destroyed.”

They dragged her toward the doors. Ilyra looked back at the wall above the auxiliary pipe. Her instructions were still visible, though spray had washed away half the words.

Open the east intake.

Close after twelve counts.

Wait for the pressure to fall.

She tried to say them again. An officer struck the back of her knee, and she fell against the wet floor.

The lens-carrier moved closer. Its red aperture widened.

It recorded her arrest.

It did not record the pump.

It did not record the bodies below.

It did not record Pell’s clean boots.

Outside, the civic lenses began broadcasting.

*The Barrage Butcher has been apprehended.*

The phrase moved faster than the rescue boats.

By noon it was painted on walls that had not dried from the flood. By evening, broadsheets showed Ilyra standing before a wall of water, a knife in one hand and the stolen civic seal in the other. The water was real. The knife and seal had been added.

Pell showed her the image the following morning.

She sat in a narrow examination room beneath the Hall, wrists chained to a ring in the table. A drain ran between her feet. Her coat was gone, and her shirt remained stiff with silt.

Pell placed the broadsheet before her.

“Do you recognize yourself?”

“Yes.”

“The weapon?”

“No.”

“The seal?”

“Yes.”

“Then the likeness is substantially accurate.”

“You use likeness to mean whatever survives after the facts are removed.”

Pell opened a folder. “This is your first warning, dated three weeks before the Feast.”

Ilyra read it.

*The eastern embankment remains within acceptable tolerance. Engineer Voss expresses concern regarding nonessential western structures and recommends unauthorized alteration of the barrage sequence.*

“That is not what I wrote.”

“It bears your signature.”

“My signature was attached to a hydraulic table. The paragraph was added afterward.”

“Can you prove that?”

“The table begins on the next page. The numbering is wrong.”

Pell gathered the paper. “You expect the court to believe clerical irregularities prove a conspiracy.”

“I expect the court to compare the original.”

“The original was confiscated.”

“By whom?”

“By civic order.”

“Whose?”

Pell’s voice remained mild. “You are still attempting to direct the examination.”

“I am establishing the sequence.”

“The sequence is simple. You were angry. You stole a seal, entered a restricted barrage, opened a gate, and the city flooded. You were found at a pump station with tools, maps, and a mechanism capable of further intervention.”

“I was trying to stop it.”

“After forging an authorization order.”

“After my license was suspended because I reported a failure.”

“Because you had become politically agitated.”

“Because the Council had altered the surveys.”

“By the Council?”

“By the engineers acting for it.”

“My office does not operate the barrage.”

“Your office certifies the orders that do.”

Pell returned the warning to the folder. “Every answer returns to the same accusation. You cannot describe your actions without placing the city on trial.”

“The city is not on trial.”

“No,” he said. “You are.”

The door opened. Two archive officials entered carrying a wooden crate stamped with the insignia of the Civic Water Office.

Ilyra recognized it from the Annex basement.

“My maps.”

“Your professional materials,” Pell said.

“There should be three copies of the older survey.”

“There are twelve documents here.”

“Show me the western relief gates.”

Pell unfolded a map and held it toward her. The page showed a narrow central channel and blank space to the west.

“The western gates are missing.”

“They were maintenance hatches.”

“They were pressure valves.”

“They were marked as maintenance hatches in the current survey.”

“The current survey was altered.”

“Master Engineer Arce will provide expert testimony.”

“Where is Arce?”

“Recovering from injuries sustained during the evacuation.”

“He was on the ceremonial platform. He knew the valves had been removed.”

“That is an allegation.”

“He signed the reservoir-transfer schedule.”

“That is an allegation.”

“I saw the private bypass.”

“You saw water and assigned it a meaning.”

The map disappeared back into the crate.

“Your materials will be retained as evidence,” Pell said.

“Evidence of what?”

“Intent.”

“You mean evidence that proves the barrage was unsafe.”

“I mean evidence that shows you understood the consequences of opening it.”

The officials lifted the crate. At the doorway, one corner struck the frame. A strip of oilskin slipped beneath the lid and fell to the floor.

Ilyra saw blue ink: part of the old survey, the divided river and the western basin.

An official kicked it beneath the table.

He bent to retrieve it.

Ilyra could have pointed.

Instead she kept her eyes on Pell.

His gaze flicked down, then returned to her face. Neither of them spoke. The official tucked the oilskin beneath his coat and carried the crate away.

That evening, the Hall broadcast the Council’s formal statement.

The voices were calm. They spoke of grief, resilience, and a city attacked from within.

An unstable engineer had exploited a moment of civic celebration.

She had acted alone.

Her resentment toward the hereditary districts had curdled into hatred of all Veyr.

The flood was not a failure of design, preparation, or governance. It was terrorism.

In her cell, Ilyra listened through the wall.

*An isolated criminal.*

*Personal grievance.*

*Deliberate mass killing.*

*No prior warning was substantiated.*

Pell came to her after midnight.

He stopped beyond the bars, hands folded behind his back.

“Do you know why the statement worked?” he asked.

“Because people are afraid.”

“Everyone is afraid. That does not explain acceptance.”

“Because the dead cannot contradict you.”

“That helps.”

“Because survivors need someone to blame.”

“That helps more.”

He stepped closer. “The city accepted you because you made the story easy.”

“I did not make the flood easy.”

“No. You made yourself visible. You entered the barrage. You carried the seal. You stood at the controls while the platform broke apart. You were found with the tools in your hands.”

“I was trying to stop it.”

“Perhaps. But the public does not consume perhaps. It consumes sequence. A face. An act. A result.”

“You removed the Council from the sequence.”

“We placed it where it belongs.”

“Outside responsibility.”

“Above panic.”

Ilyra looked toward the stairway leading up to the Hall, the lenses, and the city waiting for its story.

“You think the city wants a monster.”

“The city wants a shape for its grief.”

“And you gave it mine.”

“You offered it.”

She remembered the ceremonial platform tipping beneath her, the white canopy tearing loose, Governor Dault’s face as water rose through the central channel.

For one bright, shameful instant, she had been glad.

She had wanted him to understand—not the calculations or the warnings, but the fear. She had wanted those who called the Low Quarter a pressure sink to feel pressure in their own bones.

Pell saw the change in her expression.

“There,” he said.

“What?”

“The reason they believe you.”

“You do not know the reason.”

“I know you chose the date when the governors would be gathered.”

“So they could not suppress what happened.”

“So they would be present.”

“I needed witnesses.”

“You needed an audience.”

The corridor seemed to narrow around them.

Ilyra gripped the bars. “You sealed the evacuation records.”

“We secured them.”

“You confiscated my maps.”

“We preserved them.”

“You altered my warnings.”

“We corrected the record.”

“You named the dead before searching for them.”

Pell’s mouth tightened.

“You see?” he said. “You cannot speak without making yourself the center of every event.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “You have made me the center. That is the point.”

She understood then what the Council had done. It did not need to disprove her warnings. It did not need to explain the missing valves, the private bypass, the erased western gates, the cleared fields, or the Crown wall crews.

It needed only to make her character more memorable than the records.

A resentful lowborn engineer.

A woman with a stolen seal.

A woman who had chosen a child-sized hand over a brass key, then chosen the key.

Every warning could become an intention. Every intention could become a motive. Every motive could become a verdict.

Pell touched the bars with two fingers.

“Tell the court you acted alone,” he said. “It will make the truth easier to survive.”

“What truth?”

“That you opened the gate.”

Ilyra looked down the corridor, toward the Hall and the city waiting to watch her be explained.

“Yes,” she said.

Pell waited for more.

She gave him none.

Behind the walls, water knocked once.

Then twice.

Then stopped.

chapters.name: The Trial Begins
chapters.content:
The Hall of Civic Judgment had been built to make a person feel observed before anyone spoke.

Its walls rose in pale tiers above the trial chamber, each tier fitted with black glass lenses. They turned with small, insectile clicks as Ilyra entered between two guards. Above them, behind a lattice of bronze, the citywide transmission apparatus waited with its polished mouths open. Every lens in Veyr could receive the proceedings. Every household with a civic receiver would see the chamber, the magistrates, the witnesses, and, most often, her.

The galleries were full.

People stood along the aisles despite the posted restrictions. They crowded the upper balconies in festival colors, some wearing white masks painted with blue tears, others with red slashes across the mouth. A child near the front held a sweetcake shaped like a woman beneath a wave. Its sugar hair had been dyed black.

Ilyra looked away before the child could bite into it.

“Prisoner,” called the clerk.

The word went through the chamber and returned from the stone.

Ilyra stopped at the marked place before the magistrate’s bench. Her wrists were shackled in front of her, the chain short enough to prevent her from lifting either hand above her chest. A restraint designed to appear humane in the broadcast. Her ankles were free, though two guards stood close enough to catch her if she moved.

Senn was one of them.

He did not look at her. His jaw was tight, his eyes fixed on the bench. Maret stood on Ilyra’s other side, watching the lenses with frank curiosity. She had braided silver thread into her hair for the occasion.

The clerk began reading the charges.

“Unlawful seizure of the North Barrage. Theft and fraudulent use of a civic seal. Destruction of public infrastructure. Deliberate release of floodwater into inhabited districts. Incitement against the hereditary civic order. And the deaths of four thousand eight hundred and twelve persons.”

The number settled over the chamber with the weight of a verdict.

Ilyra listened for the missing names.

There was no mention of the storage fields. No count for the workers in the lower ropewalk, the families outside the district registers, the people whose lodging permits had been revoked before the Feast. No girl in a yellow sleep shirt with one red boot. No Nera Vale. No workers calling through a maintenance tube.

The clerk continued.

“By authority of the Council of Veyr, this proceeding shall be transmitted for public instruction, civic reassurance, and the preservation of the historical record.”

At that, several people in the galleries applauded.

Magistrate Oren Pell raised one hand. The applause ceased in uneven pieces.

He had dressed in dark green, the color of old bronze after rain. His hair, usually swept back from his forehead, had been trimmed close for the broadcast. He looked less like the man who had questioned her beneath the Hall and more like the face carved above its entrance: stern, patient, designed to outlast weather.

“Let the record show,” he said, “that the accused is present and understands the charges.”

“I understand the charges as they have been written,” Ilyra said.

A murmur moved through the chamber.

Pell’s eyes rested on her. “Do you deny them?”

“I deny that the number is complete.”

The murmur sharpened.

“And do you deny opening the North Barrage?”

“No.”

There it was: the first clean piece of the story. The thing the city had been waiting to hear.

Pell inclined his head. “Do you deny taking the bronze seal of the Civic Water Office?”

“No.”

“Do you deny entering the barrage under a forged authorization?”

“No.”

“Do you deny that you knew water would enter inhabited districts?”

Ilyra felt the chain between her wrists press into the bones. “I knew water would move through districts that the Council had designated as expendable.”

Pell turned to the clerk. “The accused offers a political qualification to a factual question.”

“I offer the fact,” Ilyra said.

He looked back at her. “You will have an opportunity to speak when recognized.”

“You asked me whether I deny it.”

“I asked whether you knew people would die.”

“Yes.”

The answer struck the room harder than any denial could have done.

Someone in the gallery shouted, “Murderer!”

Another voice cried, “Let her burn!”

Senn’s shoulders shifted. Ilyra saw his hand tighten around the baton at his belt.

Pell waited until the noise became useful rather than disruptive. Then he said, “The accused has acknowledged planning the intervention, executing it, and understanding its likely consequences. The prosecution will establish the remainder.”

Ilyra looked up at the lenses.

There were twelve visible in the chamber and more hidden behind the bronze screens. Each held a small reflected version of her face. The city would be shown her silence after the admission. It would not be shown the storage fields, or the removed valves, or the private bypass that had sent Crown water toward Governor Dault’s gardens. It would be shown a woman who had confessed to knowing.

Pell called the first witness.

He was a narrow man in a gray engineer’s coat, perhaps forty, with a civic badge pinned high at his throat. Ilyra recognized him as Halven Rusk, a survey assistant who had worked two levels below her in the Water Office. He did not meet her eyes as he took the witness stand.

“State your name and occupation,” Pell said.

“Halven Rusk. Junior hydraulic surveyor.”

“Did you know the accused?”

“I worked in the same office.”

“Was she dissatisfied with her position?”

Rusk swallowed. “She believed her work was not properly credited.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“She was dissatisfied.”

“Did she express hostility toward the Crown and the hereditary districts?”

Rusk glanced toward the galleries. “She said the maps were drawn to protect people who already had walls.”

Several spectators hissed.

“Did she make threats?”

“Not directly.”

“Did she say that the Feast of Renewal would be a memorable day?”

“Yes.”

“What did you understand her to mean?”

Rusk’s hands curled against the edge of the stand. “I thought she meant the water transfer would be completed.”

Pell paused. “And now?”

“Now I understand that she meant to make the city remember her.”

Ilyra let out a breath through her nose.

The answer was not a lie exactly. That was the method. Pell did not need witnesses to invent words. He needed them to place familiar words under a different light.

“Did the accused possess the technical knowledge required to open the North Barrage?”

“Yes.”

“Could an untrained person have done so?”

“Not without killing themselves.”

“Did she know the sequence?”

“Yes.”

“Then she was not acting impulsively.”

“No.”

“Thank you.”

Ilyra lifted her shackled hands.

Pell looked toward her. “You may question the witness.”

She stood. The chain made a small bright sound, amplified by the chamber.

“Rusk, when did you first see the old survey showing the western relief channels?”

His eyes moved to Pell.

“Answer the question,” Pell said.

“We did not use such a survey.”

“You did. It was in the archive room beneath the eastern stacks. The river was divided around an island. There were two western spill basins.”

“Not on the current plans.”

“Why were the current plans changed?”

“I don’t know.”

“Were you present when the western gates were relabeled as maintenance hatches?”

“No.”

“Were you present when the pressure valves were removed?”

“No.”

“Did you see orders for the Crown reservoir bypass?”

Rusk’s mouth opened, then closed.

Pell leaned toward him. “Witness?”

“I saw transfer schedules,” Rusk said.

“From whom?”

“From the reservoir office.”

“Were they related to the flood?”

“I can’t say.”

Ilyra turned to the bench. “The prosecution has introduced testimony about my technical capacity while excluding the documents that explain what the system had been altered to do.”

Pell’s expression did not change. “You are not questioning the witness.”

“I am identifying the limits of his evidence.”

“You are attempting to make a speech.”

“The documents exist.”

“The documents have been reviewed and found immaterial to the charge of unlawful entry and deliberate release.”

“Immaterial?” Ilyra’s voice rose despite her effort. “The altered survey, the removed valves, and the private bypass determine where the water went.”

Pell struck the desk once with the flat of his hand.

“Prisoner, you will not convert this chamber into an engineering lecture.”

“I am not asking for a lecture. I am asking why the Council’s prior knowledge is excluded from a trial about the flood.”

The gallery erupted.

Some people shouted for her death. Others shouted questions. A woman in the upper tier cried, “My son was in the ropewalk!” and was immediately answered by a chorus of “Agitator!”

Pell waited. He had the patience of someone watching a mechanism complete its intended cycle.

When the guards stepped toward Ilyra, he raised his hand again.

“Let the record show that the accused interrupts repeatedly, rejects the authority of the court, and attempts to introduce unverified political allegations in place of evidence.”

“They are not unverified,” Ilyra said.

“Your persistence does not make them admissible.”

“Your refusal does not make them false.”

For the first time, something like irritation crossed his face.

“Sit down.”

Ilyra remained standing.

Pell’s voice softened. “You have been granted the opportunity to question a witness. You are using it to perform defiance for the galleries. Sit down, or I will have you removed and the examination will continue in your absence.”

She looked at Rusk. His face had gone pale.

“Did you sign any report stating that the western channels did not exist?” she asked.

“No.”

“Did you write that the storage fields were unoccupied?”

“No.”

“Did you see who did?”

Pell rose. “Enough.”

The guards took Ilyra by the arms. She allowed them to lower her into the chair, but not before saying, “You know the answer.”

Rusk flinched as if she had struck him.

Pell called the next witness.

A woman from the Low Quarter was brought in by two attendants. She wore a brown coat too large for her and carried one arm close to her ribs. Ilyra recognized the break in the way she held herself before she recognized the face.

Lysa Renn.

The chamber seemed to tilt.

Lysa had survived the old flood. Her testimony had been excluded during the preliminary hearings because she could not explain the readings on the pump station gauges. She had been a child then, crossing a collapsed tenement roof while Ilyra held a valve key in one hand and watched another child disappear below the water.

Lysa saw her and stopped.

Pell turned to the clerk. “Record the witness’s name.”

“Lysa Renn,” the woman said.

“Occupation?”

“Dye worker.”

“Were you present during the North Barrage flood?”

“Yes.”

“Did you see the accused?”

Lysa’s eyes remained on Ilyra. “Yes.”

“Where?”

“At the pump station. Near the lower street.”

“Tell the court what she did.”

Lysa’s throat worked. “There was a child on the roof.”

Ilyra closed her eyes.

“She was small,” Lysa continued. “Yellow shirt. One boot. She reached for the engineer. The engineer had a key in her hand.”

Pell’s voice was gentle now, almost compassionate. “What happened?”

“She chose the key.”

A sound went through the galleries—not outrage, not grief, but recognition. The city had been given the image it wanted. The woman. The child. The choice.

“What did the accused say?” Pell asked.

“She said if she dropped it, more people would die.”

“Did she try to save the child?”

“No.”

“Did she appear distressed?”

Lysa looked at Ilyra then. “She looked at the child.”

“That was not my question.”

“She looked.”

Pell’s gaze sharpened. “Did she attempt a rescue?”

“No.”

“Thank you.”

Ilyra stood before Pell could dismiss her.

“You were there,” she said to Lysa.

“Yes.”

“You saw the eastern wall?”

“I saw the water.”

“You saw the tenement collapse after I opened the drainage run.”

“Yes.”

“Did you see the three children who crossed over the fallen roof?”

Lysa’s face tightened. “Yes.”

“Did you see me turn the east valve?”

“Yes.”

“Did the valve lower the pressure in the Low Quarter?”

“I don’t know.”

“It did. If I had abandoned the key, the pressure would have—”

Pell cut in. “The witness has already testified that she did not understand the technical readings.”

“She understood what she saw.”

“She understood that you refused a child.”

“She also saw people survive.”

“She saw you choose an object over a human life.”

“I chose between lives.”

The words left her before she could measure them.

A hush formed.

Pell slowly faced the galleries. “The accused now reduces the death of a child to a calculation.”

“That is not what I said.”

“It is precisely what you said.”

“No. I said the choice was between lives. The child was not the only person in danger.”

“But she was the person in front of you.”

Ilyra looked at Lysa. “Yes.”

The admission seemed to satisfy the room more than any explanation could have.

Lysa’s lips trembled. For one instant she looked less like a witness and more like the child Ilyra remembered crossing the broken roof. Then a man in the gallery called her a liar, and another shouted that the Council had paid her, and the old fear returned to her face.

A second witness rose from the rear benches.

“Let her speak!” he shouted. “The Crown left us there!”

The guards moved toward him.

“My wife was in the storage fields,” he continued. “They told us the fields were empty. They knew we were there. They shut the road and watched the water come.”

“Remove him,” Pell ordered.

The man resisted when the guards reached him. “Ask Dault why his barge was waiting! Ask Arce who removed the valves!”

Several people stood. A woman began crying out the names of relatives. Someone threw a paper token toward the bench. It struck a lens and fell smoking to the floor.

The Hall’s bronze doors opened. More guards entered.

Pell did not raise his voice. He did not need to.

“Any person disrupting these proceedings will be charged with contempt and incitement. This court will not permit grief to become a weapon.”

The man was dragged away.

Ilyra watched his boots scrape the floor until the doors closed behind him.

“Grief is already a weapon,” she said.

Pell turned back to her. “And you are demonstrating why.”

The broadcast lens above the bench pivoted toward her.

“Make no mistake,” Pell said, addressing the city as much as the chamber. “This proceeding will hear the suffering of Veyr. But suffering does not authorize disorder, nor does it excuse the deliberate destruction of life. We will not allow agitators to exploit the dead in order to conceal the accused’s responsibility.”

Ilyra understood then that the trial did not exclude grief. It sorted grief.

Lysa’s grief could remain because it pointed toward Ilyra. The storage-field survivor’s grief had to be removed because it pointed past her. Every account would be permitted only after its direction had been tested.

Pell dismissed Lysa. She stepped down from the stand without looking at Ilyra.

“Wait,” Ilyra said.

Lysa paused.

“I am sorry,” Ilyra said.

Pell’s hand moved toward the desk.

Ilyra continued before he could stop her. “Not because I chose the key. I am sorry because I knew what the choice made me responsible for, and I told myself responsibility could be measured by the number of people saved.”

Lysa’s face twisted.

“Do not make my pain part of your defense,” she said.

Then she left.

The chamber remained quiet longer than it had for any testimony.

Pell leaned back. “The court will recess for one hour.”

As the galleries began to spill into the corridors, the lenses continued to watch Ilyra. Maret shifted beside her, fascinated still, but less comfortably now. Senn kept his face turned away.

Ilyra sat beneath the painted seal of Veyr and listened to the city consume the first day of her trial.

By evening, they would repeat that she had confessed.

They would not repeat that the Council had known.

They would repeat the child’s yellow shirt.

They would not repeat the names shouted from the gallery before the guards dragged them away.

And somewhere beneath the Hall, behind stone and iron and the official shape of the flood, water knocked once against a buried door.

Then again.

chapters.name: Names on the Record
chapters.content:
The second day began with the clerk mispronouncing the dead.

He read from a slate while the Hall’s lenses watched his mouth.

“Ansel Vey. Marra Vey. Jorin Pellis. Tamas Rusk. Ellin—”

He stopped, frowned, and passed one finger over the line as if the name had become a smudge.

“Ellin Rusk,” he corrected. “Four thousand eight hundred and twelve confirmed deceased.”

The number settled over the chamber with the weight of a roof.

Ilyra stood between Senn and Maret beneath the witness alcove. Her wrists had been chained before her, the links short enough to prevent her from raising her hands higher than her ribs. She could not see the lower gallery from where she stood, only the black-glass face of the nearest lens and the reflection of her own mouth in it.

The clerk continued.

“Bera Holt. Cassen Dree. Venn Orlo. Sella Marr.”

At her mother’s name, Ilyra’s breath caught.

Not Sella Voss. The slate held another Sella, someone who had died in a district she had never entered, under a roof she had never measured. Still, for one instant, the name belonged to her mother as surely as the damp cold of the Flood Cells belonged to her skin.

She counted the bolts in the witness alcove.

Six on the left rail. Five on the right. One missing beneath the ledge, leaving a black crescent in the wood.

The clerk’s voice went on.

“Daro Venn. Pella Rusk. Oren Vale. Nera—”

A murmur moved through the court.

The clerk looked down again.

“Nera Vale,” he said. “Confirmed deceased.”

Ilyra forgot the bolts.

The sound that came from her was not quite a word. Maret turned sharply. Senn’s shoulders tightened, though he did not look at her.

Pell raised one pale hand.

“Strike the last entry.”

The clerk hesitated. “Magistrate, the name is listed among the recovered—”

“Strike it.”

The stylus made a wet scratching sound over the slate.

Ilyra leaned toward the rail. “You have not recovered Nera.”

Pell regarded her from the central bench. “You are not permitted to interrupt the death register.”

“She contacted me from the lower corridor.”

“Your claim is not evidence.”

“She was alive when I left the barrage.”

“Then you may submit that claim through the proper channel.”

“There is no proper channel for a person you have already declared dead.”

The spectators stirred. Some laughed. The sound came from the upper galleries in scattered bursts, as though laughter were another approved response and people were checking whether they had used it correctly.

Pell looked toward the lenses. “The accused has mistaken a clerical correction for an invitation to perform.”

Ilyra’s fingers closed around the chain. The metal was warm from her skin.

The clerk continued reading.

Names emerged and vanished. Some he spoke carefully, some quickly. A few he asked the court reporter to verify. There were children’s names among them, marked only by a small hooked sign that meant dependent, unregistered, unclaimed. There were families whose surnames appeared three or four times in succession. There were workers listed by trade instead of birth name: dyehouse hand, ropewalk boy, terrace servant, canal woman.

When the clerk reached the storage fields, he turned three pages at once.

“There are no confirmed residents recorded in the designated basins,” he said.

From the gallery came a voice: “My wife was there.”

Another answered, “My sons.”

Pell struck the sounding block.

“Order.”

The word traveled through the Hall’s speaking tubes and returned enlarged from the walls. Order. Order. Order.

Senn’s hand moved near the hilt of his baton.

Ilyra looked at him. “You knew.”

His jaw flexed.

“About what?” Maret asked.

“Nothing,” Senn said.

But his eyes had shifted to the gallery doors.

Pell called Lysa Renn.
