She came through the side entrance with her left arm bound against her chest. The splint had been replaced by a rigid white brace, and the fingers of that hand were swollen at the joints. Her face seemed smaller than Ilyra remembered. Or perhaps the Hall had made everyone small. Its high benches, elevated judges’ platform, and vertical lenses gave the impression that human beings existed only as details inside an instrument.

Lysa stood before the rail.

The clerk administered the oath. Lysa repeated it without stumbling.

Pell approached her gently. He had a way of changing his voice for witnesses, smoothing its edges until he sounded less like the maker of a sentence and more like someone receiving a confidence.

“Lysa Renn,” he said, “you were present during the flood at the eastern drainage station?”

“Yes.”

“You saw the accused there?”

“Yes.”

“Please tell the court what she did.”

Lysa looked at Ilyra.

Not at the chains. Not at the lenses. At her face.

“She was holding a key,” Lysa said.

Pell waited.

“A valve key. Bronze. Long handle. She had mud on her coat and blood on her cheek.”

“Whose blood?”

“I don’t know.”

“What happened then?”

“There was a child on the roof of the dyehouse.”

A low murmur rose from the galleries. Several people leaned forward. Ilyra saw the outline of a sweetcake in a spectator’s hand, white icing shaped like a breaking wave.

“The child reached for her,” Lysa continued. “Ilyra reached back. She had the child’s hand.”

Ilyra closed her eyes.

Yellow sleep shirt. One red boot. The hand, slick and hot, fingers closing around hers with an infant’s confidence that the world would answer.

“Did the accused save the child?” Pell asked.

Lysa’s mouth trembled.

“No.”

“What did she do?”

“She let go.”

The Hall inhaled.

Ilyra opened her eyes. Senn was looking at the floor now.

Pell turned to the judges. “Let the record show that the witness has identified the accused as the person who abandoned the child.”

“I did not abandon her,” Ilyra said.

Lysa flinched.

The magistrate faced her. “You have already been cautioned.”

“I released her hand to keep the key.”

“Which is another way of saying you abandoned her.”

“No.” Ilyra’s voice sounded thin against the chamber. “It is a description of the action, not its meaning.”

Pell smiled without warmth. “The court is capable of understanding plain language.”

“Then let it understand all of it. The eastern wall was failing. The key controlled the drainage run. If I dropped it, the water would have reached the lower tenements before the pressure dispersed.”

“And yet the child died.”

“Yes.”

“You chose the mechanism over the child.”

“Yes.”

Lysa’s eyes shone, but she did not look away.

Pell said, “Was the child worth less than the people in the lower tenements?”

Ilyra felt the question closing around her like a sluice gate.

“No.”

“Then why did you let go?”

“Because I believed I could save more people with the key.”

“Believed?”

“I calculated.”

“A calculation is not certainty.”

“No.”

“Then you chose to gamble with the lives of the district.”

“I chose between disasters.”

“And placed yourself above everyone else as the person entitled to choose.”

The galleries began to stir again. Ilyra heard someone whisper, “There it is.”

She looked at the floor beneath Lysa’s boots. Mud had dried in the seams. Not court mud; river mud, gray and granular. Lysa had carried the flood into the Hall with her.

“Did you see the wall?” Ilyra asked.

Pell’s expression hardened. “You will answer only what is asked.”

“I am asking her.”

“You may ask questions relevant to the charge.”

“The wall’s failure is relevant.”

Lysa answered before Pell could forbid her. “I saw it.”

“Did the drainage run open?”

“Yes.”

“Did the southern tenements collapse after it opened?”

“Yes.”

“Did three children cross the fallen roof?”

Lysa swallowed. “Three crossed. Two adults were killed.”

“So the opening saved—”

“Don’t,” Lysa said.

The word was quiet, but it stopped Ilyra more effectively than Pell’s block.

Lysa’s good hand curled against her skirt. “Don’t make them into numbers.”

Ilyra stared at her.

“I know what happened,” Lysa said. “I know the water went down. I know some people lived because you turned that valve. I know you believed the child had to die. But she was still a child. She had a hand. You had her hand.”

The lenses glimmered.

Ilyra had thought the worst part was being accused of choosing wrongly. She had not understood that Lysa could accept the choice as effective and still refuse to call it right.

Pell thanked the witness. His voice softened again.

“Your account is sincere and clear.”

Lysa looked toward the gallery, perhaps toward Senn, perhaps toward a place beyond the Hall.

“It is what I saw.”

“And therefore the truth.”

Lysa’s face changed.

“No,” she said. “It is what I saw.”

For the first time, Pell seemed displeased by her.

He dismissed her anyway.

As Lysa passed the guards, Senn moved half a step toward her. His hand rose, then stopped in the air between them. Lysa did not touch him. She walked through the side door alone.

Pell called the next witness.

A ropewalk foreman named Derren Kalt testified that Ilyra had spoken of “teaching the Crown a lesson.” He had received two months of ration credits for appearing, though he called them compensation for lost wages. When Ilyra asked whether he had heard the phrase before or after the flood, he said he could not remember.

Pell asked whether he feared losing his ration allotment if he refused to testify.

Derren glanced at the clerk.

“No.”

The answer came too quickly.

A woman from the western terraces said Ilyra had laughed when the ceremonial platform tilted. She had been offered a relocation permit in exchange for her statement. She admitted this when Ilyra asked, then added, “The permit does not change what I saw.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “It changes what you are willing to risk by seeing it.”

Pell objected.

The woman began to cry. The judges allowed her answer to stand because her tears made it useful.

A porter from the Merchant District testified that the accused had planned to drown “the upper people.” His eviction notice had been suspended for thirty days after he signed the deposition. He kept touching the folded notice inside his coat.

“I never said all upper people,” Ilyra told him.

“You said the water should reach the platform.”

“Yes.”

“That is where the upper people stood.”

“That is where the officials stood.”

“You wanted them afraid.”

Ilyra thought of the white canopy tearing loose, of Governor Dault clutching the rail as the platform dipped, of Arce’s ceremonial sash snapping in the wind.

“Yes,” she said.

The porter stared at her, relieved perhaps to receive an answer that did not require interpretation.

Pell let the silence grow.

Ilyra had once believed that truth became stronger when stripped of decoration. Give the city the exact sequence, the correct pressure, the altered survey, the removed valves. Let every fact lock against the next and form a structure no argument could enter.

But facts did not stand alone. They stood in rooms built by those who selected them.

The porter had been afraid. She had wanted him to be afraid. Both things were true. His ration credits did not erase his testimony, and her anger did not erase the Crown’s orders. The court did not need one truth to defeat another. It needed only to arrange them so that one cast the proper shadow.

The clerk resumed the death register.

This time Pell ordered the names read between witnesses.

“Jessa Or. Hal Rook. Minna Tave. Corin Voss.”

Ilyra looked up.

“Voss” was common in the Low Quarter, but she knew Corin. A boy who had repaired pump belts with his older sister. He had brought Ilyra a pear once, green and hard, after she fixed the ration office’s water meter.

She saw him on the first flood’s third night, though she had not thought of him since the trial began. He had been on the roof of a storage shed with six others while the eastern drain choked on timber. Ilyra had reached the shed by wading through water that tugged at her knees. The pump assembly had been jammed. The relief lever was behind the shed, beneath a fallen beam.

There had been one minute, perhaps less.

She had chosen the lever.

The beam had shifted. The shed roof had collapsed.

Six people had gone under. Corin had not been among the three pulled from the water.

At the time she had written: six lost, pressure reduced, east line preserved.

She had written the numbers because the numbers were what the next operator needed.

Now the clerk said his name, and the chamber expected it to become one unit in the number 4,812.

“Stop,” Ilyra said.

The clerk did not.

“Corin Voss,” she repeated. “He was in the ropewalk sheds. He should be listed there.”

Pell turned. “The witness is not permitted to amend the register.”

“He was not an unlocated casualty. He was known to me.”

“Many of the deceased were known to someone.”

“I know the circumstances.”

“Then you may provide them to the inquiry staff.”

“There is no inquiry.”

“There will be no inquiry if you continue to confuse this proceeding with one.”

The clerk moved on.

Ilyra said, “Sura Pell. Aven Dorr. Tavin Or.”

The names came faster now, each one striking some hidden surface in her.

Sura had been trapped behind the old filter room. She had shouted through the maintenance tube while Ilyra worked the gate. Aven had been one of the workers who answered. Tavin had carried a child to the pump station, then returned for his wife.

The court had not asked what they had been doing. It had not asked which doors were sealed, which channels were blocked, who had removed the valves, or why the storage fields had filled with people beneath a sky the official maps marked empty.

It asked only whether Ilyra had opened the gate.

She had.

The clerk reached the final page.

“Four thousand eight hundred and twelve confirmed deceased,” he said again.

Lysa’s account hung behind the number like a painted backdrop: the yellow shirt, the single boot, the hand released.

Ilyra looked toward Senn.

His face was rigid, but his eyes were wet.

“Your sister told the truth,” she said quietly.

He did not answer.

“She did not see everything.”

His grip tightened on the baton.

“No one does,” he said.

The words were almost lost beneath the clerk’s voice.

Ilyra turned back toward the bench. “That is what the court is doing. Treating one person’s sight as the whole flood.”

Pell leaned toward the speaking tube. “The accused appears determined to make a philosophy of her guilt.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “I am trying to name it accurately.”

“Your guilt requires no further naming.”

“It does if you are using it to hide the people who made the conditions.”

The guards moved before he ordered them. Senn caught her arm. Maret seized the other.

Ilyra did not resist. The chain between her wrists swung once and struck the rail.

In that small metallic sound she remembered the child’s fingers slipping from hers.

Not a calculation. Not a pressure line. Not a district.

A hand.

She had saved the lower wall. She had saved the three children crossing the roof. She had killed two adults when the drainage run opened. She had allowed the western camps to flood when she eased the gate back from red. She had held the key. She had released the child.

Each statement was true.

None of them could carry the others.

Pell announced that the witness schedule would continue after the midday recess. The lenses remained fixed on Ilyra as the guards led her from the chamber.

Behind her, the clerk began reading the names again, slower this time, as if the dead had become a punishment that required savoring.

At the side door, Senn’s sister stood waiting in the corridor.

Lysa did not speak to Ilyra. She looked at Senn instead.

He stopped.

For one moment brother and sister faced each other beneath the Hall’s dim lamps, while water knocked somewhere below the stones.

Then Lysa said, “I told them what I saw.”

“I know,” Senn answered.

“They kept saying it was all of it.”

His eyes moved to Ilyra, and his expression held no forgiveness, but no simple hatred either.

“I know,” he said again.

The guards pulled Ilyra onward.

At the threshold she heard Lysa call after them, not to her, but to the clerk inside the chamber.

“There are more names.”

The door closed before anyone answered.

chapters.name: The Verdict Before Judgment
chapters.content:
## The Verdict Before Judgment

The final day began with the sounding of the block.

Three strikes traveled through the Hall of Civic Judgment and reached the Flood Cells as vibrations in the stone. Ilyra felt them through the cot frame.

The first meant the court was convened.

The second meant the lenses were awake.

The third meant the city was listening.

She had been awake for hours. At dawn, seven knocks had come from beneath the floor, followed by silence. The sound might have been a trapped person. It might have been a pipe contracting in the cold. She had assigned both possibilities a measure of likelihood and hated herself for doing so.

Maret opened the cell door. Senn waited behind her, his expression shut.

“You are wanted upstairs,” Maret said.

“Has the clerk corrected the names?”

“No.”

“Has Nera Vale been restored to the register?”

“No.”

“Have they searched the storage fields?”

Senn’s jaw tightened. “Walk.”

They led her through the lower passage. Water gleamed between the stones, carrying the smell of iron and mold. At the stair, the guards took her elbows. Above them, the Hall trembled with voices and machinery. The broadcast lenses were turning toward the courtroom.

The doors opened.

The chamber was packed. Spectators wore white-and-bronze ribbons for the Feast of Renewal. Some had painted waves on their faces. Others wore small black masks shaped like Ilyra’s, the mouth stretched into a scream. A child in the front gallery held a sweetcake molded into a woman beneath a curl of blue sugar.

Magistrate Pell sat beneath the civic seal. Three black lenses adjusted behind him with small mechanical clicks.

Ilyra was placed at the central table and chained to its metal eyelet. The prosecutor’s desk was covered with documents that had already been made harmless.

Pell struck the sounding block.

“On the forty-first day since the destruction of the eastern districts,” he said, “the civic court resumes for final address and judgment in the matter of Ilyra Voss, formerly licensed engineer of the Civic Water Office.”

Formerly.

The word arrived cleanly.

Pell turned toward the galleries. “The accused stands charged with unlawful seizure of the North Barrage, theft and fraudulent use of a civic seal, destruction of protected infrastructure, deliberate release of floodwater into inhabited districts, incitement against the hereditary civic order, and the deaths of four thousand eight hundred and twelve confirmed citizens.”

The number moved through the room like a cold draft.

Pell rose.

“The prosecution will not ask this court to understand the river. The river has been made into a screen behind which the accused hopes to hide.”

He held up one of the altered reports.

“She wishes to replace the simple fact of her act with technical language. She wishes to suggest that because she possesses specialized knowledge, she possesses specialized innocence.”

A murmur of approval came from the benches.

“She entered the North Barrage under false authority. She disabled surveillance relays. She opened a sealed gate. She did not stumble into disaster. She prepared.”

The bronze seal was displayed in a glass case. Its edges gleamed beneath the lamps.

“She stole this object. She forged the Governor’s authorization. She selected the hour of the Feast, when the Council and many citizens would be gathered above the central channel. She knew water does not distinguish between a ministry and a tenement.”

He paused.

“Yet she opened it.”

Ilyra kept her hands flat on the table. The wood was warm beneath her palms.

Pell continued. “Her supporters say she acted to save the Low Quarter. Let us examine that claim. If her aim was rescue, why choose the Feast? Why forge an order in the Governor’s name? Why disable the lenses? Why act while officials stood beneath the ceremonial canopy?”

Ilyra felt the old argument rise inside her, precise and ordered.

She had not known the western valves were gone. She had not known the storage fields were occupied. She had known the eastern wall would fail. She had known the Council intended to sacrifice the Low Quarter.

She had also wanted the governors to see the water.

Pell knew enough to use that.

“She wanted them afraid,” he said. “She wanted the Crown to feel what the lower districts had felt. She wanted to teach a lesson. The flood was not an accident that followed a rescue attempt. The flood was the lesson.”

The galleries answered with applause.

Ilyra remembered the ceremonial platform tilting beneath the white canopy. Officials scrambling over one another. The shameful satisfaction that had moved through her when the powerful finally looked helpless.

Pell raised another report.

“The accused insists her warnings were suppressed. What has she offered this court? A strip of oilskin without a date. A map with no authenticated origin. Memories of conversations no surviving witness confirms. She claims the Council changed the surveys and Master Engineer Arce concealed valves. Claims, all of them.”

His voice hardened.

“Not evidence. Claims made by a woman who had already decided that every superior was her enemy.”

Arce’s chair stood empty among the civic officials. So did Governor Dault’s. A white ribbon crossed the back of Dault’s chair.

“Those who might answer her accusations are not on trial,” Pell said. “The dead cannot defend themselves from the living, and the absent cannot be compelled to answer every fantasy produced after a catastrophe.”

Fantasy.

The word had appeared in the altered warning beside the wrong hydraulic table and false numbering. Ilyra had recognized Arce’s phrasing, though the report carried no signature.

Pell moved closer to the center of the chamber.

“Her defenders speak of hereditary districts. Of restricted education, ration ledgers, unequal walls, and the neglect of the Low Quarter. Perhaps they believe those things. Perhaps some are true in a broader political sense. But grievance is not a license to drown a city.”

The word *city* settled over the chamber. It meant the Crown, the Merchant terraces, the Hall, and whatever else the court wished to preserve. It did not mean the storage fields, the ropewalk, or the families whose names were absent from the register.

“She was not denied education,” Pell said. “She entered the Civic Water Office. She was given instruments and instruction. She rose farther than any engineer from her district in two generations.”

A merchant woman called, “And still she wanted more.”

Laughter followed.

Ilyra remembered Arce tapping her first flood model with his ring.

*Dockside resentment is not a hydraulic principle, Voss.*

She had been seventeen. Tomas had still been alive. He had brought her half a heel of bread and asked whether the Crown could be persuaded to build a wall on their side.

She had answered, “Walls are calculations.”

Pell’s voice drew her back.

“Her education did not cure her resentment. It refined it. Her grievance became technical. Her hatred learned to wear a professional coat.”

The phrase pleased the room. Several spectators repeated it.

“The accused’s anger is not irrelevant,” Pell said. “It reveals motive. She did not merely fear a flood. She hated the people who governed the water. She believed her suffering made her judgment superior to law.”

Lysa Renn sat in the survivors’ gallery, her broken arm held close. Pell turned toward her.

“Lysa Renn saw the accused choose the key over a child. The accused may dress that choice in calculations, but there was a child. There was a hand. The accused released it.”

Lysa did not look at Ilyra.

“The accused tells us she chose between lives,” Pell said. “That is meant to make murder resemble burden. But there is a difference between a person forced to choose in an emergency and a person who creates the emergency, then claims authority over every life within it.”

Ilyra saw the yellow sleep shirt and one red boot. She felt the child’s fingers slip from hers as she kept the valve key.

She had saved people with that key.

She had killed people with the decision to keep it.

Both were true. Neither made the child less dead.

Pell returned to his desk.

“The prosecution has demonstrated that Ilyra Voss took the seal, forged authority, entered the barrage, and opened the gate. We have demonstrated that she knew water would move into inhabited districts. We have demonstrated that she expressed hatred for those gathered above her. We have demonstrated that, after the first failures, she continued to operate the controls, directing water toward one population rather than another.”

That last part was true enough to hurt.

“Her supporters call this courage,” Pell said. “It is not courage to appoint oneself judge over thousands. It is not justice to make a private calculation and impose its result upon a population that has not consented. It is vengeance wearing the mask of necessity.”

The word entered her more deeply than *murder*.

Because it was not wholly false.

She had chosen the Feast partly because the governors would be there. She had imagined their fear. She had wanted the people who signed sacrifice orders to learn that walls could fail.

Pell lifted his gaze to the lenses.

“Veyr has suffered because one woman believed her intelligence placed her above the law. She believed her district’s pain made her pure. She believed that if the city would not obey her warning, she had the right to force the city to listen.”

His final words softened.

“Let the record show that she was heard. Let it also show that she chose to make herself heard through the deaths of four thousand eight hundred and twelve people.”

Silence followed.

Ilyra felt an answer forming.

She could stand and name Dault’s barge, Arce’s missing valves, the reservoir-transfer orders, the private retaining wall, and the occupied fields. She could say the Council had chosen the flood’s victims before she entered the barrage. She could name Corin Voss, Sura Pell, Aven Dorr, Tavin Or, and the children without ration marks. She could make the truth too large for the court to contain.

For one breath, she imagined it. Pell interrupting. The lenses tightening around her face. The city hearing only the loudest sentence and seeing only her anger.

They would call it a final outburst. A confession disguised as accusation. They would print the most violent words beneath her mask. The court did not fear truth. It knew how to arrange truth.

The chief clerk rose. “The accused may offer final address.”

A thousand faces turned toward her. The child with the sweetcake had stopped eating.

Ilyra stood as far as the chain allowed.

“My name is Ilyra Voss,” she said.

Her voice carried through the Hall.

“I opened the North Barrage. I stole the seal. I entered under a false authorization. I knew water would move through districts where people lived.”

The clerk dipped his pen.

“I made calculations. Some saved lives. Some killed people. I do not know the names of everyone who died because of my decisions. The court does not know them either.”

A restless murmur rose.

“I warned the Council that the eastern embankment was being made to carry pressure meant for other channels. Those warnings were altered or dismissed. The western valves were removed. The storage fields were occupied. Governor Dault left by private barge. Master Engineer Arce knew—”

Pell struck the sounding block.

“Withdraw the inadmissible allegations.”

Ilyra continued. “The court has chosen not to investigate—”

“Withdraw them.”

The lenses shifted toward Pell, then toward her. She saw the ending they wanted: her voice raised, his hand commanding, the chamber restored to order.

If she fought now, they would have their ending.

She stopped.

Not because he had silenced her. Because she would not give him the shape of her truth.

“I am responsible for what I did,” she said. “That responsibility does not become the Council’s innocence.”

Pell’s expression tightened. The sentence would not settle into confession or defiance.

“Nothing further,” Ilyra said, and sat.

The judges withdrew for less than a minute.

There was no consultation visible behind the partition. No argument. The verdict had been written before the first witness entered, perhaps before Ilyra was brought to the Hall. The recess existed so the law could imitate thought.

When the judges returned, the chief judge read from a prepared sheet.

“On the charges of unlawful seizure of the North Barrage, theft and fraudulent use of a civic seal, destruction of protected infrastructure, deliberate release of floodwater into inhabited districts, incitement against the hereditary civic order, and causing the deaths of four thousand eight hundred and twelve confirmed citizens, this court finds the accused guilty.”

The word entered her like cold water.

Applause broke across the chamber. Some spectators stood. Others began chanting.

“Barrage Butcher.”

The chant gathered strength.

“Barrage Butcher. Barrage Butcher.”

Senn stood near the side door, looking at the floor. Maret watched the crowd instead of Ilyra. The child held the half-eaten cake in both hands.

The judge continued.

“In recognition of the exceptional scale of the offense, the calculated abuse of civic knowledge, and the accused’s refusal to express adequate contrition, the court sentences Ilyra Voss to the Ember Descent.”

The chant became louder.

“The sentence shall be carried out publicly on the next Feast of Renewal, at the third hour, upon the ceremonial platform of the Hall of Civic Judgment. The accused shall remain confined beneath this Hall until that date. Her final statement, if any, may be transmitted through the civic lens network at the discretion of the magistrate.”

At Pell’s discretion.

The judge lifted the seal.

“May water receive what water has been made to bear.”

The sounding block fell.

Once.

The guards unfastened Ilyra from the table. Senn took her left arm; Maret took the right. As they led her toward the lower stair, she looked at the empty chairs reserved for Arce and Dault.

Then the doors closed, and the Hall carried the city’s applause down after her.

chapters.name: Ember Descent
chapters.content:
## Ember Descent

On the morning the city began selling her death, Ilyra woke before the bells.

The Flood Cells had no windows, but the Hall’s waking noises traveled through the walls: boilers shuddering, gates opening, feet crossing the upper galleries. Somewhere above, a bucket struck stone. A lock turned, then another. The building came awake by degrees, as if reluctant to remember what it housed beneath its foundations.

Ilyra lay still until she could separate the Hall from her body.

Four breaths to the ceiling.

Sixteen finger-widths from her shoulder to the wall.

A drain beneath the cot, iron-rimmed and clogged with gray sediment.

A seam in the nearest brick, three fingers long.

She counted because these things belonged to her. A wall remained a wall whether Pell called it a chamber or a cell. A drain remained blocked whether the Hall intended to keep her alive until the Feast or had merely forgotten it. Measurements did not flatter or accuse themselves when repeated before an audience.

The first bell struck above.

The second answered from the river towers.

On the third, a murmur rose through the stone.

The city had gathered.

An announcer’s voice entered the cell through the civic tubes, polished and resonant, with the solemn cadence reserved for funerals, coronations, and punishments.

“Citizens of Veyr, on this Feast of Renewal, witness the restoration of rightful order. Today, at the third hour, the condemned Ilyra Voss will undergo the Ember Descent. Let all districts remember: no hand may seize the city’s lifeblood without consequence. No private grievance may become a public flood.”

A pause, precisely measured.

“The woman who weaponized water will be returned to water.”

The voice was followed by a swell of orchestral strings. Even beneath the Hall, Ilyra heard the crowd answer.

She sat up.

Her body had become an inventory of small injuries. The left wrist ached where the restraint had rubbed it raw. Her right knee stiffened in the cold. There was a tender place at the back of her skull from the trial chamber floor, where a guard had pressed her down after she refused to leave the witness stand.

She moved each joint once, testing it.

The door opened. Senn stood outside with Maret behind him. Both wore Hall security blue. Maret had fastened a white cloth at her throat, a Feast color. Senn’s collar was crooked, and his eyes looked as if he had slept in a chair.

“Stand,” Senn said.

“I am standing.”

“You are sitting.”

“I’m about to stand.”

His face suggested that he wanted to dispute the distinction and had decided it was not worth the effort. He stepped inside and unlocked her ankle chain. The iron had left a dark crescent above her heel.

Maret carried a shallow basin covered by a lid. Steam curled from beneath it.

“Your washing water,” she said.

“Purification,” Senn corrected.

Ilyra looked at him. “You object to my terminology now?”

“I object to making the morning longer.”

He reattached a shorter length of chain between her wrists. The links were warm from his hand.

Maret set down the basin and lifted the lid.

The water smelled of salt, bitter herbs, and metal.

“Put your hands in,” Maret said.

“Why?”

“It is the ritual.”

“Which part of the ritual?”

Maret glanced at Senn. “The hands are washed so the condemned enters without the means of further harm.”

Ilyra looked at her bound wrists.

“Then the chains are decorative?”

Maret’s mouth tightened. “Hands in the basin.”

Ilyra placed them beneath the surface.

Heat closed over her fingers. For an instant the water reflected her face in pieces: one eye, the bridge of her nose, a mouth too thin to be forgiven. The basin trembled against the floor as someone passed in the corridor.

Then the water became the pump station.

Black water moved beneath the floor. The drainage assembly resisted her hand. Thirty-seven charcoal marks climbed the wall. Someone behind her said, *There’s someone under the west intake.*

She had answered, *The intake cannot be opened until the pressure falls.*

*Someone is under it.*

She had made the next mark.

The heat reached her knuckles. In the basin’s shining surface, a child’s red boot floated past. A yellow sleep shirt lifted and vanished.

Ilyra pulled her hands free.

Maret caught her elbows. “What happened?”

“Nothing.”

Senn stared at the water. “Did you hear something?”

“No.”

“You went pale.”

“I am about to be boiled in front of thirty thousand people. Pale is not a technical anomaly.”

Maret took a cloth and dried Ilyra’s hands. Her touch was brisk but not rough.

The cell filled with steam. Nera’s voice seemed to come through it, not memory and not entirely present.

*There are people below us.*

“I told you what the survey showed,” Ilyra had said.

*You knew the survey was old.*

“I knew it had been altered.”

*And you didn’t tell me.*

Nera had not sounded angry then. Only frightened. That was worse. Anger could be answered. Fear remained after every answer had failed.

Maret folded the cloth.

“Move,” Senn said.

They led her into the corridor.

The Hall had been decorated overnight. White streamers hung between the lamps, embroidered with bronze waves. Fresh placards marked the walls:

ORDER IS MERCY.

WATER REMEMBERS.

THE CITY ENDURES.

Wax had been poured over the cracks in the flagstones, but not evenly. Ilyra noticed a dark line of damp crossing the mortar near the stairwell.

“Water under the Hall,” she said.

Senn did not look down. “Keep walking.”

“The foundation drainage is backing up.”

“Keep walking.”

“If the river has risen enough to reach this level—”

“You have had forty-one days to discuss water.”

Maret looked toward the ceiling. “Senn.”

“What?”

“Let her walk.”

The first surveillance lens turned toward Ilyra before she reached the stairs. Its black glass reflected a chained woman, damp-haired, flanked by guards. A red indicator blinked. Somewhere, an operator was announcing her position.

The stairwell opened into the public concourse.

People crowded the balconies and stairwells. Vendors moved among them with trays of cakes shaped like waves, red icing pooled in the centers. Children wore paper masks with long teeth. Some masks showed her crowned with sluice gates. Others gave her a knife.

A woman unfolded a betting slip while leaning over the rail.

“Three to one she screams before the second gate,” she said.

“Too generous,” a man replied. “I’ve heard she doesn’t feel pain properly.”

“She feels it. That’s the point.”

“Five coppers says she begs.”

“Begging is only worth two. The judges have already promised a slow descent.”

A vendor called, “Barrage Butcher cakes! Two for a copper! Buy the condemned a last sweet!”

The woman with the betting slip laughed and bought three.

Ilyra kept walking.

The crowd saw her and broke into a chant.

“Bar-rage Butcher. Bar-rage Butcher.”

It did not sound like hatred at first. It sounded like a song learned by children. The words rose and fell together, an occupation for mouths. Above the concourse, a placard displayed the ticket prices: lower platforms one silver, upper galleries three, private viewing boxes ten. Beside it, a smaller notice promised a commemorative medal for all patrons who remained until the final bell.

The city’s appetite had been carefully accounted for.

At the foot of the stairs, a boy pulled the strings of a wooden figure until its arms jerked downward. The figure wore a black coat and held a crooked lever. The crowd laughed.

His mother noticed Ilyra looking.

“Show her the good side,” she said.

The boy turned the puppet. Its painted face had Ilyra’s mouth and no eyes.

Ilyra walked on.

They brought her into a preparation room lined with white tile. Copper pipes along one wall gave off constant heat. The air smelled of lye, steam, and the faint mineral odor of river mud.

On a table lay a pale linen robe, a bronze collar, and thin slippers with red soles.

A clerk stood beside them, holding a slate. “Remove the prison garments.”

“I can do that myself.”

“Procedure requires assistance.”

“Procedure requires how many witnesses?”

The clerk blinked. “Two.”

“There are three.”

He looked at the ceiling lens.

“The lens is not a person,” Senn said.

“It is still recording.”

“Arms out,” Maret said.

Ilyra lifted them. The prison dress was pulled away, and the room’s heat touched her skin. She saw herself reflected in the tile: narrow shoulders, bruises yellowing along her ribs, the old pale scar where Tomas had cut her while sharpening a ration-knife and then cried because she bled.

Maret took the linen robe.

Ilyra lifted it first. “The seams are designed to tear.”

The clerk frowned. “It is ceremonial.”

“The sides are reinforced. The shoulders aren’t. The lower hem is weighted.”

“For dignity,” he said.

“For a cleaner fall.”

Maret took it from him. “Arms up.”

Ilyra let her pull the robe over her head and fasten the collar. Bronze threads formed descending lines down the front, widening at the hem like water spreading through a street.

“Symbolic?” Ilyra asked.

“The robe represents surrender to the civic element,” Maret said.

“Water.”

Maret’s hand paused at the collar. “You are permitted to call it that.”

“The official announcement called it water.”

“The official announcement says many things.”

Ilyra watched Maret fasten the final clasp. Her fingers trembled once, then steadied.

“Your child,” Ilyra said.

Maret’s hand stopped.

Senn looked toward the door.

“Still in Sable Ward?” Ilyra asked.

“You don’t know that,” Maret said.

“You have mud on your left boot. Not Hall mud. Fine black foundry silt. Sable Ward’s lower streets are flooding. You have been trying to get there.”

Maret’s face changed—not into fear, but into the anger of someone whose private calculation had been exposed.

“You read too much into dirt.”

“Dirt is usually honest.”

Senn stepped between them. “Enough.”

Ilyra looked at her reflection. The collar hid the marks left by the restraints. The city would see no evidence that she had spent forty-one days beneath the Hall, fed through a slot and called lawfully confined.

“Does she have a name?” Ilyra asked.

Maret’s hand went still.

Senn looked toward the floor.

“Enough,” Maret said.

Ilyra thought of Lysa on the ruined roof, one red boot below a yellow sleep shirt. The child’s hand had been small and hot in hers. Behind them, the eastern gauge had crossed red. The valve key had cut into Ilyra’s palm.

She had calculated the distance.

She had chosen the key.

Her fingers had opened.

The mirror gave her back the face of someone who had made the choice and would continue making it long after everyone else found a word for it.

The door opened.

Magistrate Oren Pell entered in a plain gray coat, followed by two assistants carrying tablets and a case of lenses. He inspected the robe as though she were an exhibit finally arranged correctly.

“Did she cooperate with the washing?” he asked.

“She placed her hands in the basin,” Maret said.

“Good.”

“I did not consent to purification,” Ilyra said.

Pell looked at her. “No one asked you to consent.”

“Then why call it cleansing?”

“Because citizens understand symbols better than procedures.”

“Do they understand that the descent uses heated water?”

“They understand that you used water to kill.”

“I opened a barrage.”

“You directed water into inhabited districts.”

“After the Council removed the western valves and occupied the storage fields.”

Pell lifted a hand. The clerk lowered his eyes. Maret turned toward the wall.

“You persist in confusing accusation with exoneration,” Pell said.

“I persist in identifying other hands.”

“Today you are expected to speak only of your own.”

He moved closer. His hair was carefully combed, and the cuffs of his coat were unmarked. There was no mud on him.

“Do you know how many tickets have been sold?”

“No.”

“Thirty-two thousand in the first hour. The upper galleries are full. Additional platforms have been erected along the river. Civic lenses will relay the descent to every district.”

“You are proud of that.”

“I am informing you.”

“People are buying access to a killing.”

“People are attending a civic judgment.”

“They are betting on whether I scream.”

“Some people wager on weather, crop yields, bridge collapses. It does not mean they wish for rain, famine, or failure.”

“They buy cake shaped like my death.”

“Food is not ideology.”

“It is when you sell it beside the execution notices.”

Pell’s gaze flicked toward the lens.

“You have always mistaken arrangement for intention,” he said.

“No. I have mistaken nothing.”

“Your execution can end the matter, Ilyra. But there are still questions about the Council, the barrage, and whether other people knew what you intended. The galleries will be watching for a confession. Give them one, and the punishment will be easier.”

“For whom?”

“For everyone.”

“Meaning the Council.”

“Meaning the families of the dead.”

“Which families?”

His eyes hardened.

“The ones who deserve an answer.”

“Will you give them the missing names?”

“The number has been certified.”

“By whom?”

“By the Hall.”

“The Hall did not search the storage fields.”

“It searched all designated civic areas.”

“The fields were occupied.”

“They were designated unoccupied.”

“That is not a description of the people who lived there.”

“It is the legal condition of the land.”

“And if the law calls them empty?”

“Then your moral objections remain irrelevant to the count.”

Pell sighed, as though she had failed a basic exercise.

“A confession will give meaning to the dead.”

“No. It will give you a clean ending.”

“Is that not mercy?”

“Not if everyone else disappears from it.”

He nodded to an assistant, who raised a tablet. On its surface appeared the approved statement:

I, Ilyra Voss, acted alone.

The letters were large enough for a civic lens to capture. Beneath them waited further lines: I rejected lawful correction. I chose destruction. I regret the suffering caused by my private grievance.

She could say it. The crowd would quiet. Pell’s shoulders would ease. The empty chairs reserved for Arce and Dault would remain empty, and their absence would become proof of nothing.

One woman. One seal. One gate. One sentence.

A clean lever.

Behind her eyes, Nera called through the maintenance tube.

*You told us to climb.*

Ilyra had not known whether the omitted service shaft still existed. She had known only that the current plans erased it. She had sent them upward because opening the door might flood the chamber.

*You told us to climb, and then you left.*

She had left. She had turned the western gate and listened to the pressure change.

The memory offered no verdict. It held only the fact of her turning away.

Ilyra looked at the tablet.

“I will not say I acted alone.”

Pell’s disappointment was almost paternal.

“Then you will make the descent harder.”

“For me?”

“For the people watching.”

“I am not responsible for their appetite.”

“No,” he said. “You are responsible for feeding it.”

He handed the tablet back.

At the door, Senn’s gaze met hers in the mirror. There was no forgiveness in it. But there was a hesitation, slight as the pause before a gate moved.

Pell turned to leave.

“Magistrate,” Ilyra said.

He stopped.

“If I confess, will you search the storage fields?”

“No.”

“Correct the register?”

“No.”

“Restore Nera Vale’s name?”

He did not answer.

“Will you tell them Governor Dault left by private barge?”

Pell’s silence became an answer.

“Will you ask Arce why the western valves were removed?”

“You have been given every opportunity to make yourself less guilty.”

“I have been given an opportunity to make everyone else less visible.”

Pell faced her fully.

“You still think truth is a device you can operate.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “I think you are afraid of what happens when other people operate it.”

For the first time that morning, his composure slipped. Not much. A tightened jaw. A breath held too long.

Then he smiled.

“Remember this when the water rises. The city will not hear your explanations.”

“The city hears what the lenses are told to carry.”

“And the lenses are mine.”

The statement hung between them, more honest than anything he had said in court.

Steam from the ceremonial platform drifted into the room, carrying the smell of heated metal and river water. Beyond Pell, the Hall thundered with voices. Somewhere above, the announcer began describing the descent: the purified basin, the mirrored viewing galleries, the regulated temperature, the civic safeguards. It was not to be called burning. It was not to be called drowning. It was to be called return.

The city would watch her descend. It would call the water cleansing and sell sweetcakes and wagers, turning her death into something small enough to carry home. It would watch because watching allowed everyone to believe the flood had begun and ended with her.

She had wanted control of the gates.

Now they wanted control of the story.

Pell opened the door.

“Ready,” he said.

Ilyra lifted her chained hands. The last drops from the washing basin fell from her fingers to the tile.

One.

Two.

Three.

She counted until the door closed behind them, and then she walked toward the water.

chapters.name: The Survivor’s Daughter
chapters.content:
The woman who came to see Ilyra wore mourning without having been invited to mourn.

Her dress was black, but not the cheap black of the Low Quarter, which faded green at the seams after a season of washing. This cloth held the light in a dense, expensive sheen. A narrow silver chain circled her throat. At its end hung a seal, turned inward against her skin.

Ilyra noticed the seal before she noticed the woman’s face.

The guard unlocked the outer grille and stood aside. “You have twelve minutes.”

“Pell gave me twenty,” the woman said.

“Senn gave you twelve.”

The woman glanced at him. She had pale gray eyes, the same color as the river beneath winter ice. “Then I’m grateful to Magistrate Pell for his generosity.”

Senn did not smile. Maret, stationed behind him, did.

“Researcher?” Maret asked.

“That is what I told them.”

“Researching what?”

“The flood.”

Maret’s smile widened. “You’re late. Everyone in Veyr has already decided what happened.”

“Then I suppose I’m researching why they decided it so quickly.”

Senn pushed the grille open. The woman entered, and the door shut behind her with a thickness that seemed excessive for a visitor. The bolts settled one after another.

Ilyra remained seated on the edge of the cot. The execution robe had been removed from her for the visit, but the salt and herbs still clung to her skin. Her hands were unchained only because Pell wanted her able to make a final statement. The permission felt less like mercy than an instrument left within reach.

The woman stopped three paces away.

“I am Elian Dault,” she said.

Maret’s amusement disappeared.

Senn’s hand moved to the baton at his belt. Not drawing it. Remembering it was there.

Ilyra looked at the silver seal again. “Governor Dault’s daughter.”

“His eldest.”

“The surviving governor.”

“Yes.”

The title hung between them, polished and intolerable.

Elian’s family name had appeared in the courtroom every day without Elian herself. Governor Arven Dault had been described as absent due to illness, then as engaged in relief coordination, then as unavailable for testimony on grounds of civic security. His chair had stood empty beneath a white ribbon. Ilyra had watched the ribbon move whenever the Hall’s ventilation shifted and had thought of the governor’s private barge cutting through the flood.

She had not known he had a daughter.

“Have you come to see the monster before the descent?” Ilyra asked.

“No.”

“To confirm that I have horns?”

“I already know what you look like.”

“From the broadsheets?”

“From a drawing commissioned by my father’s office.”

That answer was too exact to be casual. Ilyra felt the first small alteration in the room, the way pressure changed before a gate opened.

Elian removed a leather folder from beneath her cloak. She did not offer it. The folder was tied with blue cord and bore no seal.

“I told Pell I wanted to study the language used in flood proceedings,” she said. “How the city turns catastrophe into a criminal narrative. He thought this demonstrated intellectual seriousness.”

“Pell thinks anything that can be placed in a report demonstrates seriousness.”

“He also thinks I am harmless.”

“Are you?”

“No.”

The answer landed without drama. Elian sat on the single chair bolted to the floor. It had been placed there for visitors who might otherwise stand too close to prisoners.

Ilyra looked toward the observation slit. The lens above it had been polished. A dark circle watched from the brass housing.

“Is he listening?”

“Pell?” Elian asked.

“Who else?”

“Almost certainly.”

“Then you should be careful.”

“I have been careful for six months.”

“That is not what I said.”

Elian’s expression tightened. “You prefer that I speak plainly?”

“I prefer that people stop pretending the room has no walls.”

“Then plainly: yes, Pell is listening. Yes, I know that. And yes, I came because I need information you possess.”

There it was. Not sympathy. Not curiosity. Need.

Ilyra folded her hands over her knees. “You have twelve minutes.”

“I have records.”

“Everyone has records. The city is made of them.”

“Not these.”

Elian untied the folder. Inside were sheets of thin archival paper, some fresh and white, others browned at the edges. She laid the first on her lap.

Ilyra recognized the format before she could read it: Council water memoranda, copied in the narrow vertical hand of the Governor’s secretariat. The paper smelled faintly of dust and iron gall.

“Where did you get those?”

“From a private archive beneath the Dault residence.”

“Your father’s archive?”

“My father’s house. The distinction matters.”

“Does it?”

“It does to me.”

Elian turned the first page so Ilyra could see. A line of writing had been marked in red.

CROWN RETAINING WALL: REINFORCEMENT TO PROCEED WITHOUT DIVERSION.

Below it, in another hand:

EASTERN EMBANKMENT FAILURE ACCEPTABLE IF PRESSURE IS REDIRECTED BELOW THE LABOR DISTRICTS. STORAGE FIELDS TO BE CLEARED OF INVENTORY BY SECOND HOUR.

Ilyra did not move.

The cell’s drain clicked as a bead of water slipped through its clogged grate.

“What does ‘below the labor districts’ mean?” Elian asked.

“You know what it means.”

“I want to hear you say it.”

“It means the Low Quarter.”

“Not exactly. The Low Quarter begins above the old ropewalks. This line refers to the lower labor districts, including the storage fields and the eastern foundries.”

“Where people lived.”

“Yes.”

Elian watched her carefully. “The Council marked the fields unoccupied.”

“The Council marked them convenient.”

“That is not the same as proof.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “It is the reason proof disappears.”

Elian placed a second page over the first. It bore a schedule divided into columns: transfer pressure, reservoir volume, wall priority, civilian clearance. Several names had been crossed out. One remained legible.

A. Dault.

At the bottom, a handwritten note read: Platform demonstration to continue as planned. Public confidence requires visible control.

Ilyra felt the old chamber return around her—not this cell, but the North Barrage, the wet iron beneath her palms, the roar through the central sluice. She saw the white canopy above the ceremonial platform, the ministers in their bright coats, merchants leaning forward to admire the machinery. She remembered thinking that, for once, they would stand where the city’s pressure gathered.

Elian’s fingers pressed the page flat. “My father knew.”

“Your father signed?”

“Not this one.”

“Then you don’t know.”

“I know his private evacuation route was opened at the same hour.”

The page blurred for an instant.

Ilyra had seen the barge in memory so many times that it had become an argument rather than an object: a black hull sliding beyond the Crown retaining wall, a lantern under its stern, Governor Dault’s relief insignia painted in white. Pell had called it an unverified sighting. The official record said Dault had remained at the platform coordinating rescue.

“You found the route,” Ilyra said.

“I found the orders to prepare it. I found the water-depth reports from the channel beneath the old conservatory. I found a list of passengers.”

“His Council.”

“His wife. My younger brothers. Two ministers. The Master Engineer’s wife and son.”

“Arce’s family.”

“Yes.”

“Was Arce on the barge?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because he stayed behind long enough to tell the Hall that the Crown wall had held.”

Ilyra thought of the injured man on the roof, asking first about the wall. She had believed the question was delirium. Perhaps it had been loyalty. Perhaps it had been the only fact that still mattered to him.

“And your family?” Ilyra asked.

Elian’s face did not change, but the hand holding the page trembled once.

“They were on the ceremonial platform.”

The words arrived with no visible wound. That made them worse.

“Your father evacuated them?”

“He evacuated the people he considered worth saving.”

“Your brothers were there?”

“My mother insisted on remaining. She believed the platform was secure. My brothers were eleven and fourteen. My sister was seven.”

Ilyra lowered her eyes.

The platform had tilted. The canopy had torn loose. People had fallen against one another in the crush toward the stairs. She remembered a boy in a red sash clinging to a minister’s sleeve, a woman screaming that the river had changed direction, the hard bright face of Governor Dault as he turned toward the western steps.

She had wanted him to understand fear.

She had wanted all of them to understand it.

“I saw them,” Ilyra said.

Elian’s breath stopped, barely.

“Did you?”

“Not individually. I saw the crowd. I saw people trapped against the rail. When the western gate opened, the platform shifted.”

“You saw them.”

“I saw the platform.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No.” Ilyra looked up. “It is the answer I have.”

Elian studied her with open dislike. It was cleaner than the fascination Maret had shown, and more honest than Pell’s outrage.

“Did you choose the Feast because my father would be there?”

“I chose it because the Council would be gathered.”

“That was not my question.”

“It was part of the reason.”

“Was it the reason?”

Ilyra wanted to say no. The word rose easily, already shaped.

Instead she said, “I wanted them to see the system fail.”

Elian’s mouth tightened.

“I wanted the people who had designed the channels to stand beside them when the channels opened. I told myself their presence would give me leverage. It also gave me satisfaction.”

“Thank you.”

“For what?”

“For not making me call you a liar.”

Ilyra looked again at the pages. The ink seemed darker than the blood memory beneath it.

“Your family died because I opened the barrage,” she said.

“My family died because you opened the barrage, because the Council had altered the barrage, because my father knew the danger and chose a demonstration, and because the platform had been built over a channel no one intended to discuss. Those are not interchangeable truths.”

“I did not say they were.”

“You have spent your entire trial trying to make them stand beside one another until no one can tell which one belongs to you.”

The accusation struck precisely because it resembled one Ilyra had made against herself.

She rose. The cell was too narrow for the movement to be graceful. Her shoulder brushed the wall, and wax flaked from a sealed crack.

“I am not asking to be forgiven,” she said.

“No. You are asking to be understood.”

“Understanding is useful.”

“To whom?”

“To anyone who intends to prevent another flood.”

Elian stood as well, keeping the chair between them. “You still believe you are the person who should decide what happens next.”

“I am the person who knows the barrage.”

“You knew it before.”

“I knew enough to warn them.”

“You knew enough to act.”

“I acted because they would not.”

“And people died.”

“Yes.”

The answer unsettled Elian more than denial might have. She looked toward the lens.

“Say that again for Pell.”

“I have said it every day.”

“No. You have said that the Council shares responsibility. You have said the maps were altered. You have said the fields were occupied. But when they ask whether you knew people would die, you begin discussing pressure.”

“Because pressure determines where people die.”

“And that makes death a calculation?”

“It makes the choice unavoidable.”

Elian stepped closer to the chair. “My sister was seven. Was she unavoidable?”

Ilyra’s throat tightened.

“No.”

“Was my mother?”

“No.”

“My brothers?”

“No.”

“Then do not use the river to hide from me.”

The accusation opened a door in Ilyra’s mind, and behind it stood the child on the roof in the yellow sleep shirt, one red boot, the bronze key in Ilyra’s hand. She had told herself the key would save dozens. She had told herself that a person could not hold a child and operate a valve. She had not told herself that she wanted the machinery more than she wanted to be the woman who let it go.

“I have used calculations to conceal choices,” she said.

Elian’s anger faltered, but did not vanish.

“I chose the key,” Ilyra continued. “I chose to keep the western gate open when I knew the fields were occupied. I chose to protect the eastern wall when the people below it were already drowning. I do not know whether those choices saved more people than they killed. The records claim I do. The records are lying.”

“Are you?”

“I am not certain.”

“That is the first thing you have said that sounds like grief.”

“Grief is not uncertainty.”

“No. But certainty is often how the powerful refuse to grieve.”

For a moment neither spoke.

Beyond the cell, boots passed along the corridor. Somewhere above, the crowd gave a muffled roar, as if a single enormous animal had shifted in its sleep. The sound traveled through stone.

Elian gathered the papers. “There is more.”

“About the Council?”

“About my father. About Arce. About the western gates.”

“Where?”

“Not here.”

“Then why show me?”

“Because you are going to die in less than an hour, and I need to know whether you will use what I found to expose them or to justify yourself.”

“You came to measure my motives.”

“I came to decide whether helping you would create another disaster.”

Ilyra almost laughed. “You believe you can help me?”

“I believe I can get these records beyond Pell’s reach.”

“How?”

“The archive towers still accept sealed civic packets. There are clerks in the Merchant District who owe my mother money and engineers in the docks who hate Arce. If I transmit the orders before the descent, the lenses may carry them.”

“May?”

“Pell controls the central broadcast.”

“Then he will cut the towers.”

“He can cut some. Not all.”

Ilyra looked at the folder. The old instinct moved through her: ask for every map, every route, every weakness; reconstruct the network; determine which lever controlled which gate. Possession of information felt like air.

“What do you want from me?” she asked.

“Elaborate.”

“Your price.”

“I want the truth about what happened at the barrage.”

“You have the records.”

“I have the Council’s truth. I want yours.”

“Why?”

“So I do not turn you into a hero merely because my father is a coward.”

Ilyra looked at her then—not as Dault’s daughter, not as a messenger from an archive, but as a woman who had lost a family to the same water and refused to choose between two clean stories.

“You will not like the truth,” Ilyra said.

“I already dislike you.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No. Dislike leaves room for revision.”

The corridor bell sounded once. Twelve minutes.

Senn opened the grille. “Time.”

Elian retied the folder, but before she could hide it, Ilyra said, “The old conservatory channel. Is it still open?”

Elian paused. “The records say it was sealed after the flood.”

“Records say many things.”

“Why?”

“Because if the Council used it once, they may use it again.”

Elian’s gaze sharpened. “You think there is another flood?”

“I think water does not care whether a channel is politically inconvenient.”

“Can you stop it?”

“Not alone.”

The words seemed to alter Elian’s decision. She slid one page from the folder and held it out.

Ilyra did not take it immediately.

It was a passenger list. Names, titles, departure times. At the bottom, in a different hand, someone had written: lower districts not to be informed; evacuation would compromise order.

The final entry was Arven Dault.

Beside it, a notation: route confirmed.

Ilyra read the line twice.

“Your father survived,” she said.

“Yes.”

“And you want him exposed.”

“I want the city to know he survived.”

“That is not the same.”

“No,” Elian said. “It is the beginning.”

Senn reached through the grille. “Give her the paper.”

Elian folded it and pushed it between the bars. “Keep it hidden.”

“I have nowhere to hide paper.”

“You have a tongue. You have a memory.”

“Both are under surveillance.”

“Then make Pell choose which one to cut out.”

Senn’s expression darkened. “Enough.”

Elian turned to leave, then stopped. “I will return.”

“You may not be allowed.”

“Then I will come without permission.”

“That is how floods begin,” Ilyra said.

Elian looked back at her. “No. That is how locks open.”

She walked away between the guards, black cloth disappearing into the corridor’s gray light. Maret followed, glancing once over her shoulder with an expression Ilyra could not read. Senn remained at the grille until the outer door closed.

Ilyra stood alone with the passenger list pressed against her palm.

The paper was warm from Elian’s hand. On its reverse, almost invisible beneath the official ink, a second line had been written:

The eastern embankment will not hold through third hour.

Not a prediction. An instruction.

Ilyra sat on the cot. Above her, the Hall trembled faintly. Water moved somewhere under the foundations, patient and unseen.

She had wanted the powerful to feel helpless. Elian had brought her proof that helplessness had been assigned long before the gates opened.

The thought did not absolve her.

It made the room larger.

And for the first time since the sentence, Ilyra understood that the person who might carry the truth beyond the Hall did not trust her to hold it alone.

chapters.name: Pressure in the West
chapters.content:
## Pressure in the West

The first new flood announced itself by smell.

Ilyra woke with brine on her tongue and the sour mineral stink of a river moving through stone. For several breaths she lay still, listening past the drip in the ceiling and the scrape of rats behind the wall.

A tremor ran beneath the floor.

She turned toward the drain. Water gathered in its iron holes and quivered there. The grate had been clogged since yesterday with hair, wax, and a strip of red sealing cloth. Now water was rising through it.

“Guard,” she called.

No answer.

She counted the sounds beyond the cell. Two steps across the corridor. A cough near the western stair. The records door lifting and falling. Maret’s patrol was late by half a minute.

The water reached the first crack in the floor.

The latch opened. Maret entered with a lantern and a folded packet under her arm. Black silt marked the hem of her uniform.

“You were supposed to be asleep,” she said.

“I was listening.”

“To what?”

Ilyra pointed to the drain.

Maret crouched and prodded the grate with her lantern. Water shivered around the iron.

“Has Pell sent a plumber?” Ilyra asked.

“Pell sent three clerks to say the foundation is sound.”

“Did they touch the floor?”

“No.”

Maret unfolded the packet. “Someone left this in the herb room. It was addressed to the prisoner who knows how water moves.”

She held it out, then paused.

“If this is another trick—”

“Everything is a trick when Pell owns the record.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “It is the condition.”

Maret handed her the pages. They had been cut into narrow strips and covered on both sides with cramped figures.

WEST CHANNEL, THIRD HOUR: 14 HANDS.

CROWN RESERVOIR 6, THIRD HOUR: RELEASED.

SABLE WARD, FOURTH HOUR: 3 HANDS ABOVE STREET.

Ilyra aligned the torn strips across her cot. A map emerged from the readings. Reservoir Six had emptied into the western channel, followed by merchant cisterns beneath the glassworks and a chain of garden basins near the Crown retaining wall. The releases were moving water west, away from the Crown District and toward Sable Ward.

“Where did you get these?” she asked.

“A boy came through the service stairs.”

“Who?”

“He had two fingers missing and would not give a name.”

“A pump worker.”

“Likely.”

“Did he say how long?”

Maret looked toward the polished lens in the ceiling. “He said people were being told to leave Sable Ward.”

Ilyra returned to the figures. “No. They are being told not to leave.”

Maret stared at her.

“These releases are timed,” Ilyra said. “The western gates are opening in increments, but the relief channels downstream remain closed. The water is being forced into the foundries and tenements. If the ward empties, the pressure moves farther south. If it remains occupied, the buildings absorb the first surge.”

“Why would anyone do that?”

“To protect the Crown.”

“The Crown wall already held.”

“It held once. A wall is a delay, not a promise.”

Maret snatched up the strips and crushed them. “My child is in Sable Ward.”

Ilyra had seen the black silt on her boot. “I know.”

“I tried to reach the south blocks. The gates were locked. They told me the ward was under inspection.”

“Inspection means clearance.”

“Do not use their words.”

“I am telling you what they mean.”

Maret’s face tightened. “You think because you can name a thing, you own it.”

The words opened the old corridor in Ilyra’s mind.

Nera’s voice through the maintenance tube. Water above the first landing. Families trapped below. The survey was old. Ilyra had known enough to warn her, but not enough to predict every failure. She had withheld the uncertainty because uncertainty weakened command. A worker who knew the full danger might refuse the sequence. An apprentice might choose the person in front of her over the pressure line.

She had called that protection.

It had been possession.

“I do not own this,” Ilyra said.

“You opened it.”

“Yes.”

“And now you want to tell us how to close it.”

“Yes.”

Maret laughed without humor. “Then tell me where my child is.”

“I cannot.”

“Tell me whether she is alive.”

“I cannot.”

“Tell me something useful.”

Ilyra pointed to the packet. “Bring me the western gauge readings.”

“You have twenty minutes. Then the procession begins.”

She turned.

“Maret.”

The guard paused.

“If Pell asks where you went—”

“He will know.”

“Then why ask?”

“Because I am still asking people to choose.”

Maret looked back at her. “You are late learning that.”

When she left, Ilyra gathered the strips and held them near the lantern. The last mark was not a number but a small hooked line, perhaps a warning, perhaps a signature.

Seven knocks sounded beneath the floor.

Three slow, then four rapid.

Not a pipe. Not settling stone.

Ilyra lowered herself beside the drain. Water whispered below. Something scraped against the underside of the grate.

“Hello?” she called. “Can you hear me?”

A single strike answered.

“Are you in the foundation channel?”

Two knocks.

The old conservatory channel.

Elian had said records claimed it was sealed after the flood. If the Council had reopened it, private reservoirs could be emptied beneath the Hall and sent west without passing through the public gauges.

The door opened again.

Elian Dault entered in a dark traveling coat, her hair pinned badly and no papers in her hands.

“You came back,” Ilyra said.

“I said I would.”

“People who say that usually mean they hope to.”

“Jorren found me.”

“Who is Jorren?”

“Jorren Pell. A rescue diver. No relation to the magistrate. He lost his wife and two sons in the ropewalk collapse. The official count included his wife and omitted the boys.”

“Where is he?”

“Below the old dye market with survivors. Thirty-six confirmed, perhaps more trying to reach them. They are using boats made from doors and pump housings to pull people out of Sable Ward.”

“Those tunnels will flood.”

“They know. They are the only routes the wardens do not control.”

Ilyra held out the readings. “The Council is draining private reservoirs into the western channels.”

Elian read the top strip. “Jorren said the water was rising from below.”

“Pumps fail irregularly. This is timed release. They are protecting the Crown wall by making Sable Ward take the pressure.”

“Can you stop it?”

The old hunger rose in Ilyra: give me the gauges, the keys, one uninterrupted hour. She could make the Crown feel the weight it had assigned to everyone else.

“Perhaps,” she said.

“That is not an answer.”

“It depends which gates still function.”

“Tell me what to bring.”

“Live readings. Gate positions. Reservoir volumes. And the names of every occupied building.”

“People are already sending scraps through the archive runners.”

“Then connect them.”

Elian’s expression hardened. “You think I can connect an entire ward while Pell controls the Hall?”

“I think you can connect people who have already decided not to wait for permission.”

The lens above them clicked.

“He is listening,” Elian said.

“He always listens.”

“Then why tell me this?”

“Because he cannot close every channel at once.”

A metallic groan passed beneath the cell. Water at the drain trembled.

“Jorren wants to speak with you,” Elian said.

“He cannot come here.”

“He has a route through the lower channel.”

“He is a rescue diver, not a ghost.”

“He has a route.”

Ilyra looked down at the drain. “What does he want?”

“Instructions that do not require trusting you.”

That answer held more truth than an appeal would have.

“I need the full readings first,” Ilyra said. “Maret is bringing them.”

“And after that?”

“After that, they intend to kill me.”

“I know.”

“If you want my help, you will need to get me out before then.”

“I came for your help.”

“No. You came for my account. You wanted the shape of my guilt so your father’s would have somewhere to stand.”

Elian flinched.

“Now you need someone who can read the pressure network,” Ilyra continued. “Those are different requests.”

“My family died because you opened the barrage.”

“Yes.”

“My father escaped because the Council opened a private route.”

“Yes.”

“Do not make those equal.”

“I am not.”

“Good. Because if you get people out of Sable Ward, it will not erase the child you left on the roof.”

“No.”

“Or Nera.”

“No.”

“Or the people in the storage fields.”

“No.”

Elian studied her. “Then what do you want?”

“To be right.”

“That is honest.”

“No.” Ilyra looked at the water. “Not entirely.”

She remembered the Feast lights above the barrage and the satisfaction of imagining Dault on the platform, watching the system fail. She had wanted the powerful to feel fear. Not necessarily to die, but to understand that the river did not recognize their rank.

“It pleased me to make them afraid,” she said. “That is not the same as wanting them dead. It is not innocence either.”

“Jorren does not need innocence. He needs a route.”

“Then tell him to bring every reading he has. Tell him no channel is empty because a map says so. Tell him to mark children, the sick, and anyone who cannot climb before he marks pressure.”

“And then?”

“Then I will tell him where the water is going.”

The drain gave a violent gurgle. A scrap of blue cloth rose through the grate and caught on the iron.

Elian reached for it.

“Do not,” Ilyra said.

“Why?”

“The water may be carrying more than cloth.”

Footsteps rushed along the corridor.

Maret appeared, soaked to the knees, carrying three brass gauge plates and a bundle of keys. Her face had gone pale.

“The western stations are gone,” she said.

“Cut,” Ilyra replied. “Not gone.”

“Sable Ward’s lower street is under water. The wardens cut the lines.”

“Which reservoirs?”

“Six, eight, and the old conservatory cistern.”

“That is supposed to be empty.”

“It is not.”

Elian stepped forward. “Evacuation?”

Maret shook her head. “Permits go to Crown and Merchant households. The notices are written as maintenance orders. Blue stripe means immediate departure. Red means shelter in place.”

“There is no shelter,” Ilyra said.

“My child is near Foundry Row.”

Ilyra picked up the warmest gauge plate. Its needle trembled just past red.

“Then we reach Foundry Row before the next release.”

“Can you stop it?” Maret asked.

“I can tell you where to open. I cannot promise what opening will save.”

“Tell me anyway.”

Beneath them came another knock, followed by another and another. The sound multiplied through the foundation.

Elian went still. “Someone is down there.”

“Jorren,” Maret said.

Ilyra knelt beside the drain.

“Jorren Pell,” she called. “Can you hear me?”

Three knocks answered.

“Are you in the conservatory channel?”

Two knocks.

“Do you have people with you?”

A pause. Then a storm of strikes from several places beneath the floor.

Ilyra pictured the Hall, the cistern, the western channels, and Sable Ward waiting in the dark. The pattern was larger than her hands. For once, the answer could not be a single person taking every lever.

“Listen carefully,” she said. “The water is being released from the old cistern. Do not take the eastern tunnel. It will become a trap. Go toward the dye market, then climb at the third maintenance shaft. Mark every occupied room. Do not open a gate unless someone on the other side confirms they can receive the water.”

The knocks stopped.

Elian stared at her. “You expect him to obey?”

“No.”

“Then why give the order?”

“Because he may improve it.”

Maret lifted the keys. “And us?”

Ilyra looked at the gauge, the flooded drain, and the two women who had chosen to remain in the cell with her.

“Us,” she said, “we find a way out before the Hall becomes another basin.”

Above them, the Feast bells began to ring.

Below, the water answered.

chapters.name: The People Beneath
chapters.content:
Senn learned that the dead were easiest to move after they had been counted.

The prison clerks carried their ledgers in oilskin sleeves beneath their coats. They did not carry stretchers. They carried names.

He watched them cross the Hall’s lower passage as the Feast bells began above: seven bright notes, a pause, then seven more. Renewal. Continuity. The promise that Veyr would remain itself no matter what happened beneath its floors.

Water seeped between the flagstones.

One clerk stumbled. His sleeve came loose, and a ledger struck the floor. Senn stooped before the man could retrieve it.

The page had opened to Sable Ward, Foundry Row, lower ropewalk.

Names filled narrow columns. Some were crossed out. Others bore a black hook.

The hook meant confirmed dead.

Senn knew the mark. During the first flood, he had helped fill out casualty rolls. He had written his sister’s name on a ration form because the official ledger had no place for residents of her building. The Hall had called the quarter disordered, undocumented, difficult to verify.

Now he saw names he recognized.

Jessa Vale, rope spinner.

Orren and Pala Renn, children.

Mik Tarrow, foundry hand.

Not dead. Not all of them.

He had seen Mik three nights ago in the southern holding pens, alive and furious, his ear bandaged with curtain cloth. He had seen Pala Renn in the infirmary corridor, clinging to her mother’s coat.

Senn turned the page.

The names had not merely been marked dead. They had been transferred.

“Discharged to flood,” the clerk said.

Senn looked up. “Where were they taken?”

“Give it back.”

The second clerk, a woman with a scar through one eyebrow, reached for the ledger.

Senn read the next lines. Unregistered dependents. Storage-field residents. Ropewalk laborers. Several names had been marked with the hook, then annotated in cramped handwriting: *held below.*

Below.

“Why are they dead on this page?” Senn asked.

“The magistrate’s order,” the scarred clerk said.

“Pell’s?”

“Civic order.”

Three knocks sounded beneath the passage: slow, deliberate, hollow.

Four rapid knocks answered from farther under the Hall.

The clerks froze.

Senn looked at the water darkening the grout.

“Give me the book,” the first clerk whispered. “If they find it with you—”

“They already know.”

“No,” she said. “They know what they wrote.”

Senn handed it back. He did not know whether he meant to warn Pell or find the people marked dead. He only knew that when the clerks hurried away, their hands were shaking.

At the next bell, he left the Hall.

He crossed the drowned streets in uniform and carried the Hall’s brass key ring beneath his coat. The route to Jorren Pell’s network led through a grating behind a ruined tannery, down into the old dye channels.

A boy with a knife blocked the opening.

“I’m looking for Jorren,” Senn said.

“You found him?”

“I’m looking for him.”

The boy’s eyes dropped to the uniform.

Senn set the key ring on the stone. “Tell him the prison has falsified the death rolls. Some of the people they marked dead are being held below the Hall.”

The boy took the keys and disappeared. A moment later, a hand appeared through the grating.

The tunnels beneath the dye market smelled of lamp smoke, dye, wet brick, and too many bodies. People occupied the chambers on pallets and overturned crates. Two men repaired a boat made from a warehouse door. Along one wall, charcoal lines marked the rising water.

Jorren stood beside a large dye vat with a map spread across its rim. He was younger than Senn had expected, though grief had put gray in his beard. A brass diving valve hung loose at his throat.

“You’re a Hall guard,” Jorren said.

“Senn.”

“I know who you are.”

“Then you know I lost someone.”

“Everyone here lost someone.”

Senn told him about the ledger and gave him the names he remembered. A woman took a scrap of sailcloth and began writing them down.

An old man watched her. “You signed the first rolls?”

“Yes.”

“Did you mark them?”

“I marked the bodies I saw.”

“Did you look for names?”

Senn felt heat rise in his chest. “I was ordered to clear the Hall.”

“You were ordered to do a great many things.”

Jorren lifted a hand. “Enough.”

The old man’s gaze remained fixed on Senn. “A guard comes with keys, and we call it luck.”

Senn had no answer. He wanted to say he wanted his sister’s name restored. He wanted Pell dragged into the street to read every omitted child aloud. He wanted Ilyra Voss to explain why she had kept a valve key while a child slipped from her hand.

Instead, he said, “I want to know whether the woman in the Flood Cells is still alive.”

Several people laughed.

“She’s being executed,” said the woman with the sailcloth.

“The Hall is flooding,” Senn said. “The execution may not happen as planned.”

“That is your concern?” demanded a man with a split lip. “Her?”

“She knows the gates.”

“She opened them.”

“She may know how to stop them.”

The room tightened around the words.

The man rose from his crate. “My brother was in the storage fields. Did she know those fields weren’t empty?”

“She knew the maps said they were empty.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No,” Senn said. “It isn’t.”

Jorren folded the map. “You’ve spoken to her?”

“Many times.”

“Does she regret it?”

Senn remembered Ilyra in the cell, counting bolts and drains as if measurement could hold back the world. He remembered her refusing Pell’s confession and insisting she had not acted alone.

“She says she is responsible,” he answered. “She won’t say she was the only one responsible.”

“A clever answer,” the man said.

“It may be the true one.”

Senn had not meant to defend her. The realization unsettled him.

Jorren studied him. “What do you want from her?”

“To keep her alive.”

“Why?”

“To make her face us. Not a lens. Not Pell. Us.”

The woman with the sailcloth folded her arms. “You want her punished.”

“Yes.”

“Then you want her dead.”

Senn remembered the execution masks and the betting boards. He remembered his own first thought when he heard the sentence: *Good. Let the city watch her burn.*

He had called that justice because vengeance sounded too honest.

“I don’t know,” he said.

Jorren nodded. “That is the first useful thing you’ve said.”

The argument began.

Some wanted Ilyra taken from the Hall and forced to open the gates. Others said she would seize control and drown whoever stood in her way. A woman whose husband had died in the first flood said no one should risk saving the person who had chosen the Crown bypass. A young engineer insisted that without Ilyra the western channels could not be read in time.

Jorren let them speak until the lamps guttered.

Then he struck the vat with his palm.
