“We are not building another execution platform below the city,” he said. “If Ilyra knows how to stop the water, we get the knowledge. If she can help, we help her reach the controls. But exposing the Council cannot require another mass death.”

The man with the split lip stared at him. “And if she refuses?”

“Then we find another way.”

“There may not be one.”

“There was no other way the first time,” Jorren said. “That is what they want us to believe.”

The silence that followed was not agreement. It was consideration.

Senn saw the difference between Jorren and Ilyra. Both read maps as if lines could become moral laws. Both believed water could be compelled by understanding it. But Jorren counted the people around him before he counted the channels.

“What do you need?” Senn asked.

Jorren looked at him.

“Access to the Flood Cells,” Senn continued. “I can pass through the Hall until the procession begins. After that, Pell will lock every door.”

“And you’d free her?”

“I’d open the cell.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No.”

Jorren glanced at the keys. “She may not come.”

“Then she stays and dies.”

“Perhaps she should.”

Senn felt anger rise, then recognized what lay beneath it: shame.

“She should live long enough to answer,” he said. “To the people she harmed.”

“And after that?”

Senn looked at the names on the sailcloth. The city had already buried them with ink.

“After that, she can hear what we decide.”

Jorren nodded. “Then we need to know whether she can still read the city.”

They assembled a packet.

The first item was a map copied from an abandoned pumping station. It showed the old conservatory channel beneath the Hall, running west toward the dye market. The second was a brass gauge plate from a cut station, its needle fixed just beyond red. The third was a fragment of gear teeth from a Crown reservoir mechanism, scored with fresh wear.

“Proof?” Senn asked.

“Proof she can understand,” Jorren replied.

The woman with the sailcloth added a list of occupied buildings along Foundry Row. Each room had been marked with a dot: children, elderly, injured, anyone unable to climb. The list was incomplete. No one trusted a map that called a building empty.

Senn took the packet.

“How do I get it to her?”

“Through the herb room,” said the boy from the grating. “A kitchen woman trades salt for messages.”

“Her name?”

“Don’t use names.”

Jorren caught Senn’s wrist before he climbed. “If the Hall collapses, you leave her.”

Senn looked at him.

“I mean it,” Jorren said. “You leave everyone you cannot carry.”

“That is not a rescue plan.”

“It is what keeps a rescue from becoming another flood.”

The route led through a disused drain and up behind the infirmary wall. Senn emerged beneath a table stacked with dried fever leaves. The kitchen woman accepted the packet without looking at him and gave him a small tin cup.

Inside lay a thin metal pin.

“From the prisoner,” she whispered.

Senn knew it. The pin had been hidden beneath Ilyra’s tongue during washing, discovered by no one—or by someone who had chosen not to report it.

“She has a plan,” he said.

“Everyone has a plan.”

“Does she know about the false rolls?”

The woman looked at him. “She knows the city counts what it wants.”

Senn returned to the corridor.

The execution procession had begun above. Through the stone came the muffled roar of thousands, while the bells rang their bright, patient pattern.

He entered the lower passage and found the guard at the Flood Cells staring at the water around his boots.

“Where have you been?” the guard asked.

“Checking the western drain.”

“And?”

“It’s blocked.”

The guard swore.

Senn fitted a key into the lock. Before turning it, he heard metal scraping stone inside.

He opened the hatch and pushed the packet through.

A hand appeared in the darkness. Ilyra took the map, the gauge plate, and the gear fragment. Her fingers paused over the list of occupied rooms.

“Who sent these?” she asked.

“People beneath the city.”

“That is not a name.”

“It is the only one that matters.”

Her face came near the hatch. “Are they alive?”

“Some.”

“Names?”

Senn almost laughed. “You ask that now?”

“I asked before.”

“You recorded six lost, pressure reduced, east line preserved.”

The words struck her. She did not deny them.

“I remember,” she said.

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“Then remember that some of the people you killed are still alive.”

She looked at the packet. “How many?”

“We don’t know.”

“Where?”

“Below the dye market. In the conservatory channel. Foundry Row.”

Her gaze sharpened. “The conservatory channel is open?”

“Yes.”

“Who opened it?”

“We don’t know.”

She pressed the gear fragment between her fingers. “The releases are timed?”

“Jorren has readings.”

“Jorren?”

“Rescue diver. Lost his family.”

Something shifted in her face—not recognition, but calculation interrupted before it could become control.

“Tell him not to open any channel unless the receiving district confirms it can take the water.”

“He knows.”

“Does he?”

Senn leaned toward the hatch. “He says he won’t make another execution platform.”

For the first time, Ilyra looked directly at him.

“Good,” she said.

The guard at the corridor’s end called that Pell was coming.

Senn began closing the hatch.

“Ilyra,” he said.

She waited.

“I don’t know if I want you saved.”

Her mouth tightened. “You should not save me for what you want.”

“I want you alive long enough to hear the names.”

“You may not like what they ask of me.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

The question held no challenge, which made it worse. Senn saw his sister beneath the fallen roof, the child in the yellow shirt, and Pell’s clerks turning living people into black hooks.

“I don’t know,” he said.

Ilyra nodded. “Keep the uncertainty. It may save someone.”

Pell’s footsteps approached with two guards and the soft clicking of a civic lens.

Senn shut the hatch but kept his hand on the lock.

“Guard Senn,” Pell said. “Why is this door open?”

“Inspection.”

“Who authorized it?”

Senn held his gaze. “The water.”

Pell looked down at the damp stones. “You’ve been listening to the prisoner.”

“Yes.”

“And?”

Senn thought of the people beneath the city, waiting in tunnels built to carry waste away from respectable houses. He thought of the ledger and the names made dead by a clerk’s hand.

“And she is not the only one who opened the gates,” he said.

Pell’s expression barely changed. “That is not an answer I can use.”

“No,” Senn said. “It isn’t.”

Behind the cell door, something tapped once against the metal.

Not a signal. Not yet.

A reminder that the machinery was listening, and that beneath every official silence, people were still alive enough to make a sound.

chapters.name: A Second Barrage
chapters.content:
## A Second Barrage

The packet lay open on Ilyra’s knees.

She had arranged its contents by function: the gauge plate beside the gear fragment, the old channel map beneath the list of occupied rooms, the copied readings at the top where she could see the times without turning her wrist. The thin metal pin rested beneath her thumb.

Pell had taken away the civic lens, but its afterimage still trembled on the wall. Beyond the cell, the Hall groaned. Water moved somewhere below them—not through the steady pulse of a drain, but in a deeper body gathering against stone.

Ilyra placed the gauge plate against the map.

“Again,” she said.

Elian Dault stood near the bars, watching the corridor. “You’ve asked me three times.”

“I asked whether Reservoir Six is feeding the conservatory channel.”

“You asked whether the notation meant that.”

“It means that if the person who wrote it understood the distinction between transfer and relief.”

“It was my father’s route ledger,” Elian said. “He understood every distinction that kept water away from his house.”

Ilyra ignored the answer. She ran a finger along the old conservatory channel. The line began beneath the Hall, passed through the foundation cistern, and descended west beneath gardens that had not existed when the map was drawn. From there it split: one branch toward the dye market and Foundry Row, another climbing toward the Crown terraces.

The line to Foundry Row had been marked with a faded red bar.

“Closed,” Ilyra murmured.

“Jorren says the old channel is open.”

“The old channel. Not this branch.”

“Then what is happening beneath us?”

“Someone has opened the cisterns and left the receiving gates shut.”

She spread the readings across the floor. They had been copied in hurried hands, but the pattern was clear. Reservoir Six had dropped twelve inches in the last hour. Reservoir Eight had dropped nine. The conservatory cistern was rising. Merchant cisterns released water in uneven intervals, as though separate crews were working from separate instructions. Garden basins spilled into channels meant for rainwater.

“It is not a failure,” Ilyra said.

“No,” Elian replied. “It isn’t.”

“It is a transfer.”

“To where?”

“Here first.” Ilyra tapped the conservatory cistern. “Then west. They are filling the lower channels until the pressure breaks through Sable Ward. Once the ward is under water, they can call it an infrastructure loss. They’ll say the old conduits failed.”

“Can you stop it?”

Ilyra looked again at the map.

The question had no simple shape. A gate could be closed, but pressure did not disappear when denied. It moved. Every locked channel became a decision made elsewhere.

“Not from this cell.”

“That is not what I asked.”

Ilyra reached for the gauge plate. Fresh wear brightened its teeth against the dull brass. She held it near the light.

“Where is the central control?” she asked.

“The execution platform,” said Elian. “Pell told me the ceremony uses the Hall’s original waterworks. The platform stands over the old settling chamber.”

“Not the platform. Beneath it.”

“The control chamber is beneath the platform?”

“The central flood controls were built into the settling chamber before the Hall was expanded. The Council wanted the waterworks hidden but accessible during civic displays.” She shifted the map. “If the conservatory channel is carrying Crown water, the central manifold is still connected to the private reservoirs.”

Elian came closer. “Could you open those channels from the platform?”

“From the control chamber.”

“Which is beneath the platform.”

“Perhaps.”

“You don’t know?”

“I know what the original design required. I don’t know what Arce altered afterward.”

At Arce’s name, the cell seemed to contract. Ilyra remembered his fingers covering the western spill basins on an old survey as he explained that the copy was easier for the Council to read. Later she understood what the simplification had done. Water, like records, could be narrowed until it traveled only where power found it convenient.

She turned the map over.

“There.”

On the reverse, almost invisible beneath gray wash, three circles marked the old conservatory cistern. One had been crossed out. The second bore a notation: emergency isolation. The third was unmarked.

“The unmarked line leads beneath the ceremonial platform,” Ilyra said. “It was probably sealed when they built the galleries. But the pin—”

She stopped.

Elian noticed. “What?”

Ilyra raised the thin metal pin. “A retaining pin for a governor arm. Old pattern. The head has been filed down.”

“Can it open the chamber?”

“Not by itself.”

“Then why did they give it to you?”

“It can hold a bypass lever in the open position.”

“And that is good?”

“It depends which bypass.”

Ilyra rose so quickly that her chain snapped taut. She barely noticed. The packet scattered across the damp floor. She gathered it and spread the papers again, this time in sequence.

“Reservoir Six drains into the Crown garden basin. The basin overflows into the conservatory cistern. Eight feeds the Merchant terraces, then the same cistern through a secondary line. If we open the central manifold while both reservoirs are releasing, the cistern will empty toward the Crown District.”

“Toward the gardens.”

“Gardens, terraces, warehouses, the lower ceremonial road. The water would run through the Crown side before it reached Sable Ward.”

“And stop the flood?”

“It would reduce the western pressure.”

“By flooding another district.”

“By flooding the district that is sending the water.”

Elian’s eyes hardened. “You say that as if geography makes it justice.”

“I say it as if volume and elevation are real.”

“People are real too.”

Ilyra looked down at the map. “I know.”

She did. That was the trouble.

“If the Crown channels open,” she continued, “the water will expose the hidden transfer lines. Silt will tear through the ornamental conduits. Garden walls and covered pipes will rupture. Everyone watching the ceremony will see where the water came from.”

“Everyone will see officials running.”

“Good.”

The word came too quickly.

Ilyra heard the old roar in it—not the river, but the moment before she had opened the North Barrage. Governors gathered above her, gold sleeves bright in festival lamps. She had imagined their faces when water reached their shoes.

Not dead, she had told herself then. Only afraid.

Fear had been the private reward she carried into the tunnel like a second tool.

Elian watched her. “This is the plan? Use your execution to open the Crown reservoirs and drown the people who came to watch?”

“I use the controls beneath the platform.”

“The crowd is part of the access.”

“I use the access.”

“You use the crowd.”

Ilyra did not answer.

Above them, the city began to chant. The sound rose and fell through the stone. Her name was somewhere inside it, perhaps joined to the title they had given her. The Barrage Butcher.

She imagined the galleries: white masks, bronze ribbons, children lifted onto shoulders. They would watch heated water descend around her. They would buy cakes stamped with the shape of a woman falling.

And beneath their feet, the central controls waited.

“If the ceremony proceeds,” Ilyra said, “the galleries will be full. The lenses will transmit every movement. Every guard will watch the platform. The control chamber will be understaffed.”

“How many?”

“Four at most. Two platform wardens, one manifold keeper, one lens technician.”

“You know the rotations?”

“I have watched them for forty-one days.”

“From a cell.”

“From a cell with a drain, two surveillance reflections, and guards who believe I am too proud to listen when they talk.”

Elian glanced toward the corridor. “Which means?”

“The chamber can be reached during the sentence reading. Pell will be on the east dais. He will inspect the platform and speak with the lens crews. He will not inspect the lower manifold because he believes its keeper loyal.”

“Can you recruit the keeper?”

“I can frighten him.”

“That is not recruitment.”

“It may be sufficient.”

“Everything is sufficient to you if it opens a gate.”

Ilyra stopped.

For a moment the cell held another room: the maintenance corridor at the barrage, Nera’s voice through the speaking tube, workers pounding against the sealed emergency door.

Open it.

Ilyra had watched the gauge. She had known opening the door would flood the control chamber. She had known people were behind it. The mathematics had not made the choice for her.

Her hand had moved to the seal anyway.

Elian’s voice brought her back. “You’re thinking about the first flood.”

“I think about it every time I close my eyes.”

“Then think about it while you make this plan.”

“I am.”

“No. You are thinking about how to be right this time.”

“There is no time for a committee.”

“Then make a committee that moves.”

“The gates have pressure limits.”

“So do people.”

Ilyra’s hand closed around the pin.

“Foundry Row has two hundred and fourteen occupied rooms,” she said. “That is the minimum. The list is incomplete. If the western relief channel opens without confirmation, water enters the lower floors in under four minutes. If the central manifold opens first, the Crown discharge takes perhaps ninety seconds to establish. During that interval, the conservatory channel rises. Anyone below the Hall may be trapped.”

“The people marked held below.”

“Yes.”

“Can they be warned?”

“Possibly through the maintenance tubes.”

“Can you speak to them?”

“If the old network is still connected.”

“Then that is the first command.”

Ilyra shook her head. “The first command is confirmation from the receiving districts.”

“From Sable Ward?”

“From both sides. If Crown refuses to take the discharge, we cannot force it through their gardens without knowing where their workers are.”

Elian’s mouth twisted. “You care whether the Crown’s workers are warned?”

“I care whether people are in the channel.”

“Even now?”

“Especially now.”

Ilyra set the list beside the map. “Jorren’s group can confirm Foundry Row. Maret knows the lower Hall passages. Senn can reach the platform wardens, if he is still free. You can get the archive runners to the towers. We need the commands distributed before the ceremony.”

“And if Pell shuts the towers?”

“Then the water still moves.”

“That is not enough.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “It isn’t.”

She paced the cell, three steps from wall to wall, turning at the chain’s limit. The movement steadied her. A gate had a travel distance. A pressure rise had a curve. A guard rotation had an interval. Even fear could be measured if one observed the breathing of the people who carried it.

“Partial lift first,” she said. “Ten degrees. Thirty seconds. Read the gauge. Then the western relief gate. Then the Crown discharge.”

“And who opens each gate?”

“I do.”

“No.”

Ilyra looked up.

“You said Jorren would not let you control the gates alone,” Elian said.

“I said I agreed with him.”

“Your agreement lasted until you saw a mechanism.”

“It is not the same situation.”

“It is exactly the same situation. You see a system, an error, and a correction no one else can make quickly enough.”

“There may not be time.”

“There is always time to let another person confirm what you think you know.”

“If they refuse?”

“Then you explain the cost.”

Ilyra stared at her.

“Tell them the truth,” Elian said. “Not the version that makes the decision clean. All of it.”

Ilyra looked at the folded list. A line of ink could hold a catastrophe still. Six lost, pressure reduced, east line preserved. She had written it because numbers seemed more honest than names.

She pulled the pin across the map, marking three points.

“No command opens without three confirmations,” she said. “The receiving district. The district taking the discharge. Someone at the manifold reading actual pressure.”

“Who gives the final order?”

“No one.”

“That is not how gates work.”

“It is how these gates will work.”

She drew separate lines between the controls. “Each district receives only its own command. The manifold keeper cannot open the Crown discharge without confirmation from Crown and Sable. Sable cannot open its relief gate without a pressure reading from below the Hall. If one channel fails, the others hold.”

“It will be slower.”

“Yes.”

“It could collapse into confusion.”

“Yes.”

“You hate that.”

“I hate water rising while people argue.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “It is not.”

A knock sounded at the bars.

Maret stood beyond them, pale beneath her bronze collar. Her hands were empty.

“Pell is assembling the procession,” she said. “The washroom attendants are coming.”

“Your child?” Elian asked.

Maret’s face closed. “No word.”

Ilyra folded the occupied-room list and held it out. “Take this to Senn.”

Maret did not move.

“If he is free, he will know how to reach Jorren’s people. Tell them Foundry Row must confirm every opening. Tell them the old conservatory channel may contain people.”

“You’re planning to use the ceremony.”

“I’m planning to stop the flood.”

“By opening the Crown channels.”

“By opening every channel in an order that gives people time to move.”

Maret’s eyes flicked to the maps. “And if it doesn’t?”

“Then do not open it.”

“My child is near Foundry Row.”

“I know.”

“If I hear nothing—”

“Do not open it.”

Maret stared at her. Ilyra saw the old mistake in the guard’s face: the belief that certainty belonged to the person closest to the lever, the person who could see the gauge and knew enough to act.

Maret took the list.

“And you?”

Ilyra looked toward Elian.

“No,” she said. “Not alone.”

The wash attendants arrived with white cloths and a brass basin. Pell’s voice carried from the stair, smooth and practiced, explaining to someone that the condemned engineer had become unusually cooperative.

Ilyra gathered the maps. Her pulse quickened. The old exhilaration had returned, bright and poisonous. Pressure windows. Guard rotations. A city built on hidden channels could be made visible in one hour.

Elian saw it in her face.

“You want them afraid,” she said.

Ilyra did not deny it.

“I want Sable Ward alive.”

“That is not what I asked.”

Ilyra looked at the pin, at the blood on its point, at the lines she had drawn between districts that had spent generations refusing to share water.

“I want them to understand,” she said.

“Those are different things.”

“Yes.”

The Hall’s foundation shuddered. Somewhere below, seven knocks answered from inside the walls.

Ilyra slid the pin beneath her tongue. Its metal taste spread through her mouth.

“Then we will have to make them different,” she said.

chapters.name: The Shape of Vengeance
chapters.content:
## The Shape of Vengeance

The Hall shuddered.

Dust sifted from the arch above the infirmary door. Somewhere below, water struck stone with the patient rhythm of a hand seeking admission.

Ilyra held the brass gauge plate against the map and watched its needle tremble just beyond red.

“Again,” she said.

Elian glanced at it. “It has not changed.”

“Nothing holds steady under pressure.”

“That is not the same as changing.”

Ilyra took the gauge from her. The map showed the old conservatory channel branching beneath the Hall toward the dye market and Foundry Row on one side, and the Crown terraces on the other. Between them lay the original settling chamber, now buried beneath the ceremonial platform. Arce had narrowed the lines, renamed them, or concealed them. The map could not say which.

She had drawn three circles around the central manifold.

One for confirmation from Sable Ward.

One for confirmation from the district receiving the discharge.

One for a pressure reading beneath the Hall.

No gate was to open without all three.

Three voices, if the voices could reach one another in time.

Elian leaned over the table. “You have redrawn the manifold six times.”

“Five.”

“I watched you draw the sixth.”

“Then you watched poorly.”

Elian’s mouth tightened. She had Dault’s narrow eyes, though grief had made them less certain than his. “You keep saying this plan is different from the North Barrage.”

“It is.”

“Because three people will touch the controls instead of one?”

“Because no person will.”

“You will still be there.”

“I understand the pressure sequence.”

“That is not what I asked.”

Ilyra looked back at the map. She had marked a possible route through the Crown gardens, another beneath the Merchant terraces, and a third along the lower ceremonial road. The last was cleanest. It would carry reservoir water away from Sable Ward and into streets occupied by the people who had come to watch her die.

It would also flood stores, carriage houses, servants’ quarters, and perhaps the Hall’s lower galleries.

The thought had entered her mind without permission.

Not as a calculation.

As an image.

The governors in white and bronze robes, their jeweled collars darkened by spray. Their attendants scrambling over the polished platform while the mirrored lenses tilted to follow them. Pell’s careful mouth opening in astonishment. The Crown’s banners dragging in brown water.

She had seen it before.

Years ago, on the night she stole the seal.

Nera had stood at the records-room door while Ilyra spread the copied survey across the floor. Ilyra had explained the pressure windows and the danger to the eastern embankment. She had spoken of lives, failure points, and necessity.

But beneath every sentence had been another thought.

They will be there.

The governors would gather on the ceremonial platform for the Feast demonstration. They would applaud the engineers who maintained the barriers. They would raise cups to renewal while families in the Low Quarter slept beneath cracked walls.

When the sluice opened, she had wanted the powerful to feel the ground tremble.

She had wanted them to look down.

The Hall shook again. Maret crossed herself in the old Low Quarter fashion.

“What do you want?” Elian asked.

“I want Sable Ward evacuated.”

“That is an answer about the ward.”

“You asked what I want.”

“I asked what you want from this. From the platform. From the governors. From everyone watching you.”

“I want the gates opened in time.”

Elian gave a humorless laugh. “You want the gates opened by people who agree with you.”

“I want them opened by people who can see the pressure.”

“You want everyone to understand that you were right.”

Ilyra’s fingers curled against the table.

“Being right matters when people are drowning.”

“So does why you are right.”

“When the first flood came,” Ilyra said, “the Council had already decided which districts could be sacrificed.”

“Yes.”

“They altered the maps.”

“Yes.”

“They removed the valves that would have relieved the western pressure.”

“Yes.”

“They left families in the storage fields while clearing out inventory.”

“Yes.”

“Then tell me how wanting them to experience fear is vengeance.”

Elian did not answer immediately.

Ilyra remembered the barrage chamber: the wheel under her hands, the pressure hammering through the walls, the thin brightness of festival music drifting down from above. She had disabled the surveillance relays. Nera had warned that the western line was not responding.

Ilyra had told her the pressure would fall.

Above them, the crowd had cheered.

She had imagined the governors turning toward the river, their faces stripped of ceremony. Dault running first. Arce giving orders and finding no one listening. Pell—before he became the man who sentenced her—standing with empty hands.

She had not imagined the dead.

Not at first.

The memory shifted. A lantern in the storage fields. Then another. Then hundreds, folding into darkness as the water took them.

“I knew they were there,” Ilyra said.

“When?”

“No.”

Elian’s voice sharpened. “You knew before the second gate opened. You knew there were workers behind the emergency door.”

“I did not know how many.”

“You knew enough.”

“I knew the eastern wall would rupture if I closed the central sluice.”

“And you knew opening the western relief would drown the camps.”

“I chose the lesser failure.”

“You chose the failure you could describe.”

Ilyra pushed away from the table.

She was back in the lower corridor, her palm against the emergency door. Nera’s voice came through the maintenance tube, muffled by iron and distance.

Ilyra? Are you there?

She had been there.

She could have opened the door. It would have flooded the control chamber, destroyed the manifold, and perhaps killed the people inside. It might also have let the trapped workers reach a higher corridor. The calculations were uncertain.

The one certainty was that the gates would become uncontrollable.

She had sealed the door.

She had told them to wait.

Then she had opened the western relief.

“I saved the eastern line,” she said.

Elian stepped closer. “You saved the eastern line.”

“If it had ruptured, the death count would have been—”

“Do not give me the count.”

Ilyra stopped.

“Do not make them into a number so you can survive choosing,” Elian said. “My mother died on the platform. My brothers died there. My father escaped beneath it. I know what numbers conceal.”

“Your father’s orders created the conditions.”

“And you opened the gate.”

“Yes.”

“Both things must remain true.”

Ilyra wanted to tell her that she had not seen the broken valve, the rising water, or the pressure threatening the eastern embankment. She wanted to insist that a city could not be saved by people who refused to choose.

But that was Pell’s language.

The language of sealed records and emergency powers.

The language that made every person an obstruction between certainty and the desired result.

“I was trying to stop the flood,” she said.

“You were also trying to punish them.”

“I did not intend for—”

“Intent is not a gate.”

A line of water ran down the wall behind Elian and vanished beneath the floor.

“I wanted the governors to be afraid,” Ilyra said.

She had not meant to speak the admission aloud.

“I wanted them to understand that the walls did not make them safe. I wanted them to feel the city move beneath them. I thought if they were afraid for one hour, they might understand what the Low Quarter endured for generations.”

“And if they did not understand?”

“Then they would at least be afraid.”

Elian nodded once. “That is vengeance.”

“No.” The answer came too quickly. “Vengeance is personal.”

“Was the Low Quarter not personal?”

“The flood was structural.”

“You keep speaking as if structure cannot contain hatred.”

Ilyra looked at the map. The lines had blurred where dampness reached the paper. Each channel seemed to end at a body.

“Justice requires consequence,” she said.

“Justice does not require you to deliver it.”

“If no one else would—”

“There. That is the sentence.”

The old mechanism turned inside her.

No one else understood. No one else had the courage. No one else could act before the pressure rose.

The argument had always been true enough to be dangerous.

She had been the only engineer with the corrected figures. The only one who knew the embankment had been weakened. The only one with access to the controls after her forged seal opened the door.

She had mistaken singular knowledge for sovereign right.

Elian touched the edge of the map. “What happens when you are wrong?”

“I revise the model.”

“What happens when there is no time?”

“I act.”

“What happens when your action kills people?”

Ilyra said nothing.

“What happens when you believe the deaths prove the model was right?”

The Hall’s hidden knocks came again.

Seven.

Not random. Measured.

Maret went pale. “That was the signal.”

“From the conservatory channel?”

“Or beneath us.”

Ilyra traced the old line toward the settling chamber. The route beneath the platform could place her at the manifold. It could also place her in command of everything.

For one instant, the plan became simple.

She would take the lower stair, use the pin, threaten the keeper, open the Crown discharge, close the Sable gate, and redirect the surge through the terraces. If necessary, she would hold every lever herself until the water fell.

No delay. No argument. No district allowed to sacrifice another while waiting for confirmation.

The city would live because she had decided who must lose.

Her pulse quickened. The sensation was almost pleasure.

Elian saw it. “No.”

“I have not said anything.”

“You do not have to.”

“I can reach the manifold before the pressure peaks.”

“And take control.”

“I can prevent a collapse.”

“You can choose the victims.”

“There are already victims.”

“And you want the right to name them.”

Maret’s hand closed around the knife at her belt. “You always say there is no time.”

Ilyra turned toward her.

“That is what you said in the first flood,” Maret continued. “No time to open the door. No time to find everyone. No time to do anything except hold the key.”

There had been no safe time.

But there had been time to ask.

Time to tell Nera what she knew.

Time to admit the map was wrong.

Time, perhaps, to put down the key.

Maret’s face twisted. “My child is in Foundry Row. Choose.”

The command struck the old place where every decision waited to become hers.

She could feel the manifold beneath the floor, each channel a line of pressure, each district a weight on a scale. If she took the controls, she might save Maret’s child. She might save Sable Ward. She might even save the people hidden under the Hall.

Or she might be wrong again.

“I will not open a gate without confirmation,” Ilyra said.

Elian studied her. “Say it again.”

“I will not open a gate without confirmation from the receiving district, the district taking the discharge, and the pressure reader below.”

“Even if that means losing time?”

“Yes.”

“Even if the Crown refuses?”

“Then the Crown refuses in the open.”

“Even if Sable Ward’s confirmation never comes?”

Ilyra thought of Maret’s child, the occupied-room list, and the yellow sleep shirt with one red boot. She thought of Nera behind the sealed door. Of Corin Voss and five others reduced to a line in her notebook.

“Then no gate opens,” she said.

Maret stared at her. “You would let them drown?”

“No.”

“That is what you just said.”

“I said I will not open a gate without knowing where the water goes.”

“You know where it goes now.”

“I know the channels. I do not know the people inside them.”

“My child is inside one of them.”

“I know.”

“Then choose.”

The old answer rose in Ilyra’s throat: I choose.

Instead, she looked at the pin beneath her tongue.

She removed it and placed it on the map beside the three circles.

“It will hold the bypass,” she said. “If it is needed.”

Elian’s eyes followed the movement. “Not unless the confirmations come.”

“Not unless.”

“And if they do not?”

“Then I will not make the decision for them.”

Elian searched her face. “If you find a faster way, you tell the others before you use it.”

Anger rose, familiar and hot. They did not trust her. They wanted her knowledge but not her authority, her hands but not her judgment.

Then she remembered Nera’s voice through the door.

Ilyra? Are you there?

“Yes,” Ilyra said.

The locks turned outside. Pell’s procession had begun. The wash attendants would be carrying white cloth, bronze chains, and the basin used before the Ember Descent. Beyond them, galleries were filling. The city waited to watch her return to water.

Maret straightened and wiped her face.

Below them, the hidden people knocked again.

Three. Three. Three.

A confirmation seeking a confirmation.

Ilyra put the map inside her coat and faced the door.

For forty-one days, she had measured every guard, hinge, drain, and breath in the Hall so that nothing would happen without her knowing.

Now the door opened, and she stepped toward the platform without knowing what the people below would choose.

chapters.name: Pell’s Bargain
chapters.content:
### Pell’s Bargain

Magistrate Oren Pell came without the procession.

That was how Ilyra knew the offer would be worse than a sentence.

No lens clerk followed him. No guard announced his rank. He entered alone, closed the door, and left the lock turned. A narrow seam of corridor light remained behind him.

Ilyra counted what was wrong before she looked at his face.

No witness. No recording lens. No ceremonial chain.

His right sleeve was wet to the elbow.

“Your tunnel is leaking,” Pell said.

“Your Hall is leaking.”

“It is an old building.”

“So is the government.”

He set a small black case on the table outside the bars. The table had not been there yesterday. From the case he removed a folded sheet, a glass vial, and a strip of white cloth.

Ilyra rose from the cot. The chain at her waist scraped the stone. “Is that poison?”

“A sedative.”

“Meant to resemble poison?”

“Strong enough to make the Descent painless.”

“The Ember Descent is heated water.”

“The name is older than the method.”

He unfolded the paper. “I have come to offer you a choice.”

“No.”

“You have not heard it.”

“I have heard every choice made in this Hall. They begin with my name and end with someone else’s benefit.”

“Your execution is scheduled for the third hour.”

“Everyone knows.”

“The galleries are full. The ticket houses have sold out. There are wagers on whether you will scream, pray, or address the city.”

“Then why are you here without a lens?”

“Because a public statement requires preparation.”

He slid the paper between the bars.

Ilyra did not touch it.

“You will confess that you acted alone,” he said. “You will state that your warnings were political agitation disguised as engineering, that the Council had no knowledge of your plan, and that you opened the North Barrage out of private grievance and irrational resentment.”

The words did not surprise her. They had been waiting for her before she entered the Hall.

“In exchange,” Pell continued, “the sentence will be amended.”

“To what?”

“Your death will be conducted under the closed apparatus. No audience, no lenses, no steam chamber. You will be sedated before the water reaches you.”

“How generous.”

“Several surviving engineers from your department will not be prosecuted.”

At that, she picked up the paper.

“Names.”

“Halven. Tessa Marr. Corren Dey. Nera Vale.”

The cell seemed to contract around Nera’s name.

For a moment Ilyra saw the apprentice on the western catwalk, a coil of copper wire over one shoulder, ink beneath her fingernails. Nera had been nineteen and perpetually offended by the world’s failure to respect her calculations. When she thought, she tapped her thumb against her forefinger: three taps, a pause, two taps.

“She is being held,” Ilyra said.

“She is being questioned.”

“For forty days.”

“She is alive.”

“That is not the same as safe.”

“It is the condition under which I can make her safe.”

Ilyra read the statement again.

I, Ilyra Voss, acted alone.

I rejected every lawful correction offered to me.

I allowed class grievance to corrupt professional judgment.

I conceived the opening of the North Barrage as an act of mass violence.

The Council did not know.

The Crown did not know.

No engineer, official, or civic department instructed or assisted me.

Every lie had been given enough truth to stand upright. She had acted alone at the gate. Her hands had opened the lock. Grievance had entered her judgment. She had conceived the intervention.

The Council had known about the flood.

Arce had known about the maps.

Dault had known enough to save himself.

Pell watched her. “You see the advantage.”

“I see the workmanship.”

“You wrote half of it.”

“I wrote warnings.”

“Warnings that can be interpreted as threats.”

“By men who had already decided which district to drown.”

“There is no lens here,” Pell said.

“There does not need to be one for you to remember what I say.”

He pushed the vial through the bars. It rolled across the floor and stopped against her boot.

“You have spent your life insisting that systems matter,” he said. “This is one system you can still influence.”

“What happens to the records?”

“The official records remain.”

“Altered surveys. Missing valve reports. Evacuation orders.”

“Those matters have been reviewed.”

“By whom?”

“By the Council’s legal office.”

“So no one.”

“You are confusing lack of public agreement with lack of truth.”

“I am confusing nothing.”

He tapped the case. “The people want an ending. They want a person who can be blamed. If you give them one, the city can heal.”

“The city can forget.”

“Forgetfulness is sometimes mercy.”

“For whom?”

“For the living.”

“Then name the four.”

His expression tightened. “You know them.”

“Names are not an inconvenience.”

“Senior Engineer Halven. Surveyor Tessa Marr. Valve specialist Corren Dey. Apprentice Engineer Nera Vale.”

“Arce?”

“Is not included.”

“Arce altered the surveys.”

“Arce is under medical supervision.”

“Arce helped remove the valves.”

“Arce is not part of this negotiation.”

“Then it is not a negotiation.”

Pell folded his hands. “You have always believed that every person must be brought into the calculation.”

“I believe people are not numbers.”

“No. You believe people are numbers when you are the one doing the counting.”

The accusation struck because it was true enough to wound.

She remembered the maintenance corridor: the gauge trembling above red, the emergency door shuddering in its frame, water rising on the other side.

Nera’s voice had come through the speaking tube.

“Ilyra, the west wall is going.”

“I know.”

“There are thirty-two here. Maybe more.”

“Find the service shaft.”

“You said there was a shaft.”

“There is supposed to be one.”

A silence.

“Supposed to be?”

Ilyra had stood with the valve key in one hand and the pressure chart in the other. If she opened the door, the control chamber would flood. If she kept it sealed, the trapped workers might drown. Thirty-two against a rupture that could kill thousands.

She had made the calculation.

She had also imagined the governors on the ceremonial platform, looking down and seeing water where their shoes had been.

Pell said, “You are not being asked to say no one else was negligent. You are being asked to say no one else planned the flood.”

“That is not what your statement says.”

“It says what the city can understand.”

“The city understood the ration ledgers. It understood the gates.”

“The city understands spectacle.”

Above them, a crowd began to chant.

Voss.

Voss.

Voss.

The sound fell through the Hall like gravel.

Pell’s voice remained mild. “They do not want hydraulic design. They want to know why you did it.”

“Because the eastern embankment was being sacrificed.”

“Because you hated the Crown.”

“Those things are not mutually exclusive.”

“Not in your mind.”

“In the city.”

He sighed. “You are making this difficult because you think difficulty proves integrity.”

“I am making it difficult because it is difficult.”

He pushed the vial farther across the floor. “You have until the procession reaches the east stair.”

“How long?”

“Less than an hour.”

“And if I refuse?”

“The four engineers will be charged.”

“On what grounds?”

“Conspiracy. Obstruction. Misuse of civic instruments. Sedition, perhaps.”

“Halven signed the reinforcement orders.”

“He will be accused of hiding your intent.”

“Tessa reported the altered surveys.”

“She will be called an accomplice attempting to conceal her own involvement.”

“Corren was ordered to remove the valves.”

“By whom?”

Pell’s gaze held hers.

The unspoken name entered the cell.

Arce.

Ilyra could see how it would proceed. Halven would become the senior engineer who failed to stop a madwoman. Tessa would become a frightened clerk. Corren would be made to name others. Nera would receive the same choice Pell now offered her: speak the authorized truth, or watch the people beside her disappear.

Ilyra picked up the vial. It was warm.

“Painless,” she said.

“As painless as anything can be.”

“After I speak?”

“Before the sentence is read.”

“So I will not hear the crowd.”

“No.”

“I will not see the lenses.”

“No.”

“I will not stand on the platform.”

“No.”

The vial weighed almost nothing.

She imagined swallowing it. The quiet spreading through her hands. No steam, no chains tightening over her wrists, no public statement forced from her while the city listened for madness or repentance.

Instead, she would give them a composed voice.

I acted alone.

The sentence could become a wall. Behind it, Halven, Tessa, Corren, Nera. Perhaps they would live. Perhaps Nera would leave the Hall and find no place in the city, but alive meant possibility. Alive meant testimony. Alive meant someone might someday find the maps.

And Ilyra could determine what the city heard at the end.

She turned toward the wall.

Her mother’s hands appeared there, sorting grain from sawdust. Tomas laughing when Ilyra said the ration scales were false. Tomas arrested for stealing a ledger he had taken only to show her the altered columns.

They had called it theft.

A clean word. A person shaped around it.

Pell said, “You could still do one useful thing.”

She looked back.

“Do not mistake this for kindness,” he said. “I am offering order where there would otherwise be disorder.”

“You are offering to kill me in a way that protects the people who made the killing possible.”

“I am offering to prevent four lives from being consumed by your refusal to distinguish responsibility from association.”

“Those are your words.”

“They are accurate.”

“No. They are useful.”

His hand flattened against the table. “You have been given an opportunity most condemned criminals would beg for.”

“Most condemned criminals are not asked to erase the conditions of their crime.”

“Your crime is not conditions. Your crime is the flood.”

“Yes.”

The answer unsettled him.

Ilyra touched the statement. “If I sign this, Nera survives under a story that makes her silence part of my crime. Halven becomes the engineer who failed to stop a madwoman. Tessa becomes a frightened clerk. Corren becomes an accomplice who received mercy. The Council keeps its maps. The governors keep their orders. Arce keeps his name.”

“Arce will be dealt with.”

“By whom?”

“By the proper authorities.”

“The proper authorities are why he is still alive.”

Pell leaned close. “You are not in a position to demand justice for anyone.”

“No,” she said. “But neither are you.”

A knock sounded beneath the floor.

One.

The stone trembled.

Pell looked down.

Another knock.

Then another.

Three in all, measured and deliberate.

“Buildings settle,” he said.

“Buildings do not knock in threes.”

“Your imagination has always been fertile.”

Water slid from the drain in a thin brown thread, carrying grit and something pale that caught against the grate.

Pell did not look at it.

“The offer expires when the procession reaches the east stair,” he said. “After that, the statement is withdrawn. The engineers will be charged before noon.”

“Then they should know who charged them.”

“They will know you chose not to save them.”

“I know.”

That was the terrible part. She did know.

Pell had placed four names before her because he understood that she still thought in gates.

Open this, and they live.

Close this, and they drown.

He wanted her to believe refusal was another form of control.

Perhaps it was.

She lifted the vial. The crowd above roared. The drumbeat began, slow and ceremonial.

Ilyra imagined taking the bargain. A painless death. Four lives spared. One final arrangement intact.

But she also imagined her statement being preserved beneath a seal, brought out at anniversaries, taught to children as the whole truth: the Low Quarter had produced one brilliant monster and no civic engineers.

She wanted to write the ending so perfectly that no one could alter it. She wanted her last words to become the map everyone used. Pell had recognized that hunger and was feeding it.

A surrender could still be a conquest.

Ilyra set the vial beside the paper.

“I will not sign.”

Pell’s face went blank.

“Ilyra.”

“I will not say I acted alone. I will not say the Council did not know. I will not turn Nera’s survival into proof that your system worked.”

“You are condemning them.”

“I may be.”

“Then you are exactly what they say.”

“No.” She pushed the statement back through the bars. “I am refusing to make their innocence depend on my lie.”

He did not take the pages. They protruded between the bars like a tongue.

The corridor lock clicked. A guard called, “Magistrate?”

Pell kept his eyes on her.

“You will beg for this before the third hour,” he said.

“Perhaps.”

“You will hear them name you.”

“They already do.”

“You will discover that truth does not save anyone.”

Ilyra looked at the vial, the paper, and the dark seam beneath the floor.

“No,” she said. “But lies choose who gets to keep hurting people.”

Pell snatched the statement from the bars. It tore at one corner. He returned the vial to its case and turned toward the corridor.

“Tell Nera I refused,” Ilyra said.

He paused.

“Tell all four of them. Tell them I did not purchase their lives. Tell them you offered them to me.”

Pell looked over his shoulder.

“You still think this is about what you say.”

“No,” she said. “I think it is about what you can no longer prevent others from saying.”

He left.

The lock turned. His footsteps receded toward the east stair, swallowed by the wet corridors of the Hall.

Ilyra stood beside the table.

The vial was gone. The paper was gone. The choice remained inside her, heavy and warm as the metal pin hidden beneath her tongue.

She pressed her teeth against it.

For one breath she imagined pulling it free, taking the nearest lever, deciding the shape of the water herself.

Then the stone knocked from below.

Three.

Three.

Three.

Ilyra stepped away from the table and waited for an answer that was not hers alone to give.

chapters.name: Sable Ward Rising
chapters.content:
### Sable Ward Rising

The first water entered Sable Ward through the foundries.

It came beneath the western doors in thin black tongues, sliding over the iron thresholds and carrying ash, filings, and the sour glitter of oil. The night shift workers saw it before the bells did. They lifted their boots onto the casting tables and watched the water spread between the rails.

A foreman ran to the district office for an evacuation permit.

The office had closed its shutters.

Behind them, a clerk read from a prepared notice: infrastructure instability, temporary restrictions, remain in assigned housing, await authorized transport. The foreman pressed his stamped work token against the wood and shouted that the furnaces were going under.

A guard answered from the other side.

“Upper districts are receiving displaced persons. No passage without a Crown permit.”

The foreman looked back toward the foundry. Steam had begun to rise where the flood touched the hot channels.

By dawn, the water was at the knees of the tenements.

Ilyra learned this in pieces.

First, through the damp air entering the cell. Then through the drain, which burped and settled, burped and settled, each time leaving a darker stain around the iron grate. After that came the sounds from beyond the walls: a runner’s boots on the upper corridor, a door slammed against its frame, voices lowered when they passed her cell.

She counted the intervals.

The drain released twice in the space between the third and fourth bells. The pressure was increasing, though not yet violently. Water had reached the old conservatory channel or one of its branches. The Hall stood on raised foundation stone, but the original settling chamber beneath it had been built to receive sudden surges from the river. If the chamber was filling, the flood was no longer merely entering Sable Ward. It was being brought under the Hall.

That was the part the Council would call an accident.

She put her palm against the wall.

The stone trembled.

Not from the city above. The Hall was always full of movement: guards, clerks, lens operators, prisoners being dragged toward the courts. This vibration came through the foundation, a deep continuous shudder like an animal trying not to breathe.

Ilyra closed her eyes and saw the first flood.

The eastern embankment had broken in three stages. First the hairline crack beneath the dyehouses. Then the long splitting sound under the market tower. Then the water rising through the floorboards while people stood on counters and shouted names into the dark.

She had heard those names and sorted them.

Not consciously, not at first. The mind did it before the conscience could intervene. A child’s voice, a woman’s cry, the crash of a wall: noise. Pressure, flow, capacity: numbers. She had been able to preserve the eastern line if she abandoned the lower pump. She had been able to save the pump if she released the relief lever. Six lost, pressure reduced, east line preserved.

The sentence remained because she had written it.

She had once believed that writing a thing clearly was a form of honesty.

A key scraped in the lock.

Ilyra opened her eyes.

Maret stood outside with her hair coming loose from its binding and her uniform dark at the hem. She held a folded sheet in one hand. There was mud on her cheek.

“You’re being moved,” she said.

“When?”

“Now.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the only one I have.”

Maret looked over her shoulder before entering. The corridor beyond was empty except for a lens mounted near the ceiling. Its glass eye had been turned toward the cell.

“The third hour is not far off,” Maret said. “Pell wants the procession started before the galleries fill.”

“Why are you wet?”

Maret’s mouth tightened.

“Because the lower passage is flooding.”

Ilyra rose from the cot. The chain at her wrists pulled taut, and the room tilted briefly around her. She steadied herself against the wall.

“Foundry Row?”

“Water in the foundries. Sable Ward’s lower tenements have been blocked from the upper road.”

“Blocked by whom?”

Maret did not answer.

Ilyra looked at the folded sheet. “Reports.”

“Read them.”

Maret pushed the paper through the bars.

The first page bore the Council’s blue seal. It described an infrastructure emergency caused by “unlicensed interference with western drainage architecture.” Residents were instructed to remain calm and await authorized relocation. The second page was handwritten in a hurried, slanting script. Water in Foundry Row. Three buildings emptied. Four still occupied. No boats. Guards at North Steps. Permits denied to anyone without Crown or Merchant registration.

At the bottom, someone had written: THEY ARE KEEPING THE ROAD CLOSED.

Ilyra read it twice.

“Who wrote this?”

“Someone who got past the first barricade.”

“Did they see the channels?”

“They saw the water.”

“That’s not enough.”

Maret gave a humorless laugh. “People are drowning. Perhaps you can forgive them for failing to take measurements.”

The paper shook slightly between them. Ilyra noticed the tremor in Maret’s fingers and the pale crescent where her nails had cut her palm.

“Your child,” Ilyra said.

Maret stared at her.

“You said she was near Foundry Row.”

“I said nothing.”

“You didn’t have to.”

For a moment, Maret looked as though she might strike her. Instead she folded her hand around the edge of the paper.

“Lenn is in a room above the ropewalk,” she said. “Her grandmother cannot walk. The permit office told me the district was under controlled evacuation and no family movement was authorized.”

“Controlled,” Ilyra repeated.

“That is the word.”

“It means they are holding the exits.”

“It means they have a list.”

Ilyra looked again at the Council notice. The language was familiar. She had read its earlier versions before the first flood: inventory transfer, temporary clearance, protection of strategic assets. Words made smooth enough to pass over people without catching.

“Take me to the manifold,” she said.

Maret’s expression changed. “No.”

“If the pressure is already beneath the Hall—”

“You’re being taken to the platform.”

“Then take me there by way of the lower chamber.”

“I said no.”

“The old conservatory branch is filling. If the receiving channel remains closed, the water will return against the cistern wall.”

“Your execution is in less than an hour.”

“Then you should move quickly.”

Maret folded the reports and shoved them back through the bars. “You think this is another one of your gates. You see a lever and believe the city has given you a purpose.”

“I see people trapped in a district the Council has decided to sacrifice.”

“You saw that before.”

The words struck more cleanly than any accusation Pell had made.

Maret stepped closer to the bars. “You saw the storage fields. You knew there were families there.”

“I knew some workers used the fields.”

“You knew.”

“I did not know how many.”

“You knew enough to ask.”

Ilyra held her gaze. “If I had stopped to verify every occupied structure—”

“Then perhaps some people would be alive.”

The corridor seemed to narrow around them. Water ticked somewhere below.

Maret’s voice broke, but she did not lower it. “Do not stand there and tell me that knowing less made you innocent.”

Ilyra looked down at the drain.

The water in it moved backward.

A dark bubble rose, broke, and vanished.

Behind Maret, someone called for the procession guard. Boots answered from the stair.

“Open the cell,” Ilyra said.

Maret’s hand went to her keys.

“Why?”

“Because the city is being flooded.”

“I know that.”

“Because they will use my death to make it look like the flood ended with the first one.”

“I know that too.”

“Then open the cell.”

Maret did not move.

From farther down the corridor came a cry, muffled by stone. Then another. Not a guard’s command. A child, perhaps, or someone calling through a blocked passage.

Maret turned toward the sound.

Ilyra felt the old impulse rise inside her, swift and bright. Take the key. Open the door. Reach the machinery. Give the water a direction. Every delay was a death. Every question was a body behind a wall.

She could feel the manifold in her mind though she had never seen this altered version of it. The Crown cisterns would be releasing in timed intervals. Reservoir Six and Eight, likely. The pressure entered through the garden channels, passed beneath the Merchant terraces, and collected in the conservatory basin. If the Foundry Row branch was closed, the basin would climb until the old masonry failed. The failure would tear through Sable Ward first, then announce itself as a natural collapse.

Unless someone opened the central discharge.

Unless someone reached the keeper.

Unless someone took control.

The thought warmed her like fever.

Maret’s keys chimed as she closed her hand around them.

“Guards are coming,” she said.

“Then decide.”

“You make it sound simple.”

“It is simple. Open the cell.”

“No.” Maret stepped back. “If I do this, they will call it an escape. They’ll shoot everyone in the lower passages.”

“They are already killing people.”

“And if we rush the controls, they’ll call every person who helps you a conspirator. They’ll close the districts, seize the boats, arrest the engineers. They’ll have exactly the story they want.”

A second voice came from the stairwell.

“Not if the story gets there first.”

Elian Dault emerged from the shadows with a soaked cloak over her shoulders. Her boots left a trail of water across the stone. She carried no guard’s insignia, only a leather case strapped beneath her coat.

Maret spun toward her. “How did you—”

“Your colleague let me through.”

“He’ll lose his post.”

“He already lost his house.”

Elian approached the cell and looked at Ilyra. Her face was pale from cold, but her eyes were steady.

“The east archive tower is still answering,” she said. “The Crown has shut down the central announcers, but not all the district lenses. I can send the evacuation orders through the towers if we get them connected.”

“Orders won’t open gates,” Ilyra said.

“They may open people’s eyes.”

“People need boats.”

“Jorren is moving them.”

“How many?”

“Enough for one route. Perhaps two.”

“Then he needs the channels opened.”

“Yes.”

“And the channels need control.”

Elian nodded. “Shared control.”

Ilyra laughed once. It sounded unpleasant in the cell.

“Now?”

“Especially now.”

Maret looked between them. “What are you talking about?”

“Your child’s district is being deliberately flooded,” Elian said. “The Council is forcing water into Sable Ward while keeping the upper roads closed. If the records are broadcast, residents may break the barricades. If they break the barricades without routes, they’ll be driven into the water.”

“Then we open the roads and the gates.”

“With whose authority?”

Maret’s face hardened. “Mine, if you give me a weapon.”

“That is the authority they understand,” Elian said. “It is also the one they will use to condemn us.”

Ilyra pushed her hands through the bars. “Give me the pin.”

Elian’s expression sharpened.

“You have it?”

“Not here.”

The thin metal pin lay hidden beneath Ilyra’s tongue, warm from her body. She could feel its edge whenever she swallowed. It had seemed absurd when she first accepted it: a sliver of old governor-arm hardware, too small to matter. Now she imagined setting it into the bypass housing and forcing the lever past its damaged stop.

The old instinct returned with perfect clarity.

Reach the control chamber. Remove the keeper’s hand. Open the Crown discharge. Let the gardens and terraces take what they had sent below. The water would rise around the ceremonial platform. Governors would run in their white coats. The galleries would scream. The people watching her die would discover that the city’s foundations did not belong to them.

She wanted it.

The wanting was not a metaphor. It had weight, shape, temperature. It pressed against her teeth.

Elian saw something in her face.

“No,” she said.

“I haven’t done anything.”

“You’ve already chosen.”

“The Crown district is the discharge path. If we reverse the flow—”

“You will be sending water into a place you cannot see.”

“I can calculate the capacity.”

“You can calculate stone, not people.”

“I can save Sable Ward.”

“You can choose Sable Ward.”

The corridor filled with the sound of water moving through hidden pipes.

Ilyra gripped the bars. “If we wait for confirmations, the cistern may rupture.”

“If you take the controls alone, the cistern may rupture somewhere else.”

“There is no time for a council meeting.”

“Then don’t hold a council meeting. Get two people to confirm the receiving district. Get one pressure reading from beneath the Hall. Let the keeper know which gate is being opened. Make the decision fast, but do not make it yours alone.”

Ilyra’s mind rejected the proposal on instinct. Three confirmations. Three points of failure. A delayed runner, a broken lens, a frightened keeper. The system would become hesitant precisely when hesitation killed.

She remembered the first flood.

The valve key had been in her hand. Lysa Renn’s fingers had closed around hers. The child’s red boot had slipped against the roof tiles. Behind them, the water had swallowed the street.

If Ilyra released the key, she could lift the child. If she kept it, she could stabilize the eastern line.

She had called it an impossible choice because impossible choices absolved the chooser. But it had not been impossible. It had been cruel. She had chosen the key.

She had preserved a structure and lost a child.

Not all choices were equations. Some were simply made.

“I need the reports,” Ilyra said.

Maret frowned. “You have them.”

“Names. Occupied rooms. Every route Jorren has.”

Elian unfastened the leather case and drew out several folded sheets. “Jorren sent these.”

Ilyra scanned them.

Foundry Row: six occupied buildings confirmed, three uncertain. Ropewalk: grandmother and child, location presumed upper floor. Old dye market: boats delayed by debris. Conservatory branch: passable to the third bend. North Steps: guarded. Sable infirmary: patients immobile, no permits issued.

“No boats at the infirmary?” Ilyra asked.

“Two,” Elian said. “Jorren had to send them toward the lower foundries.”

“Then the infirmary will be empty before the next rise.”

“Perhaps.”

“Perhaps is not a route.”

“No,” Elian said. “It is the truth.”

Ilyra looked at her.

Elian’s face held no triumph. Only exhaustion, and beneath it the hard refusal to let certainty become another kind of lie.

“What do you want me to do?” Ilyra asked.

“Help us reach the controls without becoming the controls.”

The guards appeared at the end of the corridor.

Pell walked between them, dry now, immaculate in his ceremonial black. Behind him came the lens crew carrying their tripod and mirrored apparatus. The glass lenses turned toward Ilyra, catching her reflection in fragments: one eye, half a mouth, a white strip of forehead.

Pell saw Elian first.

“Lady Dault,” he said. “You have no authorization to be below the Hall.”

“Nor do you have authorization to drown Sable Ward.”

“An unfortunate allegation.”

“It’s in your orders.”

Pell’s gaze moved to the papers in her hand. “Those are stolen records.”

“They are signed records.”

“Then they will be examined after the emergency.”

“After the district is underwater?”

“After the condemned woman has been properly delivered to judgment.”

Ilyra stepped toward the bars. “You know the cistern is filling.”

Pell’s expression did not change, but a muscle moved beneath his eye.

“You know the old manifold cannot take the pressure,” she continued. “You know the Foundry Row branch is closed.”

“The city’s systems are under strain.”

“You are directing the strain.”

“Your talent for accusation is the reason you are here.”

“No. My talent for opening things is the reason I am here.”

The lens operator adjusted the focus.

Pell glanced at Maret. “Unlock the cell.”

Maret’s face emptied.

Ilyra heard the three knocks beneath the floor.

One.

Two.

Three.

Pell heard them too. His eyes flicked downward before he could stop himself.

“Settling stone,” he said.

“Buildings don’t knock,” Ilyra replied.

“Move her.”

Maret did not take out her keys.

Pell’s voice sharpened. “Guard.”

From the stair came a shout, then a crash. Somewhere above, a bell began ringing—not the measured Hall bell, but the frantic alarm used for fire or breach.

Elian slipped the papers into her coat.

“Now,” she said.

Ilyra touched the pin beneath her tongue.

For one instant, she could take the cell door, the corridor, the guards, the entire submerged machinery of Veyr, and force it into a single decision. She could become the hand on every gate.

Then she looked at Maret.

“Your child is in Foundry Row,” Ilyra said. “I will not open a channel toward that district without confirmation that the people there can survive it.”

Maret’s hand closed around the keys.

“And if we cannot get confirmation?”

“Then we find another route.”

“That may take too long.”

“Yes.”

The answer frightened them all.

Pell ordered the guards forward.

Maret unlocked the cell.

Not toward the platform, not yet. She pulled the door wide as the Hall shuddered around them, and brown water surged through the drain, spilling across the floor between their feet.

Ilyra stepped into it.

Above, Sable Ward was rising. Below, something knocked three times again.

And for the first time since the water had become her weapon, she did not reach for the nearest lever.

chapters.name: The Archive Plan
chapters.content:
### The Archive Plan

The corridor beyond the cell sloped downward.

Ilyra felt it before she saw it: the water gathered more heavily beneath her left foot, then pulled toward the wall as if the Hall had developed a hidden current. Brown foam curled around the stones. The drain behind them gave a wet cough and expelled a scrap of pale cloth.

Maret gripped Ilyra’s arm. “Move.”

“I can walk.”

“Then walk faster.”

Elian came behind them, one hand braced against the wall, her archive satchel held above the water. Pell’s guards shouted somewhere beyond the intersection. Their voices struck the stone and returned in fragments.

“—under sentence—”

“—Magistrate ordered—”

“—stop them—”

Ilyra counted the corridor’s arches as they passed. Four to the conservatory stair. Seven to the old settling chamber, if the western wall had not shifted. The water stood three inches deep at the first arch and five at the second. It rose in pulses, not steadily. A release upstream. Another reservoir transfer.

“They’ve opened something,” she said.

Elian glanced at her. “You sound surprised.”

“I’m measuring.”

“You always call it that when you’re afraid.”

Ilyra nearly stopped. Maret pulled her onward.

The conservatory stair had once carried dignitaries from the Hall to a glass-roofed garden above the cistern. Now most of its steps were buried beneath mud and fallen plaster. The air smelled of wet copper, coal oil, and the sharp mineral stink of water forced through old masonry.

At the landing, a man in a soaked engineer’s coat emerged from a side passage. He was broad-shouldered, gray-haired, and carried a brass hand lamp in one fist. His face tightened when he saw Ilyra.

“That’s her.”

“Mara Venn,” Elian said. “Manifold keeper.”

“I know who she is.”

Mara looked at Ilyra’s chains, then at Maret’s keys. “You brought the condemned engineer to the controls?”

“She is the only person who can read the old manifold,” Maret said.

“She is the person who opened the North Barrage.”

“And you are the person who has let the cistern fill while Foundry Row drowns.”

Mara’s mouth shut.

Beyond her, the passage shook. Dust drifted from the ceiling. Something struck metal in the darkness: once, twice, then three times.

Ilyra raised her head.

Three knocks.

Elian heard them too. Her eyes moved toward the blocked passage.

Mara crossed herself in the old dock fashion. “That route has been sealed since the first collapse.”

“Sealed does not mean empty,” Ilyra said.

“No,” Elian replied. “It means someone decided not to look.”

The words entered Ilyra like a thin blade. She turned toward the passage, but the stone there had buckled inward. A maintenance grille showed beyond the rubble, its bars black with rust. Behind it, water moved in the dark.

“Later,” Maret said. “If there is a later.”

Mara led them down.

The settling chamber lay beneath the Hall’s oldest foundation, where the city’s first engineers had allowed river silt and pressure to calm before distributing water through the district channels. The Crown had built over it, then around it, then forgotten its purpose while preserving its machinery. A circular room opened below the stair. Four iron walkways crossed a basin whose bottom could not be seen. Pipes climbed the walls in sweating bundles. At the center stood the manifold: a wheel of bronze gates, each marked with a district seal.

The water had risen to the lower grating.

A pressure gauge trembled beside the central column.

Mara hurried to it. “Redline is gone.”

“Gone where?”

“Past the marked scale.”

Ilyra stepped toward the gauge. The needle quivered against its stop. Elian caught her chain before she could lean over the basin.

“Reading,” Elian said.

Mara gave a short, bitter laugh. “The instrument is broken.”

“Then we need another.”

Ilyra reached into the seam of her execution garment and drew out the brass plate Senn had given her. It was no larger than her palm, scored with a hairline pointer and three notches.

Mara stared. “That’s from the lower intake.”

“It was fixed below the Hall.”

“Was?”

“Fresh wear on the gear teeth,” Elian said. “Senn found it in a Crown reservoir transfer housing.”

Mara took the plate and held it near the gauge. The pointer on the plate jerked toward the second notch.

“Pressure is rising beneath us,” she said. “The old chamber is taking the load.”

“For how long?” Elian asked.

Mara looked at the water. “Not long enough.”

Ilyra studied the manifold. The Crown discharge wheel was on the east side, joined to a descending pipe that ran beneath the ceremonial road. The Sable branch was lower and narrower. Foundry Row split from it at the third bend. If she opened the Crown wheel and locked the Sable gate, the water would rise through gardens, terraces, and warehouses.

The calculation formed cleanly.

“Open Crownward,” she said. “Close the western relief. We can drain the cistern into the upper districts and lower pressure here.”

Maret’s face hardened. “How many people are in the upper districts?”

“Residents have evacuation permits.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

Ilyra looked at the wheel. Behind it, unseen, lay rooms, servants’ quarters, kitchens, guard posts, market stalls, perhaps workers barred from the road. People were always behind the gate. The absence of their names did not make them absent.

Elian took the brass plate from Mara. “This is what you wanted, isn’t it? A pressure reading and a gate in your hand.”

“I want Sable Ward to survive.”

“You want to be certain.”

“Yes.”

“And if certainty is impossible?”

“Then we use the best available—”

“That is how you speak before you decide for everyone.”

The chamber shuddered. Water slapped the underside of the grating. Somewhere high above, a bell began ringing, then broke off after two frantic notes.

Ilyra looked from the manifold to Elian. “You have an alternative?”

“Yes.”

“Tell me.”

“Not here.”

They climbed a narrow ladder to an abandoned clerk’s room above the settling chamber. It had no windows, only a cracked lens housing mounted in the wall and a desk swollen by damp. A dozen cables ran from the housing into the ceiling. Elian opened her satchel and spread papers across the desk, holding the corners down with bolts and a rusted inkpot.

The records were not arranged like engineering documents. They were layered in bundles: Council orders, reservoir tallies, evacuation lists, private route diagrams, copied signatures, scraps of correspondence, and narrow strips of lens film. Some pages were stained dark with water. Others had been folded so often that the creases had become holes.

Ilyra saw Governor Dault’s seal on three orders.

One instructed the Crown wall crews to reinforce the east-facing retaining structures.

Another directed that “nonregistered congestion” in the storage fields be cleared before the Feast transfer.

The third marked a private barge route and listed its departure time.

Elian placed a fourth page over them. “The towers.”

Ilyra frowned. “The central announcer is controlled from the Hall.”

“Central is. The district towers are not all connected to it.”

“They are relay points.”

“Relay points with local maintenance locks. The Crown shut six towers this morning. The east archive tower is still answering. So are the dock tower, the Foundry tower, and two Merchant towers.”

“Mara said the lines were obsolete.”

“They are obsolete to the people who stopped using them.”

Elian unrolled a narrow diagram. It showed Veyr as a web of towers and underground cables, each marked with a district seal. “The surveillance lenses were installed to watch workers. Their image lines run through the same relay houses as the civic announcements. If we seize the relay houses, we can broadcast the records.”

Ilyra studied the diagram. “To whom?”

“To everyone who can still see.”

“By the time they understand the orders, Sable Ward will be under the water.”

“Then we broadcast warnings first. Routes, closures, pressure changes. The records follow.”

“Words don’t move water.”

“No. People do.”

Maret leaned over the desk. “People are being held behind gates.”

“Workers at the Foundry tower have refused to shut the line,” Elian said. “Dock engineers have agreed to open their maintenance locks. Three canal crews have sent word that they will not redirect water without written confirmation from the receiving district.”

Ilyra looked up. “Written?”

“They don’t trust spoken orders anymore. Pell can imitate a voice. He cannot easily imitate every district seal.”

Mara’s expression changed. “Who sent that?”

“An archive runner from the dock.”

“You have runners in the flood?”

“I have clerks, apprentices, lens operators, ferrymen, and two children who know the roof routes better than any official map.”

Ilyra felt the old impatience rise. The room was too small. The papers were too many. The pressure gauge below was climbing. Every minute spent explaining a network was a minute in which the basin filled.

“If we have engineers willing to resist,” she said, “give them the gate commands.”

“That is not enough.”

“It is the necessary part.”

“It is the dangerous part.”

Elian tapped the diagram. “A gate command without a receiving report is another weapon. We need the workers to refuse unauthorized transfers, the towers to broadcast the orders, the boats to clear routes, and the districts to confirm what is occupied. All of it has to happen together.”

“Towers cannot confirm pressure.”

“Then the gauge reader sends the reading.”

“Mara cannot be in every chamber.”

“Neither can you.”

The words settled between them.

Mara took one of the pages. “The Foundry engineers will not act on a general warning. They need proof the Council ordered the closure.”

Elian handed her Dault’s instruction.

Mara read it once. Then again. Her thumb passed over the line ordering the eastern embankment to remain “unburdened by lower-district diversions.”

“They knew,” she said.

“Yes.”

“They knew the west branch was closed.”

“Yes.”

“And they still sent the reservoir water into the cistern.”

“Yes.”

Mara folded the page with careful precision. “I can get this to the Foundry tower.”

“You can get it to three towers,” Elian said. “The relay houses have duplicate lens plates. Show the order to the engineers. Let them read it aloud.”

Ilyra looked at the cracked housing on the wall. “The images will be delayed.”

“By seconds.”

“The records will be cut.”

“Then we use every tower.”

“That multiplies confusion.”

“That is not the same as multiplying uncertainty.”

Ilyra stared at her.

Elian met her gaze. “You think a command is clean because it travels through one hand. It isn’t clean. It only hides the hands beneath yours.”

Below them, the chamber gave a deep groan.

Mara stood. “We need assignments.”

Ilyra reached for the diagram, but stopped before touching it. The plan spread outward in front of her, full of branches she could not see: towers, boats, doors, workers, confirmations. There was no central point from which she could hold the entire mechanism in her mind. No master lever. No single pressure window that would make the others irrelevant.

She hated it immediately.

“Jorren’s people confirm Foundry Row and the ropewalk,” she said. “Not merely whether they can reach it. They report occupied rooms, upper-floor access, and the direction of safe water.”

Elian nodded and marked the diagram.

“Mara carries the written orders to the Foundry and dock towers. She does not authorize a gate.”

Mara’s eyebrows lifted. “I’m the manifold keeper.”

“You are also the person who can show them why refusal is lawful.”

A shadow of approval crossed her face.

“Maret takes the occupied-room list to the platform wardens and the lower rescue crews. She confirms the Crown terraces are not empty before any discharge is considered.”

Maret looked toward the stair. “And Lenn?”

Ilyra met her eyes. “You confirm Foundry Row before the Foundry branch opens. If you cannot confirm, it does not open.”

Maret’s jaw worked. She nodded once.

“Elian broadcasts the orders and warnings. First the evacuation routes. Then the reservoir records. Then the gate conditions.”

“And you?” Elian asked.

Ilyra looked again toward the settling chamber.

“I read the manifold.”

“That is not the same as controlling it.”

“No.”

“Say it clearly.”

Ilyra’s fingers closed around the governor-arm pin hidden beneath her tongue. Its metal pressed against the soft underside of her mouth.

“I do not open a gate alone.”

Elian waited.

“No gate opens without three confirmations,” Ilyra continued. “The district receiving the water. The district taking the discharge. And a true pressure reading from below the Hall.”

“Who records the confirmations?”

“The relay keeper at each tower.”

“And if the keeper refuses?”

“Then the workers choose another.”

“And if they choose badly?”

Ilyra’s first answer rose like reflex: I correct them.

She swallowed it.

“Then we argue with them,” she said.

The chamber shook again. This time the water surged over the lowest grating and climbed the first rung of the ladder.

A voice called from the passage below.

“Mara!”

They all turned.

A young engineer stumbled into the clerk’s room, soaked to the chest. His left hand was wrapped in bloody cloth. “The Crown wardens have reached the manifold. Pell sent them down.”

“How many?” Maret asked.

“Four. Maybe five.”

“Where is Senn?” Ilyra said.

The engineer looked at her with open fear. “He was at the upper stairs. He said he would delay them.”

Elian gathered the papers. “Then we begin now.”
