Ilyra caught one sheet before it slid into the water. It was a copied Council order, unsigned but marked with Arce’s engineering notation. The line directing the western transfer ran through the center of the page.

She could take the paper. She could take the manifold. She could use the pin and make the water obey.

Instead she handed the order to Mara.

“Show them,” she said.

Mara tucked it inside her coat.

“And if they still refuse?” the young engineer asked.

Ilyra looked down at the rising water, then at the network drawn across the desk. Every route led away from her. Every decision required another person to answer.

“Then let the refusal be seen,” she said. “Let the district know who refused, and why. No hidden gate. No silent sacrifice.”

From the tower housing came a crackle.

Then Elian’s voice, transmitted through the old lens line, spoke into the flooded room.

“This is the east archive relay. By order of no single authority, hear and repeat.”

The housing flickered. A blurred image appeared on its glass: a woman in a dockside tower, holding Dault’s instruction before the lens.

Her voice trembled, but carried.

“Reinforce the Crown wall. Do not divert pressure toward the upper districts. Clear the storage fields of inventory. Residents need not be cleared.”

For a moment, nobody moved.

Then another voice answered through the line, rough and male.

“Dock relay receiving. We have the order.”

A third voice followed.

“Foundry relay receiving. We have workers at the locks.”

Mara closed her eyes.

Above them, somewhere in the Hall, the execution bells began again. This time they did not ring in sequence. One bell called from the east gallery. Another answered from the Crown platform. Then a third began below, deep and irregular, as if struck by someone in the dark.

Three knocks.

Three knocks.

Three knocks.

Ilyra placed her hand on the stair rail.

The old impulse urged her downward, toward the wheel, the pin, the single act that could turn terror into consequence.

Instead she waited for the next voice.

“Foundry Row reporting,” it said through the lens. “Six buildings occupied. Three uncertain. We will not open the branch without confirmation.”

Ilyra felt the pressure beneath the Hall rise.

“Good,” she said.

Elian looked at her. “Good?”

“It means they are still choosing.”

Another voice broke through, breathless and distant.

“Ropewalk route blocked. Child and grandmother presumed alive. Boats moving.”

Maret turned toward the stair.

Ilyra caught her sleeve. “Wait for confirmation.”

“My child—”

“Wait.”

The words were cruel. She knew they were cruel. They were also necessary, and the knowledge did not make them easier.

Maret stared at her, then tore free.

“I will confirm it myself.”

She descended into the water.

Ilyra watched her go. The chamber below groaned, and somewhere behind the sealed wall, the hidden survivors struck their signal again.

The network answered in fragments: a tower receiving, a worker refusing, a boat changing course, an engineer asking for a reading no one yet possessed.

No one voice controlled the whole.

For the first time since the flood began, Ilyra could not tell whether that was failure or the beginning of safety.

chapters.name: No Master Key
chapters.content:
The manifold had no master key.

Ilyra discovered this when she stopped looking for one.

The circular chamber shook with water moving beneath it. Bronze gates stood around the basin like spokes, each engraved with a district mark: CROWN, MERCHANT, DOCK, FOUNDRY, SABLE, LOW. The letters had been polished by generations of hands. At the center, beneath a hood of blackened iron, the original control housing had been split open.

Inside, the keeper’s lever was gone. In its place, someone—Arce, or someone following his instructions—had installed three interlocking arms. One socket bore the mark of an engineer. One carried the rough sign of a worker’s guild. The third had been hammered flat and stamped with a district seal.

Ilyra wiped grime from the metal.

“Three confirmations,” she said.

Mara Venn stood behind her, soaked to the waist, one hand against the wall. “For every gate?”

“For every transfer.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“It is if the system was built by people who feared one another.”

Mara’s mouth tightened. “You have been that someone for forty-one days.”

“And I was not innocent.”

“No one said you were.”

The words struck cleanly. Ilyra felt the part of herself that still wanted to divide the world into those who understood pressure and those who did not. She could have answered with a diagram: the narrowed sluice, the missing valves, the eastern wall, the Crown-side bypass. A diagram made grief look like an error in scale.

She crouched beside the basin and drew on the wet stone with charcoal.

“An engineer confirms the pressure and direction. A worker confirms that the gate and receiving channel are clear. A district representative confirms the occupied buildings and evacuation route.”

Mara pointed at the marks. “Which district?”

“The one sending the water and the one receiving it.”

“That makes five confirmations.”

“For a transfer between two districts.”

“And if the water must move now?”

“The engineer marks the pressure window. The worker checks the machinery. The districts speak through the relay. If one is absent, the gate remains closed.”

Mara stared at her. “People will die while we wait.”

“Yes.”

“You say that too easily.”

“I say it because the alternative is pretending they will not.”

The words carried another voice with them.

Six lost, pressure reduced, east line preserved.

She had written that sentence on a maintenance plate while Corin Voss and five others were trapped beyond a broken grating. The relief lever had been slipping beneath her palm. The sentence had seemed necessary—a record for those who would ask why she had not held the lever longer.

Later, she understood it had been a wall.

Elian watched her. “You are already arguing against the design.”

“I am identifying its weaknesses.”

“You are identifying every reason to take control back.”

“Because there are reasons. Suppose Foundry refuses to open its branch because it believes the receiving channel is occupied. Sable rises another hand. Suppose Crown refuses discharge because its terraces contain residents. Suppose a representative is corrupt, frightened, or wrong. The system locks itself while the pressure climbs.”

“And your answer?”

“An override.”

“Held by whom?”

“The manifold keeper.”

Mara gave a humorless laugh. “That would be me?”

“Or whoever is present.”

“Meaning you.”

“A temporary override could trigger when the gauge reaches—”

“The gauge is broken,” Elian said.

“The brass plate gives us a lower-intake reading.”

“A reading that cannot tell us who is in the channel.”

“It can tell us pressure.”

“People change what we owe one another.”

Another groan passed through the chamber. Dust fell into the basin. Ilyra looked toward the unseen Hall, where the execution bells rang out of time. The Council had built its ceremony to make one death visible and every other death obscure.

Elian stepped closer. “The design is not meant to prevent mistakes.”

“It will not.”

“It is meant to prevent certainty from becoming authority.”

Ilyra looked at the three sockets.

At the North Barrage, she had believed that seeing more than anyone else gave her the right to decide for everyone else. She had known the eastern wall would fail. She had known the bypass could lower pressure. She had known the auxiliary housing might open.

She had not known the child’s yellow sleep shirt until the girl was reaching for her. She had not known the red boot until the child’s hand slipped from hers.

No calculation had forced her to keep the valve key.

That was the truth she had buried under totals.

Elian touched the charcoal circle marked DISTRICT. “What counts as confirmation?”

“An acknowledgment spoken through two relay houses and entered into the public record. No verbal approval without a witness.”

“Publicly?”

“If the record is hidden, it can be altered.”

“You have faith in public records?”

“Not records. Witnesses. Records are only the marks they leave behind.”

Mara studied her. “And what are you?”

Ilyra understood.

Not a district representative. Not a worker, though she had spent half her life among machinery. Not merely an engineer, because the word had been used to excuse every decision she made.

“I read the manifold,” she said. “I do not authorize it.”

“Even if you know the others are wrong?”

“Especially then.”

The chamber doors shook.

A voice called from the stairwell. “Mara Venn! By order of Magistrate Pell, stand away from the controls!”

Senn answered from above, hoarse and furious. “By order of everyone still alive, climb back up!”

Metal struck metal. Someone shouted. The noise dissolved into splashing and the thunder beneath the floor.

Mara reached for a wrench.

Ilyra caught her wrist. “Do not fight them here.”

“If they reach the manifold—”

“They will have to choose a gate.”

“They will open Crown.”

“Then the relays will show who authorized it.”

“That will not save anyone.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “But it may keep them from making the next choice in secret.”

Mara stared at her. “You are asking me to let them take the controls.”

“I am asking you not to become the only person who can stop them.”

A wary expression crossed Mara’s face. She released the wrench.

Elian moved toward the arch leading to the conservatory channel. “I am going after the relay runners.”

“You cannot go alone,” Mara said.

“I am not.”

From the darkness came a low whistle, answered twice. Jorren’s network. Boots scraped over stone. A woman called that Foundry Row had confirmed upper rooms in three buildings, though lower floors remained inaccessible. Another voice said boats were clearing the ropewalk route.

“Not enough,” Ilyra said.

“It is what we have,” Elian replied.

“What you have is a beginning.”

He paused. “Do not improve the system while we are gone.”

“I make no promises.”

“That is why we need the locks.”

Then he was gone, carrying the archive papers beneath his coat.

Mara bent over the basin. “What do you need?”

“Read the pressure.”

“The gauge is past red.”

“Use the plate.”

Mara lifted the brass disk. Its needle trembled against the final mark. “This is not reliable.”

“No reading is reliable by itself.”

“You built your life on readings.”

“I built my life on readings no one else could check.”

Mara glanced at her.

Ilyra marked three lines beside the basin. “The plate gives us rising pressure. The east pipe’s vibration gives direction. The lower intake tells us how quickly the system is filling. We compare them.”

“And if they disagree?”

“We wait.”

“While Sable rises?”

“We find another measurement.”

Mara breathed out. “You make waiting sound like an action.”

“It can be.”

The next impact against the stairwell door was heavier. Water pushed through a crack along the floor and spread around their boots.

Ilyra’s instinct moved before thought. She saw the Crown discharge wheel and the governor-arm pin hidden beneath her tongue. She could turn it until the teeth caught, open the channel, and lower western pressure. Crown gardens would become lakes. The ceremonial road would split. The galleries would flood beneath the feet of those waiting to watch her die.

For one clean instant she imagined their faces.

Not dead.

Afraid.

The image had a sweetness she despised.

She removed the pin and held it between two fingers.

Mara saw it. “What is that?”

“A way to force the Crown bypass.”

“Can it save Sable?”

“It can lower western pressure.”

“And where does the water go?”

“Crown.”

“Who is there?”

“I do not know.”

“Then it is not a rescue.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “It is a decision.”

Mara’s eyes hardened. “You have made enough of those.”

The insult was deserved.

Ilyra placed the pin on the stone between them. For several breaths, neither touched it.

Then Mara pushed it away from the controls.

“Let them confirm,” she said.

“They may not.”

“Then we will know what we are refusing.”

The three knocks sounded again, nearer now.

Three.

Three.

Three.

Not through the floor this time. Through the wall beside the sealed passage.

Mara crossed to it and pressed her ear against the wet stone. “There are people in there.”

“Or machinery,” Ilyra said.

Mara looked back.

Ilyra closed her eyes. “No. You are right.”

Senn appeared at the stairwell arch, blood running from his brow. Behind him, the door had buckled inward. He carried a ring of keys in one hand and an iron bar in the other.

“Four wardens,” he said. “Maybe five. I bought minutes.”

“Pell?” Mara asked.

“Still upstairs, or pretending to be.” Senn looked toward the manifold. “Which gate?”

“None,” Ilyra said.

“Good.” He lifted a key stamped with the black enamel of Hall detention. “I have something else to do.”

“The prisoners?” Mara asked.

“The ones who can walk, row, climb, carry, or tell us where the Hall has hidden people.”

“Some attacked wardens,” Mara said.

“One attacked me.”

“You said he broke your nose.”

“He did.”

“And you are freeing him?”

“If he can carry a child.”

Senn turned toward the passage.

Ilyra said, “They may turn on you.”

“They already have reasons.”

“You cannot free people you do not control.”

He gave a short, bitter laugh. “That is the first good thing you have said all morning.”

He moved away.

The three knocks came again, now joined by a faint scraping. Someone struck the stone from within.

Senn stopped and examined the sealed passage. “There is no lock on this side.”

“Because it was not meant to open from this side,” Mara said.

Ilyra studied the masonry. Stones had been laid over an older maintenance door, but three vertical plates interrupted the wall at shoulder height. Each bore a shallow indentation.

Engineer. Worker. District.

The old system had not been erased. It had been buried.

“Can you open it?” Senn asked.

“Not alone.”

“We do not have time to assemble a committee for a door.”

“Then we use the people here.”

Mara put her hand against the first plate. “Worker.”

Ilyra touched the second. “Engineer.”

Senn looked at the third. “District.”

“You are not a district representative,” Mara said.

“I am the only person here assigned to keep people in this building.”

“Assigned by Pell.”

“Not anymore.”

The wall shuddered. Someone struck it from within.

Three times.

Senn placed his palm against the third plate.

Nothing happened.

“Seal?” he asked.

Ilyra drew a LOW mark on the plate with charcoal.

The bronze warmed. A tooth shifted inside the wall.

“Not a seal,” she said. “A claim.”

“Whose claim?”

“Whoever is willing to answer for what comes through.”

Senn kept his hand in place. “Then open it.”

Ilyra looked at the submerged grating, the rising water, the Crown wheel, and the pin resting on the stone.

Every mechanism offered a faster path if she was willing to become its only hand.

She left the pin where it was.

“Wait,” she said.

Senn’s face twisted. “For what?”

“For a confirmation.”

The wall struck back from within.

Three.

Three.

Three.

And from the upper stairs, the wardens began breaking through.

chapters.name: The Last Night
chapters.content:
## The Last Night

The wall struck three times.

Ilyra kept her hand on the bronze plate and felt the answer move through the stone: a shudder beneath the chamber, a tremor in the black water around her boots, then silence.

Three more blows followed.

Senn looked toward the stairwell. “They’ve reached the inner door.”

Mara Venn’s palm remained on the worker’s plate. “The passage is responding.”

“To them?”

“To us.”

Water had risen over the lowest rim of the circular manifold. Six bronze gates crouched around the basin, marked CROWN, MERCHANT, DOCK, FOUNDRY, SABLE, and LOW. Above them, three interlocking arms waited for an engineer, a worker, and a district representative.

No master lever. No single key.

Ilyra had spent the past hour explaining why the mechanism required more than three hands. The sending district had to confirm the water it was releasing. The receiving district had to confirm who remained in its path. A pressure reading had to come from beneath the Hall, not from the gauge jammed past red.

Confirmation. Witnessing. A second relay house. A public record.

Safeguards she had once called inefficient now seemed like the only barrier between intention and disaster.

The stairwell door boomed.

“What does it want?” Elian asked.

Ilyra listened. The wall struck again, three times, patient and exact.

“Not want,” she said. “Claim.”

Senn’s hand tightened on the district plate. “Then I claim them.”

“You don’t know who is behind it.”

“I know they’re behind a wall.”

“You don’t know if they’re alive.”

The next strike came softer. Scraping followed, high and thin.

Senn looked at her, hatred still present beneath exhaustion and reluctant dependence. “That distinction has been useful to the Hall.”

The stairs shook. A crack opened under the door, and water flashed through it.

“Move your hand,” Ilyra said.

“Why?”

“The passage may be a pressure release. Arce may have tied the plate to an emergency breach. If it opens, the chamber could flood.”

“And if I don’t?”

“Then you’re deciding without knowing what it does.”

“I’m deciding to open a door.”

“That is how you described the North Barrage.”

The words settled between them.

In memory, another wall appeared.

Not bronze, but gray stone sweating beneath the red lamps of the barrage. Water had reached her shins. Workers shouted through the speaking tube. Nera’s voice rose above them.

“Ilyra! The western pressure is rising. Open the door.”

“There isn’t enough clearance.”

“Then make enough.”

“We’ll lose the control chamber.”

“You said the chamber could be sacrificed.”

“The machinery cannot.”

A pause.

“The machinery or us?”

Ilyra had stared at the pressure board. The numbers had been orderly. Six lost, pressure reduced, east line preserved.

She had given the workers a route to a vertical shaft. Perhaps it remained open. Perhaps they could climb. She had not opened the door.

She had recorded the sentence before the flood took the corridor.

Three blows sounded from the bronze wall.

Ilyra flinched.

Mara saw it. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“That was not nothing.”

The hinges screamed. Senn drew the largest key from his ring and drove it into a seam between two stones.

“Help me,” he said.

Ilyra did not move.

“You want responsibility?” he said. “Take it.”

The seam widened with a wet crunch. Cold air entered, carrying the smell of bodies held too long in a sealed room.

Ilyra stepped forward.

The last night had begun with a list.

She had been alone in the Flood Cell when she made it, forty-one days after her arrest. Water whispered through the drain. She tore a strip from her shirt and wrote with a charcoal nub.

Nera Vale.

The names came slowly. Corin Voss, the pump-belt repair boy. The yellow-shirted girl with one red boot, whose name she did not know. Mik Tarrow, perhaps alive. Jessa Vale. Orren Renn. Pala Renn. The workers behind the emergency door. Three children who crossed the roof after she opened the drainage run. Two adults who did not.

She added names from ration ledgers and work rosters, people she had watched become marks on a survey. The list gave her relief. A name was fixed. It could not be altered by a clerk or hidden beneath a governor’s seal.

Then she understood what she was building: an account of remorse.

If she carried it to the execution, she could point to each name and prove she had not forgotten. The dead would become evidence.

Even grief became an instrument in her hands.

She tore the strip into pieces and dropped them into the drain. One name remained visible in the dirty water.

Nera.

Then it vanished.

Maret stumbled through the opening in the wall.

The guard was soaked to the waist, one sleeve torn away. She carried no weapon. Fear had stripped her face of its usual hardness.

“Jorren sent me,” she said. “The ropewalk route is open for a few minutes. The upper rooms are clear.”

“Lenn?” Ilyra asked.

Maret stared at her.

“Your child,” Ilyra said. “And the grandmother.”

“Alive. I heard him. They’re on the third loft, but the stairs are gone. Boats can’t reach the east side. The dye channel is backing up.”

“Did you confirm the receiving route?”

Maret’s expression twisted. “I confirmed my child.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“I know what it is.”

She moved toward Ilyra. Senn caught her arm, but she shook him off.

“You keep asking for seals while children climb furniture to keep their heads above water.”

“If I open the wrong channel—”

“You choose who drowns.”

The anger struck more cleanly than Pell’s accusations.

Ilyra saw the structure she had built in her mind. Senn had been the guard who hated her. Maret had been the guard who watched her like an exhibit. Wardens were a force at the stairs. Pell was a will behind a door.

Now Maret was a mother standing in floodwater.

Not an obstacle. Not an audience.

A person.

“I need your confirmation,” Ilyra said.

Maret laughed once. “You need me to sign the thing that saves my child?”

“I need you to tell the receiving district what the channel contains. Who is there. Which route is open. What will flood.”

“And if I don’t know?”

“Then we don’t open it.”

“Then Lenn drowns.”

“Yes.”

Maret stared at her.

“I have a route,” Ilyra continued. “Foundry can confirm the lower channel. Jorren’s people can move boats through the dye market. But they need time.”

“There is no time.”

“There may be less if I act.”

Maret’s face hardened. “You say that as though it makes you honest.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “It makes me afraid.”

That answer steadied Maret, though it did not comfort her.

The wall opened another handspan. A thin man crawled through, wrists bound with wire. A woman followed, blood dried beside one eye, then two boys carrying an old man. More figures crowded behind them.

The hidden population of the Hall was not a rumor. It was a room beneath the room, filled with people the ledgers had made convenient to lose.

One boy saw Senn and recoiled.

“You filled the rolls.”

Senn bowed his head. “Yes.”

The boy spat at him.

Senn did not raise a hand.

Maret moved among the survivors. “Can you walk? Row?”

“Some,” the injured woman said.

“If there’s a boat,” Maret replied.

“It will come,” she added, though no confirmation had arrived.

Elian appeared at the passage, breathless and wet-haired, holding sealed pages above the water.

“The east relay is still broadcasting,” she said. “Pell ordered every tower keeper detained. Halven is missing. Tessa Marr was taken from her rooms. Corren Dey’s workshop was searched.”

“Nera?” Ilyra asked.

“Alive. She sent a message through the dock relay. Pell is calling the engineers conspirators.”

Ilyra felt the old impulse rise: seize the manifold, force the Crown bypass, make the powerful afraid.

The pin waited on the stone, fashioned from old governor-arm metal.

In memory, she was back on the roof.

The child wore a yellow sleep shirt and one red boot. Ilyra had reached across the slanted tiles. The flood carried timber, doors, sacks, bodies. The valve key was clenched in Ilyra’s hand. Without it, the eastern line might fail.

The girl grabbed her wrist.

“Please.”

Ilyra remembered the exact weight of those fingers. She remembered looking at the key. She remembered deciding.

Not because there was no choice. Because the key preserved the line.

The child slipped when Ilyra withdrew her hand. Her red boot struck the gutter. Then the water took her.

Ilyra had called it an impossible exchange: one life against hundreds, perhaps thousands. But the arithmetic had never erased the choice. It had only hidden it behind a number.

She had saved three children that night. She had allowed the girl to fall. Both were true.

The wardens struck the stairwell door.

Senn moved to the choke point. “They’re coming.”

Elian set the records on a raised ledge. “Pell is suppressing everyone who can contradict him.”

“The witnesses,” Ilyra said.

Pell’s voice carried down the stairwell. “Ilyra Voss. Step away from the controls. The execution will proceed at the third hour.”

The formality was absurd in the flooded dark.

“You have made your final argument,” Pell called. “Do not turn these people into accomplices.”

A warden entered with a hooked shield. Water struck his knees.

Mara bent over the manifold. “East-pipe vibration is increasing. Filling speed has doubled.”

“Pressure?”

“Beyond the gauge.”

“Find another reading.”

“With what?”

Ilyra looked toward the survivors. “Ask where the water is moving.”

The old kitchen worker and the drainage repairer spoke over one another. A stair had flooded first. A vent was whistling. A buried culvert ran toward the settling chamber. The water was being forced from the west. The old drainage route still had capacity, but a gate near the conservatory was jammed. Opening it would send water toward Crown terraces—if the Crown channel accepted it.

Ilyra touched the pin.

One movement. One lever. A decisive correction.

She could make them afraid.

Nera’s voice returned through the speaking tube.

The machinery or us?

Ilyra picked up the pin and placed it in Maret’s palm.

Maret looked down. “What is this?”

“A bypass tool.”

“You want me to use it?”

“No. Carry it to the ropewalk. If the route collapses and you find a manual lever, don’t use it unless the receiving channel confirms who is there.”

“My child may be there.”

“I know.”

“And you still won’t tell me to open it.”

“I won’t tell you to choose for everyone else.”

Maret closed her fingers around the pin. No forgiveness passed between them. Only an agreement to remain answerable.

A relay runner appeared in the passage, a girl with red cloth tied around her arm.

“Foundry confirms,” she gasped. “Upper buildings clear where marked. The infirmary route is blocked. They need a discharge from the western channel.”

“Receiving confirmation?”

“Foundry has given it.”

“From Sable?”

The girl shook her head.

“Then no transfer.”

“People will die.”

“Yes.”

The girl stared at her.

“Tell Sable to confirm the occupied buildings,” Ilyra said. “Tell them exactly what opening the channel will flood. We wait for their answer.”

“The relay keeper says there isn’t time.”

“The relay keeper is not the district.”

The girl turned and ran.

The chamber shook. A crack opened along the manifold’s rim, and water burst through in a silver sheet.

At the stairs, Senn shouted. “They’re through!”

The first warden raised his weapon. Senn met him in the water. Metal struck metal. The survivors pressed against the wall, some reaching for the tools and keys Senn had brought.

Ilyra put both hands on the manifold.

She could no longer see the district marks beneath the water. Only feel them through the bronze.

The wall struck three times.

From somewhere above, three knocks answered.

Not one command.

A chain of replies.

The chamber filled with noise: bells, shouting, water, scraping metal. Ilyra did not reach for the pin. She did not seize the missing lever. She waited for the confirmations to come, knowing that waiting could kill them, knowing that acting alone could kill more, and knowing that neither truth belonged to her alone.

In the darkness beyond the opened wall, someone began calling out names.

Not numbers.

Names.

chapters.name: White and Bronze
chapters.content:
## White and Bronze

By dawn, Veyr had dressed itself for celebration.

White cloth hung from the bridges and balconies of the Crown District. Bronze ribbons looped around the civic lamps. Feast cakes appeared in shop windows beneath painted sugar flames. Children wore masks shaped like river fish.

On the Hall of Civic Judgment, someone had fastened a wreath of pale reeds around the eastern face, though the lower steps were already slick with water.

The city was rising toward its ceremony.

Ilyra felt it through the floor.

The settling chamber had become a bowl of noise: water shivering through cracks, boots striking stone above, voices carried by pipes and passageways. Senn was somewhere beyond the stairwell, fighting or retreating. Maret had gone toward the ropewalk with the governor-arm pin. Elian was still trying to keep the relay houses alive. The hidden prisoners, released from the Hall’s buried rooms, had been pushed toward the old channel by Mara and Jorren’s people.

No one knew how many remained below.

Ilyra kept her hands on the manifold until the last possible moment. A seam in the pipe had opened like a wet lip, spilling water over the engraved channels. The markings had been polished by generations of engineers who believed that if a system could be named, it could be governed.

Three plates. Three confirmations. A pressure reading from beneath the Hall.

Nothing opened without all three.

Nothing, except the doors the wardens were breaking through.

“Voss!”

The shout came down the stairwell.

A younger voice, strained with effort.

“By order of the Civic Council, step away from the manifold!”

Ilyra looked toward the dark passage where Senn had disappeared. A cry rose there, followed by the clatter of metal against stone.

“Ressa!”

Then another voice answered from farther in.

“Bram!”

The survivors had begun calling to one another. It was the only order left to them. Names passed through the dark like ropes.

Three wardens appeared at the foot of the stair.

The first saw the survivors and hesitated.

“Seize Voss,” he ordered. “The rest are to be detained.”

Mara Venn stepped between him and the passage.

“Detained where?”

The warden struck her with his baton. She fell against the wall.

Ilyra moved before she had decided to. Her shoulder hit the warden’s chest, and all three of them went down in the water. The bronze mask scraped her cheek. She smelled oil, wet wool, and fear.

Hands seized her arms. A cord tightened around her wrists, another across her elbows. The wardens dragged her upright while Mara shouted and someone in the passage cried her name.

Ilyra searched the chamber.

No Senn. No Elian. No Maret.

Only the wall, the water, and the survivors who had seen what the Hall had hidden.

“Look at them,” she said.

The youngest warden glanced toward the passage.

“Look at them.”

He did.

It changed nothing. But he looked.

They dragged her upstairs.

Aboveground, the Hall smelled of steam and flowers.

The transition was so abrupt that her body refused it. One moment she was in the drowned dark beneath the building; the next she was crossing a white-tiled corridor beneath chandeliers shaped like droplets. Servants hurried past carrying sugared fruit. Attendants polished brass railings. Somewhere beyond the walls, musicians practiced the first procession hymn.

A lens in the corridor turned as she passed. Its black glass followed her face. Another stared down from the mouth of a carved bronze fish.

The city had been watching her for forty-one days.

This morning it would watch more closely.

The wardens took her to the cleansing rooms, where heated aqueduct water ran through white basins. White curtains divided the stations. Bronze hooks held the ceremonial garments.

A woman in a gray apron waited beside the largest basin.

“Remove her clothes,” said the captain.

Ilyra laughed once.

“Afraid I’ll offend the water?”

He ignored her.

The attendants undressed her and lowered her into the basin. Petals floated on the surface. They clung to her skin as the woman scrubbed her arms.

“Do not resist,” the attendant murmured.

“I’m not resisting.”

“Not the washing.”

The woman’s hand paused at Ilyra’s shoulder. On her wrist was a thread bracelet knotted in the style of the Low Quarter dyehouses.

Ilyra kept her voice low. “Your name?”

“Names are not required in the cleansing room.”

“Not by whom?”

The attendant glanced toward the lenses mounted between the curtains. The Hall recorded everyone who touched the condemned.

The woman rinsed Ilyra’s hair.

“Your people are moving through the old channels,” she whispered.

Ilyra kept her face blank. “The ropewalk?”

“Some. The lower Foundry. Water is coming through the infirmary floor.”

“Are the relay towers still speaking?”

“East tower. Dock tower. Perhaps the one beyond the grain stairs.”

Perhaps. No certainty. A word with room inside it.

The attendant pressed a cloth to Ilyra’s mouth.

“Breathe through your nose.”

The water was hot. Ilyra felt the old instinct rise: measure, compare, determine. Temperature by skin. Flow by the drain. Pressure behind the wall.

Control came toward her like a hand reaching for a lever.

She closed her eyes.

For an instant she was back in the barrage chamber, watching the gauge fall from red, believing a number could become a promise.

Then she saw a yellow sleep shirt and one red boot. A small hand slipping from hers.

Ilyra opened her eyes.

“Do you know whether the child lived?”

The attendant’s expression changed.

“No.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only one I have.”

The woman wrapped her in white cloth and helped her into the execution dress. It shimmered like frost, with bronze stitching tracing the ribs and falling in three vertical lines toward the hem.

“Why white?” Ilyra asked.

“Purification.”

“Why bronze?”

“Memory.”

“No. Bronze is for heat.”

The woman said nothing.

Two civic smiths brought the chains on a velvet tray. They were polished ceremonial links, each engraved with districts that had petitioned for Ilyra’s execution: Crown, Merchant, Upper Foundry, Old Hall.

The Low Quarter was absent.

It had not been permitted to petition.

They fastened the collar around her throat, then cuffs at her wrists and ankles. The metal was warm from the brazier. A chain from collar to waist restricted her stride without making her stumble.

A civic engineer had calculated the effect.

Ilyra wondered whether the designer had come from the Low Quarter.

Probably not.

The nearest lens clicked and adjusted.

“Turn her left,” said the chain-master.

She turned.

“Raise her chin.”

She raised it.

“Hold.”

A door opened.

Magistrate Oren Pell entered wearing ceremonial black beneath a white mantle embroidered in bronze. A narrow crown of bronze leaves rested against his gray hair.

He looked at Ilyra as if inspecting a repaired bridge.

“You are late,” he said.

“Your wardens were delayed by the people you buried.”

“The condemned does not address the magistrate without permission.”

“Then you should have given me a better mouth.”

The chain-master looked down. Pell noticed.

“Leave us.”

The attendants withdrew. The captain remained.

Pell came closer. He smelled of cedar smoke and bitter herbs.

“Your accomplices have made the morning difficult.”

“Which ones?”

“The relay stations. The disturbances below the Hall. The false reports of deliberate flooding.”

“Are the floods false?”

“The city is experiencing an infrastructure emergency.”

“Then why are you executing me?”

He gestured to her chains. “The city needs a clear account.”

“No. It needs a clear villain.”

“It needs to see that law remains stronger than grievance.”

“Law?” She lifted her chained hands. “Those are theater.”

“Everything is theater to you because you believe every act is a calculation.”

Ilyra thought of the sealed door beneath the barrage. Nera’s voice through the tube. The groups of workers she had counted because numbers could stand upright when names would not.

“Not everything,” she said.

Pell lowered his voice.

“Confess as agreed. Say you acted alone. Say the Council’s decisions were unknown to you. Say your grief became a weapon. In return, the water will be cooled. The descent will be brief. Your engineers will not be charged.”

“Except Arce.”

His eyes flickered.

“Master Engineer Arce is not part of this proceeding.”

“No. He is part of the walls.”

“Do you imagine naming every official will save those people beneath the Hall?”

“No.”

“Then what do you want?”

Beyond the door, the galleries roared as they filled.

“I want them to look at the gates.”

“They will look at you.”

“That is the point.”

For the first time, Pell seemed unsettled.

He stepped back. “Do not confuse access with control, Ilyra.”

She almost asked whether he spoke to her or himself.

“Do not confuse control with justice.”

The captain returned, carrying a coded seal.

At the transfer gate, he pressed it to the lock. The seal flashed blue: two short pulses, one long, a pause, then three short.

Ilyra watched the sequence.

The seal had a cracked lower tooth. Its confirmation pulse arrived half a second late, a flaw in the Hall’s access system. She had noticed it earlier, when a guard let her borrow the seal to identify the prisoner manifest. She had pressed it against damp wax beneath her fingernail and copied its internal pattern.

Small things changed systems.

The captain pressed the seal again.

Ilyra tilted her wrist. The cuff scraped the bronze plate. A sliver of conductive metal, thinner than a sewing thread, slipped from the seam and lodged in the seal’s lower tooth.

The pulse stuttered.

The gate opened halfway, then stopped.

The captain swore and struck the seal with his palm. The gate opened.

The sliver remained.

Under Ilyra’s tongue, the thin metal pin rested against the root of her mouth. It was not the governor-arm bypass pin. Maret carried that toward the ropewalk. This piece had been filed from an old latch spring and sharpened at one end. It might lift a catch, bridge a contact, or turn a lock if the lock had not been altered.

Perhaps.

No one had searched her mouth.

The procession began.

Four wardens led her through the Hall. Pell and three Council officials followed in white mantles. The captain walked at Ilyra’s left, one hand on the chain joining her wrists.

Beyond the gallery arches, the crowd pressed against the rails.

They wore masks painted with her face: skull-faced, black-toothed, crowned with bronze sluice gates. Children held paper dolls dressed in white and dragged them through puddles.

A vendor shouted, “Barrage cakes! The Butcher’s last bite!”

Another called the odds.

“Will she kneel? Will she speak? Will she scream before the third bell?”

The crowd began to chant.

“White to water. White to water.”

A woman spat over the rail. A man raised a sweetcake in salute.

Ilyra searched for grief and found appetite.

Not everywhere. Some faces were rigid with hatred. Some were swollen from crying. Some watched with the stunned attention of people who had survived long enough to become spectators to their own ruin.

But the Hall had made room for pleasure.

It had sold the best seats.

At the central gallery, mirrored lenses surrounded the execution platform. Each stood on a bronze pole, angled toward the white basin at its center. One lens caught Ilyra’s face, another her chains, another Pell’s mantle, another the crowd and the Council seal above the platform.

Civic transmission plates carried the images through the tower network.

Every district would see her.

The Crown would watch from heated balconies. Merchants would watch between inventory counts. The Low Quarter would watch if its drowned lenses still worked. Foundry Row might hear only fragments through relay speakers. Sable Ward might already have water in its rooms.

The platform had been built over the Hall’s original manifold.

Ilyra saw it immediately. Beneath the white basin, bronze pipes descended into the floor. Three pressure gauges stood behind the execution seat. Their needles were painted gold. One trembled just beyond red.

No one in the galleries seemed to notice.

Or everyone important had noticed and decided the ceremony would continue.

Pell mounted the steps.

The crowd quieted.

Above him, the Council crest opened its carved hand. Water flowed from the bronze waves into a shallow channel around the platform. It ran clear at first. Then a thread of brown appeared, followed by grit and a pale scrap spinning against the drain.

Ilyra thought of the drain in her cell.

The knocks beneath the Hall.

The people called dead.

“Citizens of Veyr,” Pell began, his voice carried by hidden speakers, “today we gather to restore the covenant between the city and the river.”

The lenses adjusted.

The crowd leaned forward.

Pell spoke of renewal, order, and the sacred duty of government to protect the innocent from those who turned grievance into slaughter. He did not name the Council’s evacuation orders, the private reservoirs, or the families still trapped beneath the rising channels.

He named her.

Every sentence reduced the city to one woman and one choice.

Ilyra listened.

For a moment, she let him have the story. Let him pour it over her, polish it, heat it, fit it to the shape of the spectacle. Anger gathered beneath her ribs, bright and obedient.

Then, somewhere under the platform, came three knocks.

The crowd did not hear them.

Ilyra did.

Three exact strikes. A reply, or a warning.

She touched the pin beneath her tongue.

Across the galleries, the mirrored lenses caught her face and multiplied it until Veyr seemed full of Ilyras: condemned, furious, calculating, afraid.

The city had come to watch one woman die.

It had not come to ask who built the gates, who closed them, or who was still turning the wheels beneath the water.

Pell raised his hand.

The irregular bells began to ring.

chapters.name: The Names She Carries
chapters.content:
Pell raised the sentence in both hands.

The paper was white, the seal bronze, and the words upon it had been chosen to survive her.

“By authority of the Civic Covenant,” he said, “and under the witnessed judgment of the Hall of Civic Judgment, Ilyra Voss, formerly licensed engineer of the municipal water service, is condemned for murder, sabotage, unlawful seizure of civic property, incitement to insurrection, and the deliberate drowning of four thousand eight hundred and twelve citizens of Veyr.”

The crowd answered with a low, satisfied murmur.

It moved through the galleries like wind beneath a door. Some people leaned forward to hear the number again. Others lifted their masks, white faces with black lines painted around the mouths. A vendor at the rear called softly, “Last cakes before the descent. Honey and salt. Eat as the Butcher burns.”

Ilyra stood between the bronze uprights of the execution seat. The ceremonial chains crossed her chest and wrists. They were not heavy enough to prevent movement entirely. That was part of the design. She could turn her head. She could lift her hands. She could appear to struggle.

The city had engineered even her helplessness.

Behind Pell, the three pressure gauges trembled. Their needles had passed the painted red marks and quivered there, refusing either to rise or fall. A line of brown water ran from beneath the platform, darkening the white boards. It carried grit, a shaving of wood, and something pale that struck the drain and vanished.

Three knocks sounded under her feet.

Ilyra did not look down.

Pell lowered the sentence. “The condemned has been offered the mercy of a private confession and a brief descent. She has declined. The law therefore requires a public purification.”

“White to water,” someone called.

“White to water,” answered a hundred voices.

The phrase spread upward through the Hall. It was sung by children in the upper galleries and shouted by men who had come in river-worker coats, their cuffs clean, their faces flushed with festival wine. Beyond them, civic lenses turned on their brass mounts. Every lens was trained on Ilyra: the chains, the white garment, the dark hair braided tightly at her nape.

The lenses did not show the water beneath the platform.

They did not show Sable Ward, where the lower streets were already full.

They did not show the orders authorizing Crown Reservoirs Six and Eight to empty into the western channel, or the evacuation permits issued to the Crown and Merchant districts, or the lists in which the Hall had converted living people into black hooks beside a name.

They showed her.

Pell’s voice softened. “Ilyra Voss, you have been found guilty by a lawful tribunal. The sentence will now be carried out. Before the descent, as required by statute, you may make a final statement.”

He turned toward her with the expression of a man offering a cup.

The crowd quieted.

This was the moment they had purchased. Some had paid for the best seats. Some had wagered on tears, or curses, or silence. A woman near the front held a folded betting slip in her gloved hand and watched Ilyra’s mouth.

Pell had told her what to say.

You acted alone.

You rejected lawful correction.

You were overcome by private grief.

No official directed you. No engineer assisted you. No district shared your intent.

The words would make the execution easier. They would spare Halven, Tessa Marr, Corren Dey, and Nera, Pell had promised. They would spare everyone except the dead and Ilyra, who had already been made into something the city could punish without examination.

Nera.

The name moved through her before she spoke it.

Nera’s hands had always been stained with ink. Even at the barrage, with the river climbing the steps and the warning bells beating themselves hoarse, she had held the map flat against the control table and pointed to the western gate.

There are workers below.

Ilyra had told her to wait.

She had told the people behind the emergency door to climb toward the vertical shaft. She had known the shaft might be blocked. She had opened the gate by degrees anyway. She had watched the gauge settle under the red mark while voices thinned behind the wall.

Six lost, pressure reduced, east line preserved.

She had written the words herself.

The memory did not arrive as an image. It arrived as a pressure beneath her ribs, precise and inescapable.

Pell waited.

Ilyra looked past him to the galleries. At the bright masks. At the children with sugared fingers. At the survivors who had come because they wanted to see the woman whose name had swallowed their missing relatives.

She placed her chained hands on the arms of the execution seat.

“I opened the North Barrage,” she said.

The Hall went still.

Her voice was not loud, but the lenses carried it. Somewhere beyond the walls, the relay houses would be receiving the sound, if their operators had not been detained. Somewhere in the flooded districts, people might be hearing only fragments through static and water.

“I opened it knowingly.”

Pell’s face remained composed. The sentence paper rustled once in his hand.

“I knew the pressure was beyond the safe limit. I knew the eastern embankment had been weakened. I knew that the maps in my possession were incomplete. I knew that people were in the storage fields and in the lower works, though I did not know all their names or how many had been moved there.”

A murmur passed through the chamber.

She continued before it could become a shout.

“I knew people would die.”

The words seemed to disappoint them.

A man in the second gallery called, “Say murder!”

A woman answered, “Say you wanted it!”

Pell did not turn. He watched Ilyra as if she were an instrument whose reading had become irregular.

“I wanted the pressure reduced,” she said. “That is true. I wanted the Low Quarter to survive. That is true. I also wanted the people who had built the system to feel, for once, what the system did to others.”

There it was.

A change in the crowd. Faces brightened. The word they wanted was not murder. It was hatred. Hatred made her simple. Hatred made the flood a private act, born in the sealed room of one resentful woman.

Ilyra felt the old instinct rise in her: to seize the sequence, correct the interpretation, force the pressure into the channel she had chosen.

She had once believed that if she could explain the structure perfectly, the structure would be unable to deny itself.

She knew better now.

“I am not going to tell you that I was only correcting a failure,” she said. “I was correcting a failure. I was also taking revenge. Both statements are true.”

Pell’s mouth tightened.

The first gauge clicked behind her.

The audience heard it and mistook it for part of the ceremony.

Ilyra looked at the bronze pipe beneath the platform. Brown water seeped around its collar. The Hall’s original manifold lay under the boards, below the ceremonial seat, below the place where Pell stood with the sentence in his hand. Somewhere in the buried mechanism, water moved through the city’s hidden divisions.

Crown.

Merchant.

Upper Foundry.

Old Hall.

The Low Quarter absent from the chains, absent from the petition, absent from the official design until it became the place where pressure could be spent.

“Ilyra Voss,” Pell said, “you are not here to deliver a political address.”

“I am here because you made my name the explanation.”

The crowd stirred.

“You put it on cakes. You painted it on masks. You printed it on broadsheets beneath a drawing of a woman with red hands. You taught children to chant it before they learned the names of the dead. You read one number until it sounded like a person.”

Pell stepped closer. “The number is the number of citizens you killed.”

“It is the number entered by the Hall.”

“Four thousand eight hundred and twelve.”

“Four thousand eight hundred and twelve recorded deaths.”

He lifted the sentence slightly, as though reminding her that the paper outranked her.

“The tribunal heard testimony,” he said. “It heard survivors.”

“Some survivors.”

“Enough.”

The word struck harder than an accusation.

Enough.

Enough to sentence. Enough to broadcast. Enough to close the records.

Ilyra turned her head toward the lower gallery. Senn’s sister had sat there during the trial, though Ilyra could not see her now among the masks and bronze railings. Lysa Renn. She had spoken of the child in the yellow sleep shirt and the one red boot. She had said Ilyra released the girl’s hand.

Lysa had not said what came after.

She had not said that Ilyra opened the drainage run, that its collapse killed two adults, that three children crossed the roof because she had forced the lever down. She had not said it because she did not know. She had not been present for every choice.

The court had treated the part she saw as the whole.

“I want to name someone,” Ilyra said.

Pell’s eyes narrowed. “You may make your statement without theatrics.”

“I want to name Nera Vale.”

A few people in the galleries shifted. The name had appeared in the trial records only as a junior assistant who had once worked under Ilyra. Pell had used her testimony without calling her to the stand. Nera had said, in a written deposition, that Ilyra understood the barrage better than any engineer alive. The next page had been missing.

“Nera was my apprentice,” Ilyra said. “She found the western pressure anomaly before I did. She copied the old survey. She warned me that the storage fields were occupied. I did not tell her everything I knew before I entered the barrage. I decided that if she knew the whole plan, she would try to stop me.”

Pell said, “The witness is alive and will answer for her own involvement.”

“She was not my accomplice because she did not know enough to consent. I made her ignorant and then used her labor. That was my choice.”

The silence deepened.

“Nera, if you are hearing this, I am sorry. That is not a defense. It is not a request that you forgive me.”

Something cracked in the crowd—not a sound, but an expectation. They wanted her to say sorry to the city, broadly and safely. They did not want the apology to have a face.

Ilyra continued.

“I name the workers behind the emergency door.”

She did not know all of them. That was the point.

“There were at least thirty. Maintenance crews. Families sheltering in the lower access corridor. People whose names I did not ask before I made a decision about them. I ordered them toward a shaft that might not have been open. Then I opened the western gate to lower the eastern pressure. I told myself that the choice saved thousands. It may have. It also placed those people in the path of the water.”

Her fingers tightened on the seat.

“I did not know whether they lived. I do not know now.”

A woman near the front began to weep. Her grief had no obvious connection to Ilyra. Perhaps it did. Perhaps every grief in Veyr had begun to resemble every other.

“I name the child on the roof,” Ilyra said.

The Hall seemed to draw breath.

“She wore a yellow sleep shirt and one red boot. I had a valve key in my hand. If I dropped it, I could have reached her. If I kept it, I could stabilize the line and reduce the pressure moving toward the east embankment. I kept the key.”

Someone shouted, “You see? You see?”

Ilyra heard the cry but did not look toward it.

“I saved three children later through an old drainage run,” she said. “The run collapsed. Two adults died. I could have chosen another route, but I did not know whether it would hold. I chose the route I could calculate.”

She swallowed.

“I chose calculations over people more than once.”

The phrase entered the lenses and went outward.

Pell moved to interrupt her. “The condemned is attempting to confuse the issue by inventing moral equivalence between her crimes and the city’s governance.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “I am refusing your equivalence.”

She looked directly into the nearest civic lens. Its polished eye reflected a small, warped version of her face.

“I opened the barrage. I caused deaths. I made decisions that cannot be repaired by showing you a larger number of lives saved. The dead do not become acceptable because more dead might have followed. I have used that argument. It is an engineer’s way of hiding a hand inside a formula.”

Her gaze moved over the crowd.

“To the families who lost someone in the first flood: I will not ask you to call me necessary. To the families whose names were never entered: I will not use your absence to make my guilt smaller. To those who saw me refuse a hand, close a door, or choose a lever, I will not tell you that you misunderstood what you saw.”

Pell’s face had gone pale beneath the Hall’s white light.

“And to the Council,” Ilyra said, “I will not give you the solitude you purchased.”

The word Council ran through the chamber.

Several officials seated behind Pell began speaking at once. Their ceremonial collars flashed as they turned toward one another. One of them rose, then sat again when the lenses shifted to capture him.

“You knew,” Ilyra said. “You knew the eastern embankment would fail below the labor districts. You reinforced Crown walls. You cleared inventory from the storage fields and left the families there. You closed relief channels to protect gardens, terraces, warehouses, and the ceremonial road. You altered maps. You removed valves. You sent water west and called the flooding an emergency.”

Pell struck the butt of his sentence against the platform.

“Enough.”

The sound echoed.

But beneath it came three knocks.

Exact. Patient.

Ilyra felt them through the soles of her feet.

A moment later, from somewhere beyond the eastern wall, three knocks answered.

The crowd did not hear. The lenses did not turn. Pell continued speaking, but his words blurred beneath the resonance traveling through the floor.

A chain of replies.

Someone was still moving beneath the Hall.

Someone had heard her names.

Or had been waiting for them.

Pell faced the galleries. “The condemned has confessed to the essential charge. Her attempt to implicate lawful authorities is the final expression of the delusion that brought her here. The city will not be held hostage by the fantasies of a murderer.”

Ilyra watched his mouth form the word fantasies.

She could have fought him. She could have shouted the names of Dault, Arce, Halven, Marr, Dey. She could have recited dates, valve numbers, seal impressions, the placement of the private barge, the orders marked in Dault’s hand. She could have made her statement into a catalogue so precise that no one could claim ignorance.

But Pell would call it defiance.

The crowd would call it performance.

And she knew, with a clarity that frightened her, how much she wanted to win that argument. Not for Nera. Not for the child. For herself. To stand above the manifold and force the city to admit that she had understood it better than anyone.

The desire was familiar. It had the shape of a hand closing around a lever.

She opened her fingers instead.

“I will not name every dead person,” she said.

The crowd quieted once more.

“Because I cannot. Because I do not know them all. Because any list I make will leave someone outside it, as the Hall has done. I remember Corin Voss, who repaired the pump belt. I remember the five people with him. I remember the girl in yellow. I remember the workers behind the door. I remember Nera’s voice.”

She breathed in. The air smelled of hot bronze and silt.

“I remember that I wrote six lost, pressure reduced, east line preserved. Those words were mine. They made death look clean. There was nothing clean about it.”

Pell’s hand trembled around the sentence.

“I accept the judgment that I opened the North Barrage and understood people would die. I accept that my anger shaped the act. I accept that I withheld information, that I treated people as numbers, and that I chose outcomes for them without giving them the knowledge required to refuse me.”

She looked toward the upper galleries, where the masks gleamed like a second audience.

“But I did not act in a vacuum. The Council built the vacuum. The Crown filled it with water. The Hall filled it with records that erased the poor and called the erasure truth. You may execute me for what I did. You may not use my guilt to make yourselves innocent.”

For several heartbeats, no one moved.

Then the nearest lens clicked.

The sound traveled through the Hall’s relay apparatus, a small mechanical decision repeated in distant rooms.

Pell turned to the execution attendants.

“Proceed.”

The chains tightened.

Water struck the bronze pipe below with a hollow boom. One gauge needle lurched farther past red.

Ilyra closed her eyes—not to pray, and not to escape the crowd, but to hold the names in the order they had reached her.

Nera.

The workers.

The child with one red boot.

Corin.

The five beside him.

The three children who crossed the roof.

The two adults who did not.

More names waited beneath the water, beyond the reach of any list she could make.

The attendants placed their hands on the descent levers.

From under the platform came three knocks.

This time, Ilyra answered.

chapters.name: The Towers Speak
chapters.content:
The first tower spoke through the execution lens.

It did not use Pell’s measured voice or the bright cadence of the Feast. The words came cracked by distance, carried from somewhere beyond the Hall’s central relay.

“By order of the Council of Reservoirs, households in Sable Ward are to remain below the east barricade until the third hour. Evacuation permits are restricted to Crown, Merchant, and Upper Foundry residents.”

A murmur passed through the galleries.

Pell turned toward the nearest lens. “Cut that relay.”

The attendant at the control box hesitated.

“Cut it.”

The lens shuddered and widened. For one breath the execution platform vanished in static. Then the Hall’s ceremonial crest gave way to a page of writing.

CLEARANCE OF INVENTORY BEFORE EASTERN EMBANKMENT FAILURE.

Below the heading appeared the Council seal.

“Storage fields to be cleared of grain, dye stock, coal, and Crown inventory,” the announcer read. “Residents are not included in the clearance order.”

Someone laughed once, sharply. It was not amusement.

Pell climbed the steps toward the platform. “This is unlawful interference with the civic broadcast. The statement being transmitted is unverified.”

The lens turned toward him.

“Magistrate Oren Pell has declared the Council order unverified,” the announcer said.

The crowd shifted.

Pell pointed at the attendants. “Shut down the east tower. Shut down the dock relay. Shut down every lens not under Hall authority.”

A second voice answered from the far gallery.

“By what authority?”

Pell’s head snapped around.

Another lens brightened above the western doors.

“By what authority?” the voice repeated.

Then another speaker took it up from somewhere beneath the Hall.

“By what authority?”

The phrase moved through the building, not as a chant but as a question. Three knocks sounded beneath the platform. Three more answered from the eastern wall.

Ilyra felt the vibration through the soles of her feet.

“Proceed,” Pell ordered.

The executioners’ hands tightened around the descent levers. One moved a fraction. The chain at Ilyra’s wrist drew taut. Beneath her feet, brown water struck the manifold with a hollow blow.

The gauges jerked.

A lens above the north gallery filled with a map.

Ilyra recognized the old conservatory channels: the buried culvert beneath the Hall, the western branch toward the dye market and Foundry Row, the Crown-side channels, and the basin shortened on official plans. Red arrows ran from Reservoirs Six and Eight, the conservatory cistern, and the Merchant terraces toward Sable Ward.

A woman’s voice began reading.

“Reservoir Six opened at the first bell. Reservoir Eight opened at the second. Crown garden basins opened at the second bell and thirteen minutes. The receiving channel toward Foundry Row remained closed.”

Nera.

Ilyra’s throat tightened.

The lens showed a signature at the bottom of the page.

Arven Dault.

“Signed authorization,” Nera continued. “Transfer water west. Maintain Crown retaining walls. Permit no public warning until after the Feast procession.”

A man in a white festival coat rose in the lower gallery. “That could be forged.”

The voice behind him answered, “So could her confession.”

The argument spread through the chamber. People looked away from Ilyra and toward the lenses, searching the machinery for the names of offices and the hands that had directed water toward their homes.

For forty-one days the city had watched Ilyra until looking became consumption. Now it watched gates, maps, signatures, and orders.

Pell seized the young attendant by the shoulder. “Your family lives in North Quay. If this relay remains active, the wardens will classify your parents as collaborators. Your brother’s apprenticeship will end today.”

“My mother is in Sable,” the attendant said.

“Then you should understand the value of obedience.”

His fingers moved toward the switch.

A new image appeared first.

SABLE WARD—CLEARANCE PERMITS ISSUED.

The list was short: Crown households, Merchant houses, three senior engineers, two Council secretaries. No tenants. No foundry workers. No infirmary patients. No residents below the east barricade.

The civic announcer read each name.

A woman near the Crown gallery held up a paper. “You said there was no evacuation.”

“Return to your seat,” Pell ordered.

“My sister is in Foundry Row.”

“She should have applied for a permit.”

“She did.”

The lens swung toward the paper in her hand.

OCCUPANCY NOT VERIFIED.

“She has lived there twelve years,” the woman said.

A dock relay answered through the wall.

“Foundry Row occupancy verified by ropewalk crews. Upper buildings cleared where marked. Infirmary route blocked. Receiving report incomplete.”

Nera’s voice followed. “Repeat: receiving report incomplete.”

Ilyra closed her eyes. The manifold did not care about testimony. It knew only pressure, volume, direction, consequence.

“Silence the towers,” Pell ordered.

A warden ran toward the western door.

It opened before he reached it.

Three engineers stood in the passage beyond: one in a dockworks coat, one wearing the red sash of Upper Foundry maintenance, and an old woman with a brass relay key clenched in her hand. Behind them crowded ropewalk workers, canal haulers, two boys, and a man carrying a coil of copper wire.

The warden raised his baton.

The dock engineer stepped forward. “The east tower has been ordered shut.”

“Then shut it.”

“We have refused.”

The warden struck him across the mouth.

The old woman brought the brass key down on his wrist. He cried out and dropped the baton.

“No,” she said. “We are maintaining the system.”

The towers repeated her words.

WE ARE MAINTAINING THE SYSTEM.

Pell backed toward the platform. “Everyone in this chamber is subject to civic emergency law. Any worker who interferes with the Hall relay will be detained. Any engineer who refuses an authorized command will be charged with sabotage. Your families will be held as security.”

The threat moved through them. Ilyra knew that calculation: what might be done to a child, a mother, a dependent.

Pell saw their hesitation. “The families of all relay keepers are being located now. Their names are with the wardens. Do not mistake a broadcast for power.”

A lens above him flickered.

The image changed to a register.

RELAY KEEPERS AND HOUSEHOLDS.

Beside each name appeared the recorded location of a family member.

The old woman stared at her own entry. “My grandson.”

“Not yet,” said a voice from the ceiling.

Elian’s face appeared in the lens. She stood in a stone room crowded with papers and relay machinery, soot streaking one cheek.

“The list is the Council’s threat register,” she said. “It was prepared before the relay opened. No families have been detained yet. The wardens are moving toward the addresses.”

Pell looked up. “Dault.”

“You have no authority to use my family name,” he said.

“I have no authority at all,” Elian answered. “That is what the records say about everyone below the Crown wall.”

She lifted a folded document.

“Governor Arven Dault ordered the eastern embankment reinforced only where it protected Crown holdings. He ordered the storage fields cleared of inventory while families remained in place. He maintained a private evacuation route to the river platform. The route was marked confirmed.”

The lens enlarged the page.

Dault’s signature appeared beneath the order.

Below it, in another hand, someone had written:

EASTERN FAILURE ACCEPTABLE BELOW LABOR DISTRICTS.

Pell’s mouth tightened. “You are a grieving heir seeking to discredit your father.”

“My mother and brothers died on the platform he left by private barge.”

She looked directly into the lens.

“I am not asking you to call Ilyra Voss innocent. I am asking you to read the orders.”

The civic announcers began reading. Not one voice now, but many, from the east tower, the docks, the grain stairs, and the old conservatory relay.

REINFORCE CROWN RETAINING WALL.

KEEP RELIEF CHANNEL CLOSED UNTIL CEREMONIAL PROCESSION CONCLUDES.

DO NOT ISSUE PUBLIC FLOOD WARNING.

CLEAR STORAGE INVENTORY.

RESIDENTIAL OCCUPANCY NOT RELEVANT TO LOSS CALCULATION.

The last sentence came from a technical memorandum stamped with Master Engineer Arce’s office.

Ilyra felt the platform tilt beneath her.

Arce.

Her mind began separating reliable lines from uncertain ones. A memorandum could be misdated. A stamp could be borrowed. The handwriting might have been copied.

Then she saw the faces in the galleries.

They did not need her to arrange the evidence.

The water struck beneath the platform. The gauges climbed. A Crown merchant removed his festival mask. An execution attendant stared at the map as though discovering that the machine he served had always counted him among its disposable parts.

Pell seized the nearest lens housing. “Look at her. This is a diversion. She has confessed. She admitted she wanted revenge. The flood is hers. These records are her accomplices’ attempt to save her.”

The lens showed Ilyra: white cloth, bronze chains, wet hair at her temples.

The old story remained true. She had opened the gate. She had released the child’s hand. She had written six lost, pressure reduced, east line preserved.

It had simply ceased to be the whole story.

“She is guilty,” Pell said. “Anyone who helps her is guilty with her.”

The dock engineer stepped into view.

“My name is Harl Venn. I maintained the western relays for nineteen years. I received an order to close the Sable discharge. I refused it.”

The old woman followed. “Mara Venn. East tower keeper. I refused the order to cut the archive broadcast.”

A ropewalk worker raised scarred hands. “Tessa Renn. I opened the maintenance lock.”

Names rose from the passage and galleries. Not a crowd chanting one name. People identifying themselves.

Pell’s authority depended on speaking for the city. The towers had given the city back its own voice.

A warden reached the western relay box. Two workers blocked him. He drew his sword.

“Move.”

“No,” said one of the boys.

The warden lifted the blade.

A bronze shutter dropped between them. The boy had opened a maintenance lock. The shutter slammed down, severing the warden from the box. Sparks leapt through the seams.

Across the Hall, another shutter opened, then another. Workers emerged from spaces no official map acknowledged, carrying tools, relay keys, wire, and lists written on cloth.

The Hall’s hidden body was opening.

Three knocks sounded beneath the platform. Three answered from the eastern wall. Three more came from behind Ilyra.

Pell heard them. “Kill the broadcast,” he whispered.

No one moved.

He turned to the attendants. “Pull the levers.”

The attendants looked at the gauges.

“Now.”

One began to pull.

Ilyra’s hidden pin pressed against the roof of her mouth. She could feel its sharpness, the small certainty of metal. A catch. A contact. A lock. Perhaps enough to interrupt the descent. Perhaps enough to open something worse.

Before she decided, the lens above Pell flashed white.

“Pressure beneath the Hall exceeds the marked safety line,” the announcer said. “Receiving reports are incomplete in Sable Ward, the infirmary, and the lower ropewalk. No gate transfer is authorized.”

The eastern lens displayed a table.

SENDING DISTRICT.

RECEIVING DISTRICT.

PRESSURE WITNESS.

The first two columns held names and seals. The third was empty.

The network was waiting.

Pell stared at it. “You cannot let the city drown while you play at procedure.”

He was speaking to her now.

“You know the system. Take control.”

For one terrible instant, relief moved through Ilyra.

She could reach beneath the platform, use the pin, seize the manifold, and send the water through the Crown channels. She could save Sable Ward, perhaps the infirmary, perhaps those trapped under the Hall.

And she could decide who would be flooded.

The old arithmetic rose before her.

Six lost, pressure reduced, east line preserved.

Pell mistook her hesitation for surrender. “Do it. Prove that you are what the city believes you are. Take the controls. Save whom you can. Then we will have no choice but to call this another act of terrorism.”

The platform groaned.

Ilyra lifted her head.

“I will not authorize a gate alone.”

Pell laughed. “You will let them die to preserve a principle?”

“No,” she said. “I will make them answer for what they are asking another district to lose.”

The eastern lens displayed the table again.

A new line appeared beneath the empty confirmations.

SABLE WARD—REPORT REQUESTED.

Far away, a relay clicked.

Then another.

A worker in the passage pressed his ear to the wall.

“Someone is answering,” he said.

The Hall waited.

Water rose through the pipes. The execution levers remained poised above the platform. Beyond the galleries, beyond the white cloth and bronze ribbons, the towers carried the orders into every quarter of Veyr.

For the first time, the city was not watching Ilyra descend.

It was listening for the people below.

chapters.name: Everything Fails at Once
chapters.content:
## Everything Fails at Once

The first confirmation came from Foundry Row in a voice broken by static.

“Upper buildings clear where marked. Lower infirmary route blocked. Receiving report incomplete.”

The words emerged from the nearest civic lens, then repeated through the Hall in three different voices: a dock keeper, a woman somewhere beneath the eastern galleries, and a child who sounded as if he were reading from a page held too close to his face.

Pell lifted one hand.

“Silence the relay.”

No one moved.

The execution attendants stood beside the levers, white sleeves darkened at the cuffs by mist. Behind them, the ceremonial basin trembled on its bronze supports. It was meant to receive the heated water of the Ember Descent, to turn Ilyra’s death into steam and shadow. Brown water now seeped around its base.

On the lens above the platform, the table remained visible.

**SENDING DISTRICT | RECEIVING DISTRICT | PRESSURE WITNESS**

Sable’s row was unfinished. Foundry’s was unfinished. The pressure-witness column was blank.

“No transfer,” Ilyra said.

Her voice carried farther than she expected. The crowd heard it through the Hall’s stone throat and answered with a wave of muttering. Some demanded that she open the gate. Some demanded that she be drowned. A few shouted the names of districts where their families were trapped.

Pell turned toward her. “People are dying while you play at procedure.”

“People are dying because you opened the westward release.”

“You opened the North Barrage.”

“Yes.”

The admission struck the Hall more cleanly than the accusations had. She felt it settle in the room—not forgiveness, not even surprise, but a new weight. Her guilt could no longer be used as a lever unless she allowed it.

A vibration passed through the platform. The chains at her wrists rattled against the bronze rail.

In her mind, another gauge climbed.

Beyond red.

She had been standing in the North Barrage with the old survey under one hand and the valve key under the other. Nera had asked what the red line meant.

“Nothing by itself,” Ilyra had said. “Pressure is only dangerous when you refuse to account for where it goes.”

She had believed the sentence. She had built her life around believing it.

Now the water went on rising.

A relay in the western gallery clicked alive.

“Crown garden basin has no receiving crew. Repeat, no receiving crew. The channel terminates at ornamental retaining walls.”

A second voice answered. “That basin is listed as emergency storage.”

“It is a garden.”

“Confirm.”

“It is a garden. There are trees in it.”

The crowd laughed, at first. Then the laugh broke apart as the meaning entered them.

Elian stood at the edge of the platform stairs, one hand pressed against the bronze chain at her throat. She looked toward the lens, toward the maps still turning across its surface, and then back to Ilyra.

“Dault converted the basin,” she said.

“Not Dault alone,” Ilyra replied.

There it was again: the instinct to distribute blame accurately, to place each hand on the mechanism and name the finger that had moved. It was a useful instinct in an investigation. It was less useful when water was entering a district.

A harsh metallic crack came from beneath the Hall.

The floor dropped half an inch.

People screamed. The galleries lurched as one body. A child fell between two benches and vanished beneath the legs of the crowd. One of the attendants let go of his lever. The bronze handle swung back and struck his wrist.

“Hold it!” Pell shouted.

The attendant seized it again.

The ceremonial lens shuddered. Its image dissolved into white lines, then returned to show a new reading from below.

**MAIN GAUGE: CRITICAL**

Beneath it, in smaller characters:

**PRESSURE WITNESS—NO CONFIRMATION**

Ilyra closed her eyes.

Not a basin. Not a garden. A termination chamber disguised as a garden, with no crew, no report, no one authorized to receive the water. The Council had called every empty ornamental channel an emergency measure because emptiness did not argue. It did not send back names. It did not say which grandmother could not climb, which infirmary bed had wheels rusted in place, which upper room still contained a sleeping child.

A gate could be opened into a void.

A gate could also be opened into people.

“Where is the pressure witness?” she asked.

Mara Venn, still crouched beside the wounded relay keeper, looked up. Blood ran from her temple into the corner of one eye.

“Senn was trying to reach the lower gauge.”

“Trying?”

“The wardens breached the settling chamber. We lost the west passage.”

Ilyra saw the chamber again—not the present one, but the old corridor beneath the first barrage. The maintenance tube had carried Nera’s voice to her in fragments.

*There are thirty of us. More behind the second door.*

She had told them to wait.

She had told herself waiting was an instruction, not a sentence.

“Jorren’s route,” Elian said. “Can they get to the gauge?”

Mara shook her head. “The dye channel collapsed.”

As if summoned by the words, another relay flared.

“Old dye market route down! The roof has gone through! We have people trapped on the north side!”

A man’s voice followed, raw with distance. Jorren.

“Keep the boats out of the central cut. The ceiling is settling. Take the ropewalk route. Repeat, take—”

The transmission ended in a roar.

Water burst from a seam in the eastern wall. It struck the lower steps and spread in a shining sheet across the stone. The crowd on the nearest gallery surged backward, trampling benches. The execution attendants abandoned their levers.

Pell drew his sidearm.

“Return to your stations!”

No one obeyed him. The attendants ran.

The levers rose.

The pressure in the pipes changed.

Ilyra felt it through the soles of her feet: a deep, inward pull, as if the Hall itself had begun to breathe. The central manifold was under the platform. The execution machinery had been connected to it long ago, not merely to flood the basin but to draw water through a calibrated return. The Ember Descent had always been a control chamber pretending to be punishment.

Pell understood it too late. “Take the levers down!”

There was no one left to do it.

Elian caught Ilyra’s chained arm. “Can you reach the manifold?”

“Yes.”

“Can you open something?”

“Yes.”

“That is not what I asked.”

Ilyra looked at her.

Water lapped over the first stair.

“I can reach it,” she said. “I can open almost anything.”

“And if you do?”

The answer waited behind her teeth with the metal pin. She had hidden it there because it was the last place Pell’s guards would search without cutting her open. Its sharpened edge pressed against her tongue. A small, clean pain. A reminder that a tool was never only a tool. Someone had made it. Someone had carried it. Someone had trusted a hand to use it correctly.

She bent her head and spat the pin into her palm.

Pell saw the glint.

“Stop her!”

He moved first, but Elian stepped between them. Pell shoved her aside. She struck the bronze rail and went down hard.

Ilyra drove the pin into the lock of her nearest chain.

The mechanism had been designed to resist ordinary keys, not a sliver filed from an old latch spring and bent at precisely the right angle. The pin caught. She twisted.

Nothing.

The crowd pressed against the galleries. Water climbed another inch.

She twisted again, remembering the coded seal, the cracked lower tooth, the pulse that had stuttered before the gate opened. The chain lock gave with a sound like a cough.

One wrist came free.

Pell seized her shoulder.

“You will not turn this into another barrage.”

“I am trying not to.”

She struck him with the loose chain. It caught his forearm and dragged the pistol from his hand. Elian kicked it beneath the platform. Pell staggered, and for one instant his face lost its magistrate’s composure. He looked like an old man who had discovered that the flood did not recognize his title.

Ilyra freed the second wrist.

Behind Pell, a door in the side wall burst inward.

Senn stood in it.
